{"claims": [
{"id": "c1", "text": "On a released Qwen-2.5-7B layer-20 NLA, explanations pass the reconstruction test through gist rather than grounded specific claims.", "methods": ["Claim-level flip audit (minimal-pair counterfactual edits, grounding = reconstruction drop Δr̃ ≥ τ)", "Per-edit validity filtering with an open judge (Appendix A)", "Linear probe decodability of specifics vs gist", "Transform control (paraphrase, synonym, masking, shuffle)", "Late-layer logit-lens inventory"], "results": ["r̃ = 0.84 on in-distribution web text", "Grounded fraction 4.2% / 2.1% / 1.6% at τ = 0.02 / 0.05 / 0.10 (n = 1,517); described as a lower bound", "Specifics decode at ~6% vs gist ~18% chance-corrected per position; mean-pooled gist ~50%", "Transforms: paraphrase 0.75, synonym 0.70, mask function words 0.72, word shuffle 0.32, mask content words 0.04", "Flip noise floor: 95th percentile |Δr̃| = 0.017; wrong-direction drops ≥ 0.02 at rate 2e-4", "Closed-model judge: 68.4% valid edits, oversized edits inflate grounding ~7x; open judge: 99.3% valid", "Logit-lens top-50 recovery of missed values rises from 0.6% at the read layer to 10.1% at layer 27"], "conditions": ["The released NLA's missing specifics are largely absent from the tap (a storage gap), not a pure metric artifact", "Flip sensitivity is low, so grounding is undercounted"]},
{"id": "c2", "text": "Under exact synthetic ground truth, standard co-trained verbalizer/reconstructor pairs develop co-adapted private codes (grounded but false wording), detected by the comparison of grounding and truth and by the swap to an independent evaluator.", "methods": ["Two templated sandbox scenarios (story, marketplace) with retained, faded and unread slots", "Comparison of grounding and truth", "Swap to an independent evaluator, including one trained on a disjoint paraphrase family"], "results": ["Codes in 5/5 standard runs; grounded-minus-true gaps 0.30–0.80", "r̃ 0.71–0.86 while every slot is asserted confidently", "Under the independent evaluator, grounding on code-carrying slots falls from 0.53–0.89 to 0.08–0.23 while grounding of true claims survives", "Cross-evaluator r̃ gap 0.17–0.38 on standard runs vs ~0.003 on RECAP runs", "In the marketplace scenario a code occupies an unread slot", "Readout gap: slots 55–72% decodable are stated truly only 15–26% of the time"], "conditions": ["The independent evaluator is trained without exposure to the audited pair's outputs"]},
{"id": "c3", "text": "Natural fixes fail: verbalizer-side grounding rewards game the proxy, a reconstruction-pull objective collapses decodable content, and frozen probes go stale under drift, which affine realignment needing no labels reverses.", "methods": ["Rejection sampling and GRPO against a clause-level grounding reward", "Target-side objective pulling activations toward their reconstruction (λ = 0–10)", "Frozen probes under continued training", "Label-free affine realignment and its decomposition by map class"], "results": ["Grounding rewards improve the proxy while the claim-level audit stays null; RAFT/RL grounded fractions stay within the base bootstrap intervals", "Pull removes decodable slot content at every strength with perplexity unchanged; freshly retrained probes also fail", "Frozen probes reach near-chance within 1,500 steps and are at chance across seeds (6/6)", "Affine map restores probes in 9/9 cases; rotation recovers ~half; rank 16–64 non-orthogonal change recovers nearly all"], "conditions": ["Drift preserves information; collapse destroys it"]},
{"id": "c4", "text": "In the sandbox, RECAP (co-trained linear heads on external targets) makes designated content fully decodable at negligible cost, and fresh NLAs then state it truly with no private codes.", "methods": ["RECAP heads on slot values, aux weight 0.3", "Independently fitted probes for every decodability number", "Fresh NLAs with identical training on RECAP vs standard target models", "Partial-designation dose (1–3 slots)"], "results": ["100% decodability at +0.001 nats in all five runs", "Heads decode nothing on unread slots", "Fresh NLAs ~1.00 truth and grounding on designated content under both evaluators; remaining false content grounded ~0", "Codes in 0/5 RECAP runs; any designation dose prevented codes"], "conditions": ["Only content actually present before the tap can be made decodable"]},
{"id": "c5", "text": "RECAP transfers to continued pretraining of Pythia-160M under a target-design rule, at a cost that depends on target count, and decodability must be maintained.", "methods": ["Linear heads at layer 6 on self-supervised targets (presence of top-K content words, identity of the token at offset −8)", "Naive vs class-balanced presence loss", "Weight sweep, MLP head, layer-9 tap", "Head-free fine-tuning persistence test with refit probes"], "results": ["Fresh probe AUC 0.95–1.00 for K = 8/64 vs control 0.77–0.80", "Naive K = 512 minimized its loss while making nothing decodable (predicted 'absent'); balancing restores 0.97–0.99", "Tax +0.010 nats for K = 64 balanced (CI [−0.015, +0.034]); +0.14–0.20 for K = 512", "Identity target readable at w = 0.03 (0.953) with tax −0.003; naive presence drops to 0.79–0.81 below w = 1.0", "Without heads, the surplus mostly erodes within 250 steps (identity .991 → .320 → .169); applying the head loss every 10th step retains .849/.900/.891", "Never-designated bucket stays at control level"], "conditions": ["Targets must not be minimizable without genuine discrimination", "Maintenance is a running cost"]},
{"id": "c6", "text": "At scale, RECAP's decodability reaches a fresh verbalizer only partially; the shortfall is in generation, not storage.", "methods": ["AV/AR pair trained on Pythia-160M taps with the released recipe structure", "Exact truth audit against the trailing 64-token window", "Probe precision–recall comparison", "Reconstructor redesign and scale ablations"], "results": ["Word truth 0.44 (RECAP) vs 0.06 (control); 0.44–0.46 across seeds", "Recall 0.29 vs 0.07 while stating fewer words (252 vs 406)", "Grounded-minus-true gap +0.42 (control) vs +0.33 (RECAP)", "At the verbalizer's recall, probe precision ~0.80 vs verbalizer 0.44–0.63", "Redesigned reader: decode-point decodability 0.79–0.81 but generated precision 0.56–0.63; a 3B reader matches the 0.5B reader"], "conditions": ["Closed-vocabulary claims only"]},
{"id": "c7", "text": "Probe-based monitoring on RECAP-decodable content verifies claims and survives an adversary that edits the explanation to game the reconstruction score, but only for designated content.", "methods": ["Sandbox discrepancy detector (probe confidence > 0.9)", "Scale presence probe ranking true vs false claims", "Lie-ladder adversaries L1–L4", "Frozen-threshold check and held-out band (ranks 64–128)"], "results": ["Sandbox control: 27/733 lies flagged, precision 1.0, abstain 63%; RECAP: 0 false pre-tap claims, coverage 37% → 100%; post-tap claims abstained on both models", "Scale AUC 0.965 vs 0.823; flags at 0.93 recall, 0.87 precision", "L3 suppresses ~87% of lie penalty (Δr̃ 0.022 vs 0.173 for a random lie); RECAP probe AUC 0.952 vs control 0.508", "L1 0.993 vs 0.729; L4 0.909 vs 0.242", "Held-out band: RECAP 0.66 vs control 0.70 (no advantage)", "Patching the tap barely moves behavior (~0.003)"], "conditions": ["Threat model covers text edits, not activation-level attacks", "RECAP certifies storage, not use"]}
],
"items": [
{"id": "q1", "type": "failure", "claims": ["c7", "c5"], "pair": null, "question": "The RECAP monitor's robustness is shown against adversaries that only edit explanation text. Would it remain reliable against an adversary who can continue training the target model without the RECAP heads, even one that does not aim at the probe?", "answer": "No. Head-free fine-tuning alone erodes most of the designated decodability within about 250 steps, even when fresh probes are refit. The probe's advantage would therefore fade without any probe-aware attack. The text-edit robustness depends on the activation being untouched and decodability being maintained.", "rubric": ["Says the monitor would not remain reliable (its advantage would largely vanish).", "Reason: head-free fine-tuning erodes designated decodability quickly (within ~250 steps per Appendix C), and the monitor needs decodable content.", "Notes the shown robustness assumes the activation and model are not altered (a text-only threat model)."]},
{"id": "q2", "type": "failure", "claims": ["c5", "c7"], "pair": null, "question": "Suppose a team applies RECAP to 512 designated words using the naive presence loss and then deploys the probe-based monitor on those words. Would the monitor outperform a control-model monitor?", "answer": "No. With 512 rare targets the naive head minimized its loss by always predicting 'absent' and made nothing decodable to a fresh probe. Monitoring coverage and discrimination are bounded by decodability, so there would be no advantage over control.", "rubric": ["Says no (no meaningful advantage over control).", "Reason: the naive K=512 head made nothing decodable (always-absent shortcut), and the monitor depends on decodability."]},
{"id": "q3", "type": "failure", "claims": ["c5", "c7"], "pair": null, "question": "A lab trains with RECAP but then drops the heads for a long post-training stage before deploying a freshly fit probe monitor. Would the monitor's large AUC advantage over control (e.g., 0.965 vs 0.823) be expected to persist?", "answer": "No. Without the heads, the designated decodability falls toward control level within a few hundred steps, measured with refit probes. The probe would have little extra signal to exploit, so the advantage would mostly disappear unless heads are kept on continuously or applied intermittently.", "rubric": ["Says the advantage would not persist (it largely disappears).", "Reason: decodability erodes toward control within ~250–2,000 head-free steps even with refit probes.", "Condition: it would persist if the head loss were maintained, e.g., intermittently every 10th step."]},
{"id": "q4", "type": "failure", "claims": ["c3", "c5"], "pair": null, "question": "Could the label-free affine realignment that fixes stale probes after drift recover RECAP's designated decodability after 2,000 steps of head-free fine-tuning?", "answer": "No. In the persistence test, freshly fitted linear probes on the new activations already lose access. An affine map followed by a linear probe is still a linear readout, so it cannot read what fresh linear probes cannot. This is decodability loss, not reader staleness.", "rubric": ["Says no.", "Reason: fresh probes refit at each snapshot also fail, so the linear decodability itself is gone; an affine map plus a linear probe is still linear and cannot exceed a fresh linear probe."]},
{"id": "q5", "type": "failure", "claims": ["c2"], "pair": null, "question": "Would the swap to an independent evaluator still expose private codes if the 'independent' reconstructor were trained on the audited pair's own explanations?", "answer": "Probably not. Trained on those outputs, it could learn the pair's convention, so grounding on code-carrying slots would not collapse and the evaluator gap would shrink. The detector relies on the evaluator being trained without exposure to the audited pair's outputs.", "rubric": ["Says the swap would likely fail to expose the codes.", "Reason: the evaluator could learn the private convention from those outputs, so code grounding would not collapse.", "Condition: independence requires no exposure to the audited pair's outputs."]},
{"id": "q6", "type": "failure", "claims": ["c5"], "pair": null, "question": "Would watching the RECAP heads' own training loss be enough to verify that designated content has become decodable?", "answer": "No. The naive K=512 head minimized its training loss while making nothing decodable to a fresh probe, because it learned to always predict 'absent'. Only an independently fitted probe exposed this, which is why the paper takes all decodability numbers from fresh probes.", "rubric": ["Says no.", "Reason: at K=512 the naive head achieved low loss via an always-absent shortcut while a fresh probe found nothing decodable; independent probes are needed."]},
{"id": "q7", "type": "failure", "claims": ["c1"], "pair": null, "question": "On the released Qwen NLA, suppose an explanation keeps its topic but every specific fact is replaced by a false fact of the same kind. Would the reconstruction score be expected to reveal this?", "answer": "Largely no. Only about 2% of specific claims are grounded, so flipping specifics rarely moves r̃. The score survives meaning-preserving changes such as paraphrase (0.75) and synonym substitution (0.70) and collapses only when content words are removed. It tracks gist, which the false-specifics version preserves.", "rubric": ["Says the score would mostly not reveal the false specifics.", "Reason: few specific claims are grounded (~2%) and the score is carried by gist (it survives paraphrase/synonyms and collapses only when content words are masked)."]},
{"id": "q8", "type": "why", "claims": ["c1"], "pair": null, "question": "Why does flipping a specific claim in a released-NLA explanation so rarely change r̃?", "answer": "The specifics are largely not present in the layer-20 activation: they decode at only ~6% chance-corrected, versus much higher for gist. The reconstruction therefore depends on the explanation's overall meaning, and changing one specific leaves the reconstructed activation nearly the same.", "rubric": ["States that the reconstruction depends on gist rather than on specific facts.", "Reason: specifics are weakly decodable from the tap (~6% vs ~18% for gist, ~50% mean-pooled), so there is little specific content for the reconstruction to depend on."]},
{"id": "q9", "type": "why", "claims": ["c7", "c1"], "pair": null, "question": "Why does the r̃-optimal adversary (L3) suppress about 87% of the lie penalty on the RECAP model as well, even though RECAP improves decodability?", "answer": "The adversary games r̃, which comes from the reconstructor's objective. That objective is insensitive to claim values that induce similar reconstructions, whatever the target model. RECAP changes what the activation holds, not how reconstruction scores text, so the score stays gameable while the probe on the activation still works.", "rubric": ["States that r̃ remains gameable regardless of RECAP.", "Reason: the reconstruction objective does not penalize false claims that leave the reconstruction similar; RECAP changes the target model's activations, not the reconstruction-based score."]},
{"id": "q10", "type": "why", "claims": ["c7"], "pair": null, "question": "Why does the control probe fall from AUC 0.729 against random lies (L1) to 0.508 against r̃-optimal lies (L3), while the RECAP probe barely moves?", "answer": "Stronger adversaries pick absent words that are semantically closer to the real content, and these are harder for a probe to tell apart from present words. The control probe's weak margin cannot separate them, so it drops to chance. RECAP's designated words are decoded with a large margin, so the RECAP probe still separates them (0.993 → 0.952).", "rubric": ["States that the control probe lacks the decodability margin, while RECAP's probe has a strong margin on designated words.", "Reason: stronger rungs choose semantically nearer absent words, which a weakly decodable probe confuses with present ones."]},
{"id": "q11", "type": "why", "claims": ["c5"], "pair": null, "question": "Why could the naive presence head work at K=8 (fresh-probe AUC 1.000) yet fail completely at K=512?", "answer": "With 512 mostly rare targets, almost every target is absent in any window, so predicting 'absent' minimizes unbalanced cross-entropy without any discrimination. With only 8 targets, presence is common enough that the loss cannot be minimized without actually discriminating. This is the paper's design rule.", "rubric": ["Attributes the difference to base rates: with many rare targets, always predicting 'absent' minimizes the unbalanced loss.", "Reason: with few (frequent) targets, low loss requires genuine discrimination, matching the rule that targets must not be minimizable without discrimination."]},
{"id": "q12", "type": "why", "claims": ["c5"], "pair": null, "question": "Why does applying the head loss only every tenth step during the shifted fine-tune keep identity accuracy near 0.89, while head-free fine-tuning drops it to about 0.17?", "answer": "Without the heads, decodability erodes over a scale of a few hundred steps (most of it is gone by step 250). A correction every 10 steps arrives far more often than that, so erosion is repeatedly undone before it builds up.", "rubric": ["States that intermittent supervision counteracts erosion before it accumulates.", "Reason: erosion happens over roughly hundreds of steps (most gone by 250), much slower than a 10-step supervision interval."]},
{"id": "q13", "type": "why", "claims": ["c6"], "pair": null, "question": "Why does the comparison between probe precision and verbalizer precision at matched recall locate the scale shortfall in generation rather than storage?", "answer": "A fresh probe reading the same tap reaches ~0.80 precision at the verbalizer's recall, while the verbalizer reaches only 0.44–0.63. The tap therefore holds enough linearly readable content to do better. If storage were the limit, the probe would be equally limited, so the gap must arise when the verbalizer generates text.", "rubric": ["States that the information is present in the activation but lost in generation.", "Reason: the probe on the same tap achieves higher precision (~0.80 vs 0.44–0.63) at matched recall, which would be impossible if the content were not stored."]},
{"id": "q14", "type": "why", "claims": ["c1"], "pair": null, "question": "Why can grounded claims counted at the smallest threshold τ=0.02 on the released NLA be trusted as more than flip noise?", "answer": "The noise floor sits below that threshold. The 95th percentile of |Δr̃| for flips without grounding signal is 0.017, and wrong-direction drops of at least 0.02 occur at a rate of only 2×10⁻⁴. A drop of 0.02 or more is therefore rarely produced by noise alone.", "rubric": ["States that τ=0.02 lies above the noise floor.", "Reason: cites the 95th-percentile noise of 0.017 and/or the 2e-4 rate of wrong-direction drops ≥0.02."]},
{"id": "q15", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c5", "c7"], "pair": "p1", "question": "If the RECAP Pythia-160M model then underwent 2,000 steps of head-free fine-tuning, would a refit RECAP probe monitor still clearly beat the control monitor on designated words?", "answer": "No. After 2,000 head-free steps, designated decodability is close to control (b1/b2 .789/.812 vs .770/.793). The monitor's edge, which comes from decodability, would mostly disappear.", "rubric": ["Says no (the advantage is mostly lost).", "Reason: head-free fine-tuning brings designated decodability near control level."]},
{"id": "q16", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c5", "c7"], "pair": "p1", "question": "If the same 2,000-step fine-tune instead applied the head loss every tenth step, would a refit RECAP probe monitor still clearly beat the control monitor on designated words?", "answer": "Yes. Intermittent supervision kept most decodability (.849/.900/.891 at step 2,000) well above control, so the monitor would keep most of its advantage.", "rubric": ["Says yes.", "Reason: intermittent supervision retains most designated decodability above control."]},
{"id": "q17", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c5", "c7"], "pair": "p2", "question": "For a monitor covering 512 designated words, would RECAP trained with the naive presence loss give a probe advantage over the control model?", "answer": "No. The naive K=512 head made nothing decodable to a fresh probe, so the probe would have no edge over control.", "rubric": ["Says no.", "Reason: the naive K=512 head left nothing decodable (always-absent shortcut)."]},
{"id": "q18", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c5", "c7"], "pair": "p2", "question": "For a monitor covering 512 designated words, would RECAP trained with the class-balanced presence loss give a probe advantage over the control model?", "answer": "Yes. Balancing restored fresh-probe AUC to 0.97–0.99 across all 512 targets, against a control baseline of 0.77–0.80. The probe would therefore have stronger signal, though at a larger tax (+0.14–0.20 nats).", "rubric": ["Says yes.", "Reason: balanced loss gives 0.97–0.99 AUC vs control 0.77–0.80."]},
{"id": "q19", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c7", "c5"], "pair": "p3", "question": "On the K=64 RECAP Pythia model, would the probe monitor reliably flag an r̃-optimal lie that claims a top-64 designated word is present when it is absent?", "answer": "Yes. For designated top-64 words the RECAP probe holds AUC 0.952 at the r̃-optimal rung, against 0.508 for the control.", "rubric": ["Says yes.", "Reason: designated words are decodable; the RECAP probe reaches AUC ~0.95 at L3."]},
{"id": "q20", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c7", "c5"], "pair": "p3", "question": "On the same K=64 RECAP model, would the probe monitor reliably flag an r̃-optimal lie about a word ranked around 100 in frequency?", "answer": "No. Words ranked 64–128 were never designated, and the RECAP monitor there is no better than control (L3 AUC 0.546 vs 0.585).", "rubric": ["Says no.", "Reason: ranks 64–128 are outside the designated set; the held-out band shows no RECAP advantage."]},
{"id": "q21", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c4", "c2"], "pair": "p4", "question": "In sandbox scenario 1, could RECAP heads trained on the activity slot make it decodable from the tap?", "answer": "No. Activity is mentioned only after the tap, so it is provably absent from the activation. Heads recover only content the activation holds and decode nothing on unread slots.", "rubric": ["Says no.", "Reason: activity occurs only after the tap (an unread slot), and RECAP cannot create content absent from the activation."]},
{"id": "q22", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c4", "c2"], "pair": "p4", "question": "In sandbox scenario 1, could RECAP heads trained on the place slot make it decodable from the tap?", "answer": "Yes. Place is mentioned before the tap, so it is present though faded. RECAP brings designated pre-tap content to 100% decodability by independent probes.", "rubric": ["Says yes.", "Reason: place precedes the tap (a faded but present slot), and RECAP reaches 100% decodability on designated pre-tap content."]},
{"id": "q23", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c5"], "pair": null, "question": "A team using a 768-dimensional model with a tight language-modeling budget must choose between RECAP with 64 balanced targets at w=0.1 and 512 balanced targets at w=1.0. Which should it choose, and why?", "answer": "The 64-target configuration. Its tax is +0.010 nats, not distinguishable from zero, and it still gives 0.97–0.99 AUC. The 512-target setup reaches similar AUC but costs +0.14–0.20 nats.", "rubric": ["Chooses K=64 balanced at w=0.1.", "Reason: comparable AUC (0.97–0.99) at a much lower tax (+0.010 vs +0.14–0.20 nats)."]},
{"id": "q24", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c5"], "pair": null, "question": "A team wants designated content to stay decodable at almost no LM cost by using a very small aux weight (w=0.03). Should it use the naive presence target or the identity target?", "answer": "The identity target. At w=0.03 it stays readable (0.953 accuracy) with a tax within noise (−0.003), whereas naive presence falls to the control level (0.79–0.81) below w=1.0.", "rubric": ["Chooses the identity target.", "Reason: identity stays decodable at w=0.03 with near-zero tax, while naive presence loses readability below w=1.0."]},
{"id": "q25", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c3"], "pair": null, "question": "A team monitors a model that is still in continued training using a probe fitted early on, and has no new labels. What should it do to keep the probe working, and what kind of map is required?", "answer": "Fit a label-free affine map on paired activations from the old and new checkpoints to realign the probe. A pure rotation recovers only about half the drift. A non-orthogonal map of rank ~16–64 is needed for full recovery.", "rubric": ["Recommends label-free affine realignment on paired activations (explicit recalibration).", "Reason/condition: rotation alone recovers ~half; full recovery requires a non-orthogonal change of rank ~16–64."]},
{"id": "q26", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c6", "c7"], "pair": null, "question": "A team has a RECAP-trained small model and wants to check whether claims about designated words are true. Should it rely on the verbalizer's explanations or on a fresh probe, and would upgrading the verbalizer's reader to 3B change that?", "answer": "Rely on the fresh probe. It reaches ~0.80 precision where the verbalizer reaches 0.44–0.63, and ranks true over false claims at AUC 0.965. A 3B reader matched the 0.5B reader, so upgrading would not close the gap.", "rubric": ["Recommends the probe over verbalizer prose.", "Reason: the probe has higher precision/AUC than the verbalizer on the same content.", "States that a 3B reader would not change this (it matched the 0.5B)."]},
{"id": "q27", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c1"], "pair": null, "question": "An auditor replicating the flip audit uses the closed-model judge to write edits, without validity filtering. How would its grounded fractions compare with the paper's, and why?", "answer": "They would be inflated. The closed judge produced valid edits only 68.4% of the time. Invalid edits were mostly oversized, rewriting surrounding material, which inflated apparent grounding roughly sevenfold.", "rubric": ["Says the grounded fractions would be overestimated.", "Reason: the closed judge's edits are often invalid (68.4% valid) and oversized edits inflate grounding (~7x)."]},
{"id": "q28", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c3", "c4"], "pair": null, "question": "A team hopes to cut false claims by sampling five explanations and keeping the one an external truth judge prefers, instead of changing the target model. Based on the paper, how much should it expect, and which approach does the evidence favor?", "answer": "Little. Best-of-5 lowered the false-claim rate only from 0.747 to 0.688, because faithful explanations are rare among the samples. The evidence favors training the target model with RECAP, which brought designated content to ~1.00 truth in the sandbox.", "rubric": ["Predicts only a small reduction (about 0.75 → 0.69).", "Reason/recommendation: faithful samples are rare, so selection cannot reach them; training the target model (RECAP) is favored."]},
{"id": "q29", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c7", "c2"], "pair": null, "question": "In a new sandbox scenario, a verbalizer makes confident claims about a slot that appears only after the tap. Which audit tool should catch false claims about it: the probe monitor, or the comparison of grounding and truth?", "answer": "The comparison of grounding and truth. The probe monitor correctly abstains on post-tap content, because the activation provably lacks it. Such claims are then caught by checking grounding against exact truth, for example a grounded but false claim.", "rubric": ["Chooses the comparison of grounding and truth.", "Reason: the probe monitor abstains on post-tap content, since it cannot be read from an activation that lacks it."]},
{"id": "q30", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c3"], "pair": null, "question": "If freshly retrained probes had fully recovered slot content after the reconstruction-pull objective, which of the paper's conclusions would lose support?", "answer": "The conclusion that reconstruction-pull destroys information (collapse) rather than rotating it. It rests on fresh probes also failing. Recovery would instead resemble drift, which realignment could fix, erasing the paper's separation between drift and collapse.", "rubric": ["Identifies the collapse conclusion (information removed, not merely moved).", "Reason: that conclusion and the drift/collapse distinction rely on fresh probes failing after pull."]},
{"id": "q31", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c2"], "pair": null, "question": "If grounding of true claims had also dropped sharply under the independent evaluator, which interpretation of the evaluator gap would lose its support?", "answer": "The interpretation that the gap reflects co-adaptation (private codes specific to the pair) rather than a weaker evaluator. # Train the Model, Not the Reader: Decodability Supervision for Verifiable
Activation Explanations

Hiskias Dingeto, StackOne Technologies (hiskias@stackone.com)

###### Abstract

Natural-language autoencoders (NLAs) score activation explanations by reconstruction. This test is structurally insensitive to individual false claims. We show it is passed without faithfulness in two ways:
- by gist: a released Qwen-2.5-7B verbalizer reconstructs well above chance while as few as ${\sim}2\%$ of its specific claims are grounded;
- by co-adapted private codes: false wording the reconstruction depends on, found under synthetic ground truth.

Fixes that leave the target model unchanged fail. We contribute two audit protocols (grounding-vs-truth; swap to an independent evaluator) and RECAP (Readable Encodings via Co-trained Auxiliary Predictors): linear heads co-trained with the target model to keep designated content decodable. In the sandbox, codes vanish at $+0.001$ nats. On Pythia-160M:
- content becomes probe-decodable, given a target-design rule;
- a fresh verbalizer conveys it only in part (truth 0.44–0.46 vs near-zero control);
- a probe scores true over false claims at AUC 0.96 (vs 0.82), and still flags lies at 0.95 (control 0.51) under a score-gaming adversary that suppresses ~87% of its lie penalty.

## 1 Introduction

An NLA's verbalizer maps an activation to text and its reconstructor maps the text back. Round-trip quality is treated as a per-explanation faithfulness test. The gap: reconstruction only checks that the explanation suffices to regenerate the activation. The objective has no preference among claim values inducing the same reconstruction, so false additions go unpenalized, regardless of model or scale.

Figure 1: (a) NLA: AV maps activation to text, AR maps it back; only AV and AR train. The score can stay high while the text asserts an ungrounded specific. (b) RECAP trains the target model: co-trained linear heads keep designated content decodable against external targets. After training, an independent fresh probe (not the heads) recovers it (AUC 0.95) and a fresh verbalizer states it truly.

Contributions:

- **Claim-level audit.** We flip each salient claim, with per-edit validity controls. A released verbalizer passes the test with ~2% grounded specifics, a lower bound given the flip's low sensitivity. The score survives paraphrase but collapses under content-word masking.
- **Private codes.** Under standard training, co-trained AV/AR pairs develop codes (grounded−true gaps 0.30–0.80, two scenarios), detected by the grounding-vs-truth comparison and the evaluator swap. Both natural fixes fail:
  - minimizing the distance between a hidden state and its reconstruction removes probe-readable content;
  - rewarding grounding raises the score by changing which sentences the metric counts.
- **RECAP.** Trains the target model; a reconstruction objective instead collapses content, and frozen probes go stale under drift (fully reversed by label-free realignment). RECAP restores claim-level faithfulness in the sandbox and transfers to Pythia-160M at measured cost.
- **Adversarial monitor.** Results in §6. The reconstruction score must not be used as a truth signal.

## 2 Preliminaries and Experimental Setup

### 2.1 The Reconstruction Test and Audit Protocols

An NLA pairs an activation verbalizer (AV), generating explanation $z$ of activation $h$, with an activation reconstructor (AR) mapping $z$ to $\hat{h}$. With target weights $\theta$ frozen and $h$ the tap activation:

$$\mathcal{J}_{\mathrm{read}}=\max_{\mathrm{AV},\mathrm{AR}}\cos\big(\mathrm{AR}(\mathrm{AV}(h)),h\big)\quad(1)$$

The NLA authors warn nothing forces faithfulness, yet this score is what NLAs report. We use $\tilde{r}=(\cos(\hat{h},h)-\mathrm{floor})/(1-\mathrm{floor})$, where floor is the mean cosine to mismatched activations (0 = chance, 1 = perfect).

**Grounding.** Let $z_{\neg c}$ be $z$ with claim $c$ alone minimally flipped (a flip). Then

$$\Delta\tilde{r}(c)=\tilde{r}(z)-\tilde{r}(z_{\neg c})\quad(2)$$

and $c$ is grounded iff $\Delta\tilde r\geq\tau$. This measures reconstruction sensitivity, which we argue differs from the model's own. Invalid edits inflate grounding severalfold, so edits are validity-checked (App. A).

Grounded × true gives four cases. Grounded-but-false wording that is specific to the co-trained pair (shown by evaluator swap) is a co-adapted private code; the label is operational. Evaluator gap: $\tilde r_{\mathrm{co}}-\tilde r_{\mathrm{ind}}$.

**Terms.**
- Tap: the layer/position read.
- Probe: a freshly fitted linear decoder.
- Gist: overall meaning, vs specific facts.
- Designated: an auxiliary predictor is co-trained to predict it.
- Decodable: a fresh linear probe reads it.
- Faithfulness: claim-level (true of and grounded in the activation); not downstream computation or world-grounding.

#### Settings.

(i) Released Qwen-2.5-7B layer-20 NLA on in-distribution web text ($n{=}1{,}517$ claims). (ii) Sandbox of two templated scenarios (story, marketplace) with exact, judge-free truth; tap position fixes retained/faded/unread slots. (iii) Continued pretraining of Pythia-160M with self-supervised heads; tax = held-out LM loss minus a shared control. Details in App. D, K.

## 3 Auditing Reconstruction-Scored Explanations

The two failures differ:
- **Released NLA:** specifics are largely absent from the tap, so the score rests on gist and the content is genuinely missing.
- **Sandbox:** content is present but stated in wording only the co-trained reconstructor understands. This is a pure metric artifact, exposed by evaluator swap.

### 3.1 Counterfactual Audit of a Released Verbalizer

Explanations score $\tilde r=0.84$, yet only 4.2%/2.1%/1.6% of LLM-salient specific claims are grounded at $\tau=0.02/0.05/0.10$ (App. E).
- **Lower bound:** an append-and-re-rank control recovers a known-encoded topic at only 28% raw.
- **More robust statistic:** a probe recovers specifics ~3× worse than gist (~6% vs ~18% chance-corrected per position; mean-pooled gist ~50%).
- Reconstruction survives paraphrase but collapses when content words are masked.
- The effect holds across layers 16–27 and is specific to reconstruction-style readouts; the model's own output head sees late-layer specifics.
- The noise floor sits below the smallest $\tau$.

Training the verbalizer toward grounding (rejection sampling; GRPO with a clause-level grounding reward) improved the proxy. The independent claim-level audit stayed null at every $\tau$ (CIs straddle zero). Text statistics attribute the gains to merging and repackaging sentences.

### 3.2 Audit Under Synthetic Ground Truth

The toy NLA asserts every slot confidently at $\tilde r$ 0.71–0.86 (both scenarios). Truth tracks decodability loosely:
- fully decodable slot: true 0.44–0.96 across seeds, yet grounded 0.76–0.88 in all;
- partially decodable slots: 0.15–0.26;
- unread slots: chance.

**Codes.** Standard training yields private codes in 5/5 runs (grounded−true gaps 0.30–0.80). Codes can occupy several slots. In marketplace one occupies an unread slot, so the sentence serves as a channel rather than a description.

**Evaluator swap.** Under an independent evaluator never exposed to the pair's outputs, grounding on code slots collapses from 0.53–0.89 to 0.08–0.23, while grounding of true claims survives. This points to co-adaptation, not a weaker evaluator. Cross-evaluator $\tilde r$ gap: 0.17–0.38 (standard) vs ${\sim}0.003$ (RECAP, §5). An evaluator trained on a disjoint paraphrase family (different frames and slot order, shared slot words only) reproduces the pattern within ~0.05 over three seeds (RECAP slots 1.00). Codes are therefore private to the pair, not shared across templates.

**Readout gap.** In marketplace, slots 55–72% decodable are stated truly only 15–26% of the time. This is in addition to the storage gap; RECAP closes it.

## 4 Representation Collapse and Probe Drift

**Collapse.** A target-side objective pulling activations toward their reconstruction removes decodable slot content at every tested strength and initialization, with perplexity unchanged. Freshly retrained probes also fail, so the information is gone, not rotated. The reconstruction is a lossy projection; raising similarity to it removes variation outside the probe's subspace.

**Drift.** Matched probes decay to near-chance within 1,500 continued-training steps and are at chance across seeds (6/6 pairs). Yet a label-free affine map on paired activations restores native performance in 9/9 cases. Rotation alone recovers ~half; full recovery needs a non-orthogonal change of rank ~16–64 (App. H). Concurrent work reports the same on 2B/7B models.

**Consequences.** Probe monitoring of a training model needs explicit recalibration. Realignment fixes how probes read; RECAP changes what is stored. Adapter-based probe transfer across models should work.

### 5.1 Method

Linear heads read the tap hidden state and predict external targets (slot values in the sandbox; self-supervised text functions at scale):

$$\mathcal{J}_{\mathrm{model}}=\min_{\theta,\phi}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{LM}}(\theta)+w\,\mathcal{L}_{\phi}\big(h(\theta),y\big)\quad(3)$$

$\mathcal{L}_\phi$ = class-balanced BCE on content-word presence + CE on token identity; balancing prevents the §5.3 shortcut. Eq. 1 never touches $\theta$; Eq. 3 trains it. RECAP removes each failure mode at its source:
- drift: heads co-train, so no frozen probe goes stale;
- collapse: targets are external, with no self-reconstruction objective;
- codes: heads read the activation directly, with no intervening text.

Heads could co-adapt, so all decodability numbers come from independently fitted probes. RECAP is a form of deep supervision.

### 5.2 Sandbox Results

Designated content is 100% probe-decodable at $+0.001$ nats in 5/5 runs; heads decode nothing on unread slots. Fresh NLAs, given identical training (incl. cold-start SFT on gold descriptions), behave differently on RECAP models:
- designated content is stated at ~1.00 truth and grounding under both evaluators;
- remaining false content has grounding ~0;
- no codes appear in any RECAP run (App. D).

Only the target model differs, isolating its decodability as the cause.

### 5.3 Scaling to Pythia-160M

- **Decodability:** fresh probes reach 0.95–1.00 AUC for $K{=}8,64$ (control 0.77–0.80).
- **Shortcut:** at $K{=}512$ the naive presence head minimized loss by predicting "absent" and decoded nothing for a fresh probe. Class balancing restores 0.97–0.99 across all 512. Design rule: choose targets whose loss cannot be minimized without genuine discrimination.
- **Cost:** 64 targets, $+0.010$ nats (indistinguishable from zero); 512 targets into $d{=}768$, $+0.14$–$0.20$. An identity target stays decodable at $w{=}0.03$ with tax within noise of zero.
- **Scope:** the never-designated bucket stayed at control level in 8/8 runs.
- **Head and tap:** an MLP head reaches 0.98–0.99 at layer 6; a linear head at layer 9 lifts AUC from 0.77–0.79 to 0.95–0.98 at $+0.01$ nats.

### 5.4 Verbalizer Audit at Scale

An AV/AR pair trained as for the released NLA, audited against exact text truth:
- context words true at 0.44 (RECAP) vs 0.06 (control);
- control is grounded at 0.48 but true at 0.06; RECAP narrows the gap from $+0.42$ to $+0.33$ by stating more truly, not by removing codes;
- recall 0.29 vs 0.07 despite stating fewer words;
- robust to reconstructor strength; truth 0.44–0.46 over three seeds vs near-zero control (App. J).

**Shortfall is generation, not storage.** At the verbalizer's recall, a fresh probe reaches precision ~0.80 vs the verbalizer's 0.44–0.63. A redesigned reconstructor (standardized multi-token injection, MLP capacity, a decode-point presence head on window occurrence) makes content decodable at its decode point: 0.79–0.81 (two seeds) vs matched control 0.03. Generated precision still stays 0.56–0.63. None of the following closes the gap: reconstructor scale (3B matches 0.5B), reconstruction optimization, a truth reward, injection bandwidth, negative supervision. At scale, RECAP guarantees probe-verifiable decodability; prose is a lossy rendering.

**Running cost.** Without heads, decodability erodes within a few hundred fine-tuning steps. Maintain it continuously ($+0.010$ nats) or intermittently (~1/10 compute); training it in beats restoring it (App. C).

## 6 Probe-Based Monitoring

**Sandbox monitor.** One fresh probe per slot; claims contradicted by a confident probe ($p{>}0.9$) are flagged and scored by exact truth (App. B).
- Standard model: sound (every flag is false) but catches only 27/733 pre-tap lies, as most slots are too faded.
- RECAP model: no false pre-tap claims, zero abstention. Verification coverage of designated pre-tap content rises from 37% to 100%. This is coverage, not monitor precision, and not the whole activation.
- Post-tap claims are correctly abstained on both; the grounding–truth comparison handles them (one scenario, seed, threshold).

**Pythia-160M.** A fresh presence probe ranks true over false claims at AUC 0.965 vs 0.823 (disjoint 95% CIs) and flags false claims at 0.93 recall, 0.87 precision. At the 1.5% base rate, sandbox coverage does not transfer.

#### Surviving a score-gaming adversary.

The adversary edits a true stated word into an absent one, choosing the edit that maximizes recomputed $\tilde r$ (App. F).
- ~87% of the lie penalty is suppressed on both models.
- RECAP probe: AUC 0.952. Control probe: 0.508. Reading a signal that predates the report is not sufficient; decodability is required.
- Selection leakage: 0.993→0.952 as lies grow semantically nearer.
- Threat model: text edits, not activation attacks. Immunity is structural for score manipulation, empirical for candidate selection.
- A probe-aware adversary assuming monitor leakage: RECAP 0.909, control 0.242; separation grows with strength.
- A threshold recalibrated on a disjoint split leaves recall unchanged; no control threshold reaches 0.9 precision even vs random lies.
- Never-designated words (rank 64–128): no RECAP advantage (0.66 vs 0.70).

## 7 Related Work

#### Activation verbalization and its critiques.

Prior work improves the reader: QA decoders, general explainers, interpreter assistants, training-free readouts, cross-model adapters; SAEs are the unsupervised family. Plausible-but-unfaithful explanations occur in chain-of-thought, neuron explanations showed high causal error, and counterfactual faithfulness tests prefigure our flips. Verbalization critiques are benchmark-level (tasks solvable without internals). We audit the reconstruction test per claim on a released NLA, and repair it by training the target.

#### Scalable oversight.

Reconstruction scoring is a cheap automatic oversight signal; AI control designs subversion-robust protocols. We add a monitor from an independent probe that survives score gaming.

#### Steganography in learned channels.

Reconstruction objectives hide information (CycleGAN). Encoded reasoning arises under optimization pressure, process supervision, misspecified incentives and tool use. Probing detects collusion; optimization obfuscates activations against latent monitors and CoT monitors. Those channels are induced; ours emerge from the standard reconstruction recipe alone. Beyond not optimizing on the monitor, we supervise the target against external truth, with no pressure to fool probe or reconstructor.

#### Representation drift, stitching, and monitor staleness.

Representations are equivalent up to transformation, and affine maps transfer features. Tuned lenses are the affine readers whose staleness we characterize. Concurrent work reports staleness and label-free repair at 2B/7B; retraining probes restores detectability after probe-aware fine-tuning. We add the recovery anatomy, the cross-seed failure, exact evidence that information outlives readers, and the drift/collapse separation.

#### Deep supervision and intrinsic interpretability.

Deep supervision targets task labels; ours targets external content. Concept bottlenecks, concept whitening, codebooks and gradient routing constrain flow or geometry; we add linear heads without constraining flow. Explanation-side supervision exists; ours acts on the target.

## 8 Discussion and Limitations

Reconstruction scoring is fragile oversight: passable without faithfulness, and gameable. RECAP shifts oversight from trusting prose to checking an independent probe, which survives explanation edits. It covers only designated, decodable content, so it is a component of oversight, not a solution.

Evidence comes from a sandbox, one released NLA and one small model, mostly at single seeds; frontier scale is untested. Limitations:
1. Claims are closed-vocabulary and template-parsed, and the monitor covers designated content only; open-ended faithfulness is unmeasured.
2. RECAP must be co-trained in, not retrofitted, and depends on target choice; a bad target can report success while decoding nothing.
3. Decodability ≠ verbalizability.
4. RECAP certifies storage, not use: patching the tap barely moves behavior (~0.003), and computation could route around the monitored subspace.

Success is claim-verified explanations, calibrated abstention where content is absent, and monitors with recalibration protocols, not higher $\tilde r$.

## 9 Conclusion

The reconstruction test is passed via gist and private codes, and training against it yields collapse or proxy gaming. RECAP trains the target model rather than the reader. It yields claim-level faithful verbalizers in the sandbox and probe-decodable designated content on Pythia-160M, where probes read the content more reliably than verbalizers generate it. Training decodability in is more reliable than auditing after the fact.

# Train the Model, Not the Reader: Decodability Supervision for Verifiable
Activation Explanations

Hiskias Dingeto · StackOne Technologies · hiskias@stackone.com

###### Abstract

Natural-language autoencoders score activation explanations by reconstruction. The test is structurally insensitive to individual false claims: flipping one to a false alternative often leaves reconstruction unchanged, so it is never penalized. We show two ways to pass it without faithfulness: gist (a released Qwen-2.5-7B verbalizer) and co-adapted private codes (synthetic ground truth). Fixes leaving the target model unchanged fail. We contribute two audit protocols (grounding-vs-truth comparison; swap to an independent evaluator) and RECAP (Readable Encodings via Co-trained Auxiliary Predictors), linear heads co-trained with the target model to keep designated content decodable. For interpretability, the audit sets a claim-level standard of evidence. For AI safety, RECAP makes designated content checkable against probes rather than taken on trust from verbalizer prose a model can game.

## 1 Introduction

An NLA's verbalizer maps an activation to text, a reconstructor maps it back, and round-trip quality is treated as each explanation's faithfulness test. It is unsupervised and self-checking; released pairs exist for several open models. Structural gap: reconstruction checks only that the explanation suffices to regenerate the activation; it has no preference among claim values inducing the same reconstruction, so false additions go unpenalized, regardless of model or scale.

Two natural fixes fail: minimizing hidden-state-to-reconstruction distance removes probe-readable content; rewarding the verbalizer for grounding raises the score by changing which sentences the metric counts, not by grounding more claims.

Figure 1: (a) NLA: AV maps activation to text, AR back; only AV/AR train; score can stay high while text asserts an ungrounded specific. (b) RECAP trains the target model; co-trained linear heads keep designated content decodable against external targets; afterwards an independent fresh probe (not the heads) recovers it (AUC 0.95) and a fresh verbalizer states it truly.

Contributions:
- **Claim-level audit**: per-claim flips with per-edit validity controls show a released verbalizer passes while its specific claims are largely ungrounded; gist carries the score.
- **Private codes**: co-trained pairs develop them under exact ground truth; grounding-vs-truth and evaluator swap detect and quantify them.
- **RECAP**: avoids collapse and probe drift by training the target model; restores claim-level faithfulness in the sandbox; transfers to Pythia-160M, where designated content becomes probe-decodable at a measured cost.
- **Adversarial monitor**: RECAP decodability survives text gaming; the reconstruction score must not be used as a truth signal.

## 2 Preliminaries and Experimental Setup

### 2.1 The Reconstruction Test and Audit Protocols

With target weights $\theta$ frozen and tap activation $h$, AV (text $z$) and AR (estimate $\hat h$) optimize

| | $\mathcal{J}_{\mathrm{read}}\;=\;\max_{\mathrm{AV},\,\mathrm{AR}}\;\cos\!\big(\mathrm{AR}(\mathrm{AV}(h)),\,h\big),$ | | (1)

Prior work warns the objective does not force faithfulness, yet this score is the main criterion applied. We use $\tilde{r}=(\cos(\hat{h},h)-\mathrm{floor})/(1-\mathrm{floor})$, floor = mean cosine to mismatched activations (0 chance, 1 perfect).

Grounding: with $z_{\neg c}$ = $z$ with claim $c$ alone minimally flipped (a flip),

| | $\Delta\tilde{r}(c)=\tilde{r}(z)-\tilde{r}(z_{\neg c}),$ | | (2)

$c$ grounded iff $\Delta\tilde{r}(c)\geq\tau$. This is reconstruction sensitivity, which we argue differs from the model's own sensitivity. Invalid edits inflate grounding severalfold (App. A). Grounded-but-false wording that is pair-specific (evaluator swap) is a co-adapted private code (operational label, no intentional stance). Evaluator gap: $\tilde{r}_{\mathrm{co}}-\tilde{r}_{\mathrm{ind}}$.

Terms: tap = read layer/position; probe = freshly fitted linear decoder; gist = overall meaning vs. specific facts; designated = an auxiliary predictor is co-trained on it; decodable = fresh linear probe reads it. Faithfulness is claim-level (true of and grounded in the activation), not about downstream computation or world grounding.

#### Settings.

(i) Released Qwen-2.5-7B layer-20 NLA, in-distribution web text ($n{=}1{,}517$ claims). (ii) Sandbox: story and marketplace templates with exact, judge-free ground truth; tap position fixes retained/faded/unread slots. (iii) Pythia-160M continued pretraining with self-supervised heads; tax = held-out LM loss minus shared control. Details: App. D, K.

## 3 Auditing Reconstruction-Scored Explanations

Released NLA: missing specifics are largely absent from the tap; score rests on gist. Sandbox: content is present but stated in wording only the co-trained AR understands, a pure metric artifact.

### 3.1 Counterfactual Audit of a Released Verbalizer

Explanations reconstruct at $\tilde{r}=0.84$, yet only ~2% of LLM-salient specific claims are grounded ($4.2/2.1/1.6\%$ at $\tau=0.02/0.05/0.10$; App. E). It is a lower bound: reconstruction has low sensitivity; an append-and-re-rank control recovers a known-encoded topic at only 28% raw. More robust: probes recover specifics ~3× worse than gist (~6% vs ~18% chance-corrected per position; mean-pooled gist ~50%). Reconstruction survives paraphrase but collapses under content-word masking. Holds across layers 16–27; specific to reconstruction-style readouts (the model's output head sees late-layer specifics). Noise floor lies below the smallest $\tau$.

Training the verbalizer toward grounding (rejection sampling; GRPO with clause-level grounding reward) improved the proxy while the independent claim-level audit stayed null at every $\tau$ (CIs straddle zero); text statistics attribute gains to sentence merging/packaging.

### 3.2 Audit Under Synthetic Ground Truth

The toy NLA asserts every slot confidently at $\tilde{r}$ 0.71–0.86 (both scenarios). Truth tracks decodability loosely: fully decodable slot true 0.44–0.96 across seeds (grounded 0.76–0.88 throughout), partially decodable 0.15–0.26, unread at chance.

In 5/5 standard runs the pair develops private codes (grounded-minus-true gaps 0.30–0.80), possibly over several slots; in the marketplace one occupies an unread slot, so the sentence serves as a communication channel.

Under an independent evaluator (never exposed to the pair's outputs), grounding on code slots drops from 0.53–0.89 to 0.08–0.23 while true-claim grounding survives, so the gap is co-adaptation, not a weaker evaluator. Cross-evaluator $\tilde{r}$ gap: 0.17–0.38 standard vs ~0.003 RECAP. An evaluator trained on a disjoint paraphrase family (different frames and slot order, sharing only slot words) reproduces this within ~0.05 over three seeds (RECAP slots grounded 1.00): the channel is pair-private.

Readout gap: marketplace slots 55–72% decodable are stated truly only 15–26%, beyond the storage gap; RECAP closes it too.

## 4 Representation Collapse and Probe Drift

**Collapse.** Pulling activations toward their own reconstruction removes decodable slot content at every tested strength and initialization with perplexity unchanged; freshly retrained probes also lose accuracy, so information is gone, not rotated. The reconstruction is a lossy projection; raising state–reconstruction similarity removes variation outside the probe's subspace.

**Drift.** Probes matched to a training model decay to near-chance within 1,500 steps and fail across seeds (all six pairs), yet an unlabeled affine map on paired activations restores native performance in all nine cases. Rotation alone recovers ~half; full recovery needs non-orthogonal change of rank ~16–64 (App. H). Probe monitoring of a training model therefore requires recalibration. Realignment fixes the reader; RECAP changes what the representation contains. Corollary: adapter-based cross-model probe transfer should work.

### 5.1 Method

Linear heads read the tap hidden state and predict external targets (slot values in the sandbox; self-supervised text functions at scale):

| | $\mathcal{J}_{\mathrm{model}}\;=\;\min_{\theta,\,\phi}\;\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{LM}}(\theta)\;+\;w\,\mathcal{L}_{\phi}\big(h(\theta),\,y\big),$ | | (3)

$\mathcal{L}_{\phi}$: class-balanced BCE for content-word presence plus CE for token identity; balancing blocks the §5.3 shortcut. Eq. 1 never touches $\theta$; Eq. 3 trains $\theta$ against the ground truth the reader needs. Co-trained heads leave no frozen probe to drift; external targets give no self-referential objective to collapse into; heads read the activation directly, with no text to hide codes. All decodability numbers come from independently fitted probes, never heads. RECAP is deep-supervision-style decodability supervision.

### 5.2 Sandbox Results

Designated content: 100% probe decodability at $+0.001$ nats in all five runs; heads decode nothing on unread slots. Fresh NLAs on RECAP models state designated content at ~1.00 truth and grounding under co-trained and independent evaluators, flag remaining false content at grounding ~0, and form no codes in any run (App. D). Identical NLA training (incl. cold-start SFT on gold descriptions) isolates target decodability.

Figure 2: On one held-out Pile passage, fresh layer-6 probes on the RECAP model recover trailing-window content words and the offset-8 token; the control readout is scrambled.

### 5.3 Scaling to Pythia-160M

Fresh probes reach 0.95–1.00 AUC for $K{=}8$/$64$ (control 0.77–0.80). At $K{=}512$ the naive presence head minimized its loss by always predicting "absent", decoding nothing to a fresh probe; class balancing restores 0.97–0.99 on all 512. Design rule: targets whose loss cannot be minimized without genuine discrimination. Cost: $+0.010$ nats for 64 (indistinguishable from zero); 512 into $d{=}768$: $+0.14$–$0.20$. A discriminative identity target stays decodable at $w{=}0.03$ with tax within noise. Never-designated bucket at control level in all eight supervised runs. MLP head: 0.98–0.99 at layer 6; linear head at layer 9: 0.77–0.79 → 0.95–0.98 at $+0.01$ nats (App. I).

### 5.4 Verbalizer Audit at Scale

An AV/AR pair trained on Pythia-160M taps with the released recipe states context words truly at 0.44 (RECAP) vs 0.06 (control). The control shows grounded-but-false at scale (grounded 0.48, true 0.06); RECAP narrows the gap $+0.42\to+0.33$ via truer statements, not code removal. RECAP recall 0.29 vs 0.07 while stating fewer words; robust to reconstructor strength; truth 0.44–0.46 over three seeds vs near-zero control (App. J).

The shortfall is generation, not storage: at the verbalizer's recall a fresh probe reaches precision ~0.80 vs the verbalizer's 0.44–0.63. A redesigned reconstructor (standardized multi-token injection, MLP capacity, decode-point presence head on window occurrence, an external fact) makes designated content decodable at its decode point (0.79–0.81, two seeds; matched control 0.03), yet generated precision stays 0.56–0.63. Reconstructor scale (3B = 0.5B), reconstruction optimization, truth reward, injection bandwidth and negative supervision do not close it. At scale the guarantee is decodability; prose is lossy, so the monitor checks claims against internals.

Without heads, decodability erodes within a few hundred fine-tuning steps; maintenance is continuous ($+0.010$ nats) or intermittent at ~1/10 the compute; train it in from the start (App. C).

## 6 Probe-Based Monitoring

Sandbox: per-slot fresh probes read the tap; a claim contradicted by a confident probe ($p{>}0.9$) is flagged; exact truth scores it (App. B). Standard model: sound but low recall: all flags genuine, 27 of 733 false pre-tap claims caught, most in slots too faded to read. RECAP: no false pre-tap claims, zero abstention; designated pre-tap coverage 37% → 100% (coverage, not precision; not the whole activation). Post-tap claims correctly abstained on both; those fall to the grounding-vs-truth comparison (one scenario, seed, threshold).

Pythia-160M: a fresh presence probe ranks true over false claims at AUC $0.965$ vs $0.823$ control (disjoint 95% CIs); flags false claims at $0.93$ recall, $0.87$ precision. At the $1.5\%$ base rate per-claim coverage does not transfer, so AUC and precision/recall are reported.

#### Surviving a score-gaming adversary.

The adversary edits a true stated word into an absent one, maximizing recomputed score (App. F); this suppresses ~87% of the lie penalty on both models. The RECAP probe still flags lies at AUC $0.952$; the control probe, though also reading the unedited activation, falls to $0.508$: decodability is necessary. Candidate selection costs little ($0.993\to0.952$ as lies grow semantically nearer). Threat model: text edits, not activation-level attacks; immunity structural for score manipulation, empirical for selection. A probe-aware adversary assuming monitor leakage (outside the model) drops RECAP only to $0.909$, control to $0.242$; separation grows with adversary strength. Recalibrating the threshold on a disjoint split leaves recall essentially unchanged; no control threshold reaches $0.9$ precision even against random lies. On never-designated words (ranked 64–128) RECAP has no advantage ($0.66$ vs $0.70$).

## 7 Related Work

#### Activation verbalization and its critiques.

Reader-improving methods: supervised QA decoders, general activation explainers, interpreter assistants, training-free readouts, cross-model adapters; SAEs unsupervised. Model explanations pass plausibility without faithfulness in chain-of-thought; causal tests of neuron explanations found high error; counterfactual faithfulness tests prefigure our flips. Prior verbalization critiques are benchmark-level (tasks solvable without internals). We audit the reconstruction test per claim, counterfactually, on a released NLA, and repair the target model, not the reader.

#### Scalable oversight.

Reconstruction scoring substitutes cheap automatic signals for human judgment; AI control designs protocols safe under subversion. We add a monitor whose signal is an independent probe of the target, surviving reconstruction-score gaming.

#### Steganography in learned channels.

Reconstruction objectives hid information since CycleGAN; LLM encoded reasoning, steganographic collusion, tool-widened channels, probe-detected collusion, activation obfuscation, and obfuscated reward hacking under CoT monitors are all induced by incentives, process supervision, or adversaries. Our codes emerge from the standard reconstruction recipe alone, with no steganography objective. Complementing "don't optimize on the monitor": supervise the target against external truth, with no pressure to fool probe or reconstructor.

#### Representation drift, stitching, and monitor staleness.

Representations are equivalent up to transformations; affine maps transfer features across LMs; tuned lenses are affine readers whose staleness we characterize. Concurrent work reports the same staleness and label-free repair at 2B/7B; retraining probes restores detectability after probe-aware fine-tuning. We add recovery anatomy, cross-seed failure, exact evidence information outlives readers, and the drift/collapse separation.

#### Deep supervision and intrinsic interpretability.

Deep supervision targets task labels; ours external content. Concept bottlenecks route flow through concepts, concept whitening constrains geometry, codebooks discretize, gradient routing localizes; we add linear heads without constraining flow. Explanation-side supervision can track behavioral change; ours acts on the target model.

## 8 Discussion and Limitations

Reconstruction scoring is fragile oversight: passable without faithfulness and gameable. RECAP turns oversight into checking an independent probe that survives explanation editing; but it covers only designated, decodable content: a component, not a solution.

Evidence: sandbox, one released NLA, one small model, mostly single seeds; frontier scale untested. Limitations: (1) closed-vocabulary template claims only; monitor covers designated content; open-ended faithfulness unmeasured. (2) Must be co-trained in, not retrofitted; a poor target can report success while decoding nothing. (3) Decodability ≠ verbalizability. (4) Certifies storage, not use: patching the tap barely moves behavior (~0.003), and a model could route around a monitored subspace.

Success is not higher $\tilde r$ but verified claims, calibrated abstention, and recalibrated monitors.

## 9 Conclusion

Models pass the reconstruction test via gist and private codes; training against it yields collapse or proxy gaming. RECAP, training the target model rather than the reader, is the fix that survives our controls. Lesson: a model can game a learned test of its own explanations, so training decodability in beats post-hoc auditing; explanations checkable against internals are a firmer basis for trust.

## Appendix K Hyperparameters and Reproducibility Notes

#### Scale runs (Pythia-160M).

pile-uncopyrighted, 500M tokens/run, identical data/order; batch $64\times1024$; AdamW $10^{-4}$, cosine to 10%, warmup 100, wd 0.01, clip 1.0; bf16 autocast, fp32 weights. Linear heads at layer 6. Presence BCE averaged over $K$; balanced weights positives by inverse window base rate (clamp 100, first 2M tokens). Identity CE over top-$K$ at offset −8. Probes: ridge $\lambda{=}10^4$, first 80%/last 20% held-out sequences (documents may straddle); identity 64-class logistic. Earlier per-bucket $\lambda$ selection from $\{10,…,10^4\}$; fixed-$\lambda$ rerun matches to three decimals. Optimizer settings unswept. Held-out loss on 20M tokens. Significance: 95% bootstrap CIs, disjoint intervals, Hanley–McNeil. Single A100-80GB, Modal, Python 3.12, pinned versions. fp16 loading plus AdamW destroys weights in one step via epsilon underflow with finite loss; runs force fp32.

#### Sandbox runs.

0.5B AV/AR, adapter, norm-matched injection, SFT on full-story descriptions, then alternating rounds. Exact vocabulary-scan parsing; same-type flips. RECAP: $w$ 0.3, 3,000 steps, batch 128, lr $3{\times}10^{-4}$, 30,000 probe taps. Seeds 3+2 via torch.manual_seed (+ CUDA generator). Ceilings on tuple-disjoint (sc. 1)/held-out (sc. 2) splits.

# Train the Model, Not the Reader: Decodability Supervision for Verifiable Activation Explanations

Hiskias Dingeto (StackOne Technologies, hiskias@stackone.com)

###### Abstract

NLAs score activation explanations by reconstruction, a test structurally insensitive to individual false claims. On a released Qwen-2.5-7B verbalizer, explanations reconstruct well above chance while ~2% of specific claims are grounded, so the score tracks gist. Under exact synthetic ground truth, standard training develops co-adapted private codes, and fixes that leave the target model unchanged fail. We contribute two audits (grounding-vs-truth; independent-evaluator swap) and RECAP (Readable Encodings via Co-trained Auxiliary Predictors): linear heads co-trained with the target model to keep designated content decodable. In the sandbox, fresh verbalizers state it truly and codes vanish (+0.001 nats). On Pythia-160M it becomes probe-decodable (verbalizer truth 0.44–0.46 vs near-zero control). A probe ranks true over false verbalizer claims at AUC 0.96 (0.82 without RECAP). Under a score-maximizing lying adversary (~87% of lie penalty suppressed) it holds AUC 0.95; the control probe falls to 0.51.

## 1 Introduction

In an NLA, a verbalizer (AV) maps an activation to text and a reconstructor (AR) maps it back. Round-trip quality is treated as each explanation's faithfulness test: unsupervised, label-free, self-checking. Released AV/AR pairs exist for several open models. The test has a structural gap, a property of the objective at any model or scale. It checks only that the explanation suffices to regenerate the activation and is indifferent among claim values inducing the same reconstruction, so false additions go unpenalized.

The test is passed in two non-faithful ways:
- **Gist:** on a released Qwen-2.5-7B NLA, a per-claim flip audit finds grounding in only ~2% of salient specific claims. This is a lower bound, since flips have low sensitivity.
- **Codes:** in a sandbox with exact ground truth, co-trained pairs consistently develop private codes, i.e. false wording the reconstruction depends on (grounded–true gaps 0.30–0.80, two scenarios).

Two natural fixes fail. Minimizing hidden-state–reconstruction distance removes probe-readable content. Rewarding grounding raises the score by changing which sentences the metric counts. A frozen probe goes stale under drift, which label-free realignment fully reverses. What survives our controls trains the target model: RECAP.

Figure 1: (a) NLA: only AV and AR train; the score can stay high while the text asserts an ungrounded specific. (b) RECAP trains the target with co-trained linear heads on external targets. After training, an independent fresh probe (not the heads) recovers the content (AUC 0.95) and a fresh verbalizer states it truly.

Contributions:
- **Claim-level audit** with per-edit validity controls. The released verbalizer passes with largely ungrounded specifics; its score survives paraphrase and collapses under content-word masking.
- **Private codes**, detected and quantified by grounding-vs-truth and the evaluator swap.
- **RECAP** restores claim-level faithfulness in the sandbox and transfers to Pythia-160M at a measured cost.
- **Adversarial monitor:** a score-gaming adversary suppresses ~87% of the lie penalty on both models, yet the RECAP probe flags lies (AUC 0.95) while the control falls to chance (0.51). The reconstruction score must not be used as a truth signal.

## 2 Preliminaries and Experimental Setup

### 2.1 The Reconstruction Test and Audit Protocols

AV generates explanation $z$ of activation $h$; AR maps $z$ to $\hat h$. With target weights $\theta$ frozen and $h$ the tap activation:

| | $\mathcal{J}_{\mathrm{read}}=\max_{\mathrm{AV},\mathrm{AR}}\cos(\mathrm{AR}(\mathrm{AV}(h)),h)$ | (1)

The NLA authors warn nothing forces faithfulness, yet this is the reported score and users' main criterion. floor = mean cosine of reconstructions vs mismatched activations; $\tilde r=(\cos(\hat h,h)-\mathrm{floor})/(1-\mathrm{floor})$, which is 0 at chance and 1 when perfect. Released NLA: Qwen-2.5-7B layer-20 AV/AR.

**Grounding.** Let $z_{\neg c}$ be $z$ with claim $c$ alone minimally flipped (a flip).

| | $\Delta\tilde r(c)=\tilde r(z)-\tilde r(z_{\neg c})$ | (2)

$c$ is grounded iff $\Delta\tilde r(c)\ge\tau$. Thesis: reconstruction sensitivity to a flip ≠ the model's sensitivity, and the two diverge in practice. Edits changing more than their target inflate grounding severalfold (App. A). Grounded × true gives four cases; we focus on grounded-but-false. If that wording is pair-specific (shown by the evaluator swap, §3.2), it is a co-adapted private code. The label is operational, with no intentional stance. Evaluator gap $=\tilde r_{\mathrm{co}}-\tilde r_{\mathrm{ind}}$.

**Terms.**
- Tap: the layer/position read.
- Probe: a freshly fitted linear decoder.
- Gist: overall meaning, vs specific facts.
- Designated: an auxiliary predictor is co-trained to predict it.
- Decodable: a fresh linear probe reads it.
- Faithfulness: always claim-level (true of and grounded in the activation); not downstream computation, not world grounding.

#### Settings.
1. Released Qwen-2.5-7B layer-20 NLA on in-distribution web text ($n{=}1{,}517$ audited claims).
2. Sandbox: two templated synthetic scenarios (story, marketplace) with exact, judge-free truth. Tap position fixes what the activation holds (retained, faded, unread slots).
3. Continued pretraining of Pythia-160M with self-supervised heads. Tax = held-out LM loss minus a shared control.

Details: App. D, K.

## 3 Auditing Reconstruction-Scored Explanations

The mechanisms differ. In the released NLA, specifics are largely absent from the tap, so the score depends on gist. In the sandbox, content is present but stated in wording only the co-trained AR understands, which the evaluator swap exposes. Only the sandbox failure is a pure metric artifact.

### 3.1 Counterfactual Audit of a Released Verbalizer

Explanations reach $\tilde r=0.84$, yet ~2% of LLM-salient specific claims are grounded (4.2/2.1/1.6% at $\tau$=0.02/0.05/0.10; App. E).
- **Lower bound:** an append-and-re-rank control recovers a topic known to be encoded at only 28% raw.
- **Gist vs specifics (more robust):** probes recover specifics ~3× less accurately than gist (~6% vs ~18% chance-corrected per position; mean-pooled gist ~50%).
- **Layers and readouts:** holds across layers 16–27 and is specific to reconstruction-style readouts; the model's output head does see late-layer specifics.

Training the verbalizer toward grounding fails. Rejection sampling and GRPO with a clause-level grounding reward improved their proxy, but the independent claim-level audit stayed null at every $\tau$ (CIs straddle zero). Text statistics attribute the gains to sentence restructuring (merging/packaging units), not grounding.

### 3.2 Audit Under Synthetic Ground Truth

The toy NLA asserts every slot confidently at $\tilde r$ 0.71–0.86. Truth tracks decodability only loosely:
- fully decodable slot: true 0.44–0.96 across seeds, grounded 0.76–0.88 in all;
- partially decodable slots: true 0.15–0.26;
- unread slots: true at chance.

In 5/5 standard runs, private codes appear (grounded–true gaps 0.30–0.80). Codes can occupy several slots. In the marketplace one occupies an unread slot, so the sentence acts as a channel rather than a description.

Evaluator swap: under an independent evaluator never exposed to the pair's outputs, grounding on code slots collapses 0.53–0.89 → 0.08–0.23 while true-claim grounding survives. This is co-adaptation, not a weaker evaluator. Cross-evaluator $\tilde r$ gap: 0.17–0.38 on standard runs vs ~0.003 on RECAP runs. An evaluator trained on a disjoint paraphrase family (different frames and slot order, sharing only slot words) reproduces the pattern within ~0.05 over three seeds (RECAP slots at 1.00). The channel is private to the pair.

Readout gap: in the marketplace, slots 55–72% decodable are stated truly only 15–26% of the time. Content is present but not conveyed, a gap beyond the storage gap; RECAP closes it.

## 4 Representation Collapse and Probe Drift

**Collapse.** Pulling activations toward their own reconstruction removes decodable slot content at every tested strength and initialization, with perplexity unchanged. Retrained probes also fail, so the information is gone, not rotated. Reconstruction is a lossy projection, and raising similarity to it removes variation outside the probe subspace (cf. non-contrastive SSL collapse).

**Drift.** Matched probes decay to near-chance within 1,500 continued steps and are at chance across seeds (6/6 pairs). A label-free affine map on paired activations restores native performance in 9/9 cases. Rotation alone recovers ~half; full recovery needs non-orthogonal rank ~16–64 (App. H). Concurrent work reports the same at 2B/7B.

Monitoring a model still in training needs explicit recalibration. Realignment fixes how a probe reads; RECAP changes what is stored. Corollary: adapter-based cross-model probe transfer should work.
