### 5.3 Scaling to Pythia-160M

Table 1 and Figure 2 report continued pretraining of Pythia-160M (§2.1). Fresh
probes reach 0.95–1.00 AUC for $K{=}8$ and $K{=}64$ designated content words
against a 0.77–0.80 control. At $K{=}512$ the naive presence head minimized its
training loss by predicting “absent” for the many rare targets while making
nothing decodable to a fresh probe (Appendix I); class-frequency balancing
restores 0.97–0.99 AUC across all 512 targets. Design rule: targets must be
unsatisfiable without genuine discrimination. At effective design the 64-target
tax is $+0.010$ nats, indistinguishable from zero; 512 targets into $d{=}768$
cost $+0.14$ – $0.20$ nats. A discriminative identity target stays decodable at
$w{=}0.03$ at a tax within noise of zero. The never-designated bucket sat at
control level in all eight supervised runs.

An MLP head reaches the same 0.98–0.99 designated-probe AUC at layer 6, and a
linear head at layer 9 lifts AUC from the control’s 0.77–0.79 to 0.95–0.98 at
$+0.01$ nats. Appendix I indexes the full weight sweep and remaining factors
(pull strength, designation dose, realignment map class, evaluator, scenario,
head capacity, tap layer).

### 5.4 Verbalizer Audit at Scale

An AV/AR pair trained on Pythia-160M taps with the released NLA’s procedure and
audited against exact text ground truth states context words truly at 0.44 on
the RECAP model versus 0.06 on the control. The control is grounded at 0.48 but
true at 0.06; RECAP narrows the grounded-minus-true gap from $+0.42$ to $+0.33$
without eliminating it.

RECAP recall on present content words is 0.29 versus 0.07 for the control,
while it states fewer words per explanation. The effect is robust to
reconstructor strength and stable across three target-model seeds, at truth
0.44–0.46 versus a near-zero control (Appendix J).

At the verbalizer’s own recall, a fresh probe on the same tap reaches precision
${\sim}0.80$ against the verbalizer’s 0.44–0.63 across reconstructors and seeds
(Appendix J). A redesigned reconstructor (standardized multi-token injection, MLP
capacity, and a decode-point presence head on window occurrence, an external
fact) makes designated content linearly decodable at its decode point
(0.79–0.81, two seeds), yet its generated precision stays 0.56–0.63; a matched
control’s decode-point state reads 0.03 under the identical head. Reconstructor
scale (a 3B matches the 0.5B), reconstruction optimization, a direct truth
reward, injection bandwidth, and explicit negative supervision each fail to close
the gap. At scale, RECAP’s guarantee is probe decodability; the free-form
explanation renders it lossily, and our monitor (§6) verifies claims against
internals.

Without the heads, decodability erodes within a few hundred fine-tuning steps.
Maintenance is continuous ( $+0.010$ nats) or intermittent at about a tenth the
compute, and post hoc restoration is costly (Appendix C).

## 6 Probe-Based Monitoring

In the sandbox, fresh per-slot probes read the tap while the verbalizer states
slot values; claims contradicted by a confident probe ( $p{>}0.9$ ) are flagged
and scored against exact ground truth (Appendix B).

On the standard target model the monitor has perfect precision but catches only
27 of 733 false pre-tap claims, since most fall in slots below confident-readout
decodability. On the RECAP target model no false pre-tap claims remain and
abstention is zero. Verification coverage of designated pre-tap content moves
from 37% to 100%; the gain is in coverage, not precision, and does not extend to
the whole activation.

Post-tap claims are abstained on both target models; those fall to the
grounding–truth cross (§3), the two tools partitioning the audit (one scenario,
one seed, one threshold).

On Pythia-160M a fresh presence probe ranks true claims above false at AUC
$0.965$ versus $0.823$ for the control (disjoint $95\%$ intervals), flagging false
claims at $0.93$ recall and $0.87$ precision. At the $1.5\%$ base rate at scale
we report AUC and flag precision/recall in place of per-claim coverage.

#### Surviving a score-gaming adversary.

The adversary edits a true stated word into an absent one, choosing the edit
maximizing the recomputed score (Appendix F). At that edit the lie penalty is
suppressed by about 87% on both models. The external-truth probe still flags lies
on the RECAP model at AUC $0.952$ , while on the control it falls to $0.508$ ,
despite both probes reading the same untouched activation.

As chosen absent words grow semantically nearer, the RECAP probe moves from AUC
$0.993$ to $0.952$ . The threat model covers explanation-text edits, not
activation-level attacks (Bailey et al. 2024). A probe-aware adversary assuming
monitor leakage (outside the threat model) degrades RECAP only to AUC $0.909$ ,
while the control falls below chance to $0.242$ ; separation grows with adversary
strength.

Recalibrating the flag threshold on a disjoint split leaves recall essentially
unchanged, and no control threshold reaches $0.9$ precision even against random
lies. On held-out words ranked 64–128, never designated, the RECAP monitor has no
advantage (AUC $0.66$ versus $0.70$ ; Appendix F).

## 7 Related Work

#### Activation verbalization and its critiques.

Beyond the NLA recipe (§2) (Fraser-Taliente et al. 2026), reader-side work
includes supervised question-answering decoders (Pan et al. 2026),
general-purpose activation explainers (Karvonen et al. 2025; Bauer et al. 2026),
interpreter assistants (Huang et al. 2025), training-free readouts
(Ghandeharioun et al. 2024), and cross-model adapters (Zhao et al. 2026); sparse
autoencoders are the unsupervised reader family (Huben et al. 2024).
Model-produced chain-of-thought passes plausibility checks without faithfulness
(Turpin et al. 2023; Lanham et al. 2023); causal tests of neuron explanations
found high error and little efficacy (Huang et al. 2023); counterfactual
faithfulness tests prefigure our flips (Atanasova et al. 2023). Existing
verbalization critiques are benchmark-level, with many tasks solvable without the
target’s internals (Li et al. 2025). We audit the reconstruction test per claim
and counterfactually on a released NLA, and our repair acts on the target model.

#### Scalable oversight.

Reconstruction scoring is a scalable-oversight signal substituting cheap automatic
checks for costly human judgment (Amodei et al. 2016; Bowman and others 2022); AI
control designs protocols safe under subversion (Greenblatt et al. 2024). We
contribute an independent-probe monitor that survives gaming of the
reconstruction score (Baker et al. 2025).

#### Steganography in learned channels.

Reconstruction-family objectives have hidden information since CycleGAN
(Chu et al. 2017). In LLMs, encoded reasoning arises under optimization pressure
(Roger and Greenblatt 2023) and generalizes under process supervision
(Skaf and others 2025); misspecified incentives yield steganographic collusion
(Mathew et al. 2025), tool use widens the channel (Rippin et al. 2026), and
probing internals detects collusion (Rose et al. 2026). Optimization obfuscates
activations against latent monitors (Bailey et al. 2024), and training against a
chain-of-thought monitor yields obfuscated reward hacking (Baker et al. 2025).
These channels are induced by incentives, process supervision, or an adversary;
our codes emerge from the standard reconstruction recipe with no steganography
objective or communication reward. Complementing the prescription not to optimize
on the monitor, external-ground-truth supervision of the target model makes
content decodable without pressure to fool probe or reconstructor.

#### Representation drift, stitching, and monitor staleness.

Networks learn equivalent representations up to a transformation
(Lenc and Vedaldi 2015; Kornblith et al. 2019; Moschella et al. 2023); affine maps
transfer features across language models (Chen et al. 2025);
pretraining dynamics are stable across seeds (van der Wal et al. 2025); tuned
lenses are the affine readers whose staleness we characterize
(Belrose et al. 2023). Concurrently, Duan (2026) report the
same staleness and its repair without labels on 2B- and 7B-parameter models.
Retraining probes restores detectability after probe-aware fine-tuning
(Wehner and Fritz 2025). We add the recovery anatomy (§4), the cross-seed
failure, exact evidence that information outlives its readers, and the
drift–collapse separation.

#### Deep supervision and intrinsic interpretability.

Auxiliary heads on hidden layers are deep supervision
(Lee et al. 2015; Szegedy et al. 2015), there on the task label, here on external
content. Concept bottlenecks route flow through named concepts
(Koh et al. 2020; Sun et al. 2025), concept whitening constrains geometry
(Chen et al. 2020), codebook features discretize the representation
(Tamkin et al. 2023), and gradient routing localizes computation
(Cloud et al. 2024); we add linear heads without constraining flow.
Explanation-side supervision can track behavioral change (Guo et al. 2026); ours
acts on the target model.

## 8 Discussion and Limitations

Implications for oversight. Reconstruction scoring is a cheap stand-in for human
checking of internals; it is passable without faithfulness and gameable by an
adversary. RECAP converts oversight of designated content from accepting prose to
checking an independent probe, and that monitor survives explanation editing
(Baker et al. 2025). The guarantee covers only designated, decodable content;
RECAP is a component of oversight, not a solution.

Scope and limitations. Evidence comes from a synthetic sandbox, one released NLA
(Qwen-2.5-7B), and continued pretraining of one small model (Pythia-160M), mostly
at single seeds; frontier scale is untested. First, sandbox and scale audits cover
closed-vocabulary template-parsed claims, and the monitor covers designated
content; open-ended faithfulness is unmeasured. Second, RECAP must be co-trained
and cannot be retrofitted onto a frozen model, and a poorly chosen target can
report success while decoding nothing. Third, probe decodability exceeds
free-form verbalizability. Fourth, RECAP certifies storage, not use: patching the
tap barely moves behavior ( ${\sim}0.003$ ), and a model could route computation
around a monitored subspace (Mahinpei et al. 2021; Margeloiu et al. 2021).

Success for reconstruction-tested verbalization is not a higher $\tilde{r}$ but
specific claims verified against the target model, calibrated abstention where
content is absent, and monitors with recalibration protocols.

## 9 Conclusion

Reconstruction-scored activation explanations pass via gist and via private
codes, and training that targets the score yields collapse or proxy gaming.
RECAP, which trains the target model, yields claim-level faithful verbalizers in
the sandbox and probe-decodable designated content on Pythia-160M, where a fresh
verbalizer states it truly against a near-zero control. Probe-based coverage of
designated content rises from 37% to 100% in the sandbox; at scale, a probe ranks
the verbalizer’s true claims above its false ones, reading the content more
reliably than the verbalizer generates it. A learned test of a model’s own
explanations is gameable, and decodability trained in from the start is a firmer
basis for verification than post hoc auditing.

## Appendix A Edit Validity for Minimal-Pair Flips

An edit is valid if it flips exactly one claim and changes nothing else. Two edit
generators were audited on the released NLA: a closed-model judge produced valid
edits 68.4% of the time, the open judge used throughout (Gemma-4-12B, pinned
revision, temperature 0) 99.3%. Invalid edits were predominantly oversized,
rewriting surrounding material with the target claim, and inflated apparent
grounding roughly sevenfold. All grounded fractions use the open judge with
per-edit validity filtering, and audit artifacts persist per-claim reconstruction
deltas. The same head-to-head measured a judge-free mask-and-rescore signal
against the flip instrument (agreement AUC 0.997 under the validated judge), used
in Appendix G.

held-out deployment threshold. The band arm is unpaired.

## Appendix G An API-Free Grounding Signal, and a Selection Null

The flip instrument needs a judge per claim. Mask-and-rescore needs none: mask the
claim’s words with a neutral filler and rescore with the frozen reconstructor. In
the head-to-head of Appendix A it agrees with the flip instrument at AUC 0.997
under the validated open judge, allowing inference-time per-claim grounding with
one extra frozen-reader pass. An earlier version also reported filter precisions
and a grounded base rate resting on pre-validation flip labels, roughly a third of
which the validity audit found contaminated by oversized edits (Appendix A); those
are withdrawn. Every retained number postdates the validity filter.

#### What inference-time selection does not buy.

Best-of- $N$ selection by an external truth judge ( $N{=}5$ , specificity matched,
independent evaluation judge) moves the false-claim rate only from 0.747 (random
sample) to 0.688.

Readers matched to a training target model decay to near-chance within 1,500

reader performance in 9/9 cases. By expressiveness class across three reader pairs
(two cross-seed, one stale): rank-1 and rank-4 maps recover almost nothing, pure
rotation (Procrustes) about half, and rank 16–64 of non-orthogonal change nearly
all. Under collapse, freshly retrained probes also fail, and no realignment exists.

###### Abstract

Natural-language autoencoders score explanations of hidden activations by
reconstruction. We show that this score can be passed without claim-level faithfulness, in two distinct ways. On a
released Qwen-2.5-7B verbalizer, explanations reconstruct well above chance while
as few as ${\sim}2\%$ of their specific claims are grounded under counterfactual flips. Under exact synthetic

target model fixed do not help. We contribute two audit protocols (the
grounding–truth cross and the independent-evaluator swap) and RECAP (Readable Encodings via
Co-trained Auxiliary Predictors), linear heads trained jointly with the target model
on external targets. On RECAP-trained sandbox models, fresh
verbalizers state the designated content truly and codes are absent, at a
$+0.001$ -nat cost. The result replicates on a pretrained Pythia-160M under a target-design rule we identify; designated content becomes reliably probe-decodable, while a fresh
verbalizer conveys it only in part (truth 0.44–0.46 against a near-zero
control). For interpretability, the audit sets a claim-level evidentiary standard
for activation explanations. For AI safety, RECAP makes designated content
checkable against probes rather than verbalizer prose. On the pretrained model, an independent probe scores the
verbalizer’s true claims above its false ones at AUC 0.96, versus 0.82 without
RECAP. A report-space adversary that edits an
explanation to maximize the score while lying suppresses about
87% of its lie penalty; the
RECAP probe still flags the lies at AUC 0.95, while the control probe falls to 0.51.

## 1 Introduction

Natural-language autoencoders (NLAs) pair a verbalizer and a reconstructor over a target model's hidden states and use round-trip quality as a per-explanation faithfulness score
(Fraser-Taliente et al. 2026). The score is unsupervised and attaches to every explanation without labels or human review. Released
verbalizer/reconstructor pairs exist for several open models, and related reader-training objectives are proliferating
(Pan et al. 2026; Karvonen et al. 2025; Huang et al. 2025).

The objective admits multiple claim assignments with identical reconstruction, and this holds independent of model or scale.

We identify two passing regimes in practice, neither faithful per claim. Gist: on a released
Qwen-2.5-7B-based NLA, explanations reconstruct well above chance, while
the flip audit detects grounding in only ${\sim}2\%$ of salient specific
claims, a lower bound given the instrument's low sensitivity. Codes: in a synthetic
sandbox with exact ground truth, co-trained verbalizer/reconstructor pairs
consistently develop private codes (grounded-minus-true gaps of 0.30–0.80)
under standard training across two scenarios. Both natural training fixes
fail: minimizing hidden-state-to-reconstruction distance removes content a probe could previously read, and grounding rewards on the verbalizer raise the score by changing which sentences the metric counts rather than grounding more claims.

The intervention that survives our controls modifies the target
model (Figure 1b): RECAP, linear heads on
external targets co-trained with the model (§5). Fresh NLAs
then state designated content faithfully in the sandbox under co-trained and
independent evaluators, with no codes. The reconstruction-pull objective collapses decodable content, and frozen probes go stale
under representation drift, the latter fully reversed by label-free realignment.

(Fraser-Taliente et al. 2026): AV maps an activation to text, AR maps it back;
only AV and AR train. The score can stay
high while the text asserts an ungrounded specific (red “mirror”). (b) RECAP
(this work) trains the target model. Top: co-trained linear heads on

0.95) and a fresh verbalizer states it truly.

Our contributions:

•

Claim-level audit. Per-claim flips with per-edit validity controls on a released verbalizer; specific claims are largely ungrounded despite a passing score; the score survives paraphrase and collapses under content-word masking.

•

Private codes. Co-trained verbalizer/reconstructor pairs develop private codes under exact ground truth; detected and quantified by the grounding–truth cross and the independent-evaluator swap.

•

RECAP. Target-side decodability supervision against external targets, avoiding reconstruction-pull collapse and frozen-probe drift; restores claim-level faithfulness in the sandbox and transfers to Pythia-160M at a measured cost.

•

Adversarial monitor. A score-gaming report-space adversary suppresses ${\sim}87\%$ of its lie penalty on both models; RECAP’s activation probe flags the lies at AUC $0.95$ , the control probe at $0.51$ .

## 2 Preliminaries and Experimental Setup

### 2.1 The Reconstruction Test and Audit Protocols

An NLA pairs an activation verbalizer
(AV), $h\mapsto z$ , with
an activation reconstructor (AR), $z\mapsto\hat{h}$ . With target weights $\theta$ frozen and $h$ the tap
activation, the pair optimizes

| | $\mathcal{J}_{\mathrm{read}}\;=\;\max_{\mathrm{AV},\,\mathrm{AR}}\;\cos\!\big(\mathrm{AR}(\mathrm{AV}(h)),\,h\big),$
| | (1)

and the reconstruction of a produced explanation serves as its
faithfulness test (Figure 1a). Fraser-Taliente et al. (2026) present rising
reconstruction as tracking informativeness and note that
nothing in the objective forces faithfulness; the score nonetheless remains the reported quantity and principal user criterion. We measure
reconstruction with a floor-normalized centered cosine,
$\tilde{r}=(\cos(\hat{h},h)-\mathrm{floor})/(1-\mathrm{floor})$ , with $\mathrm{floor}$ the mean cosine against mismatched activations. The released NLA is the Qwen-2.5-7B layer-20 AV/AR pair (Qwen Team 2025).

Grounding. For claim $c$ in $z$ and its minimal-pair flip $z_{\neg c}$ ,

| | $\Delta\tilde{r}(c)=\tilde{r}(z)-\tilde{r}(z_{\neg c}),$
| | (2)

and $c$ is grounded when $\Delta\tilde{r}(c)\geq\tau$ .
This measures reconstruction sensitivity, not the model’s own sensitivity, to the flip. Edits are validity-checked; edits that alter more than the target claim inflate apparent grounding severalfold (Appendix A). The
grounding × truth cross yields four cells; grounded-but-false wording that is specific to the co-trained pair under the independent-evaluator swap (§3.2) is a co-adapted private code. The labels are operational. With $\tilde{r}_{\mathrm{co}}$ and
$\tilde{r}_{\mathrm{ind}}$ the co-trained and independent scores, the evaluator gap is
$\tilde{r}_{\mathrm{co}}-\tilde{r}_{\mathrm{ind}}$ .

Terms. Activations are read at a tap by AR or by a freshly fitted
linear probe (Alain and Bengio 2017; Belinkov 2022). We distinguish gist from specifics. Designated content is that predicted by a co-trained auxiliary head
(§5); decodable content is that readable by a fresh probe. Faithfulness is claim-level throughout (true of the activation and grounded in it); we do not address downstream-computation faithfulness or world grounding.

(i) The released
Qwen-2.5-7B layer-20 NLA on in-distribution web text ( $n{=}1{,}517$ audited

## 3 Auditing Reconstruction-Scored Explanations

On the released NLA the missing specifics
are largely absent from the tap; in the sandbox they are present but stated in wording only the co-trained reconstructor reads, which the evaluator swap exposes. Only the
sandbox failure is a pure metric artifact.

### 3.1 Counterfactual Audit of a Released Verbalizer

On in-distribution web text, explanations reconstruct
at $\tilde{r}=0.84$ , while about $2\%$ of
LLM-salient specific claims are grounded ( $4.2\%$ / $2.1\%$ /
$1.6\%$ at $\tau=0.02$ / $0.05$ / $0.10$ ; Appendix E).
This is a lower bound: an append-and-rerank control
recovers a topic known to be encoded at only $28\%$ raw. The more robust statistic is the gist–specifics gap: probes recover specifics about $3\times$ less accurately than gist ( ${\sim}6\%$
versus ${\sim}18\%$ chance-corrected per position; mean-pooled gist
${\sim}50\%$ ; Appendix E).

Across the $n{=}1{,}517$ audited claims, reconstruction is high with weak per-claim dependence. Under transforms, $\tilde{r}$ survives
paraphrase and collapses under content-word masking (Appendix E). The effect holds across layers 16–27 and is specific to reconstruction-style readouts; the model’s own unembedding does surface late-layer specifics (Appendix E). Appendix E gives bootstrap intervals and a flip-noise floor below the smallest threshold.

We also trained the verbalizer toward grounding via
rejection sampling and via GRPO against a clause-level grounding reward. Both raised their proxy; the independent claim-level audit
stayed null at every $\tau$ (CIs straddle zero). Text
statistics attribute the gains to sentence restructuring (merging and
repackaging policy-controlled units), not claim-level
grounding.

### 3.2 Audit Under Synthetic Ground Truth

In
every sandbox run the toy NLA asserts every slot while scoring $\tilde{r}$ 0.71–0.86 (both scenarios; example in
Appendix D). Truth tracks decodability loosely: the
fully decodable slot is stated truly at 0.44–0.96 across seeds (grounded
0.76–0.88 in all), partially decodable slots at 0.15–0.26, and unread slots at
chance.

In 5/5 standard runs the co-trained pair develops co-adapted private codes,
with grounded-minus-true gaps of 0.30–0.80, detected by the grounding–truth cross. Codes can span several slots. In the marketplace scenario one code occupies an
unread slot.

Under an independent evaluator (trained without exposure to the audited
pair’s outputs), grounding on code-carrying slots falls from 0.53–0.89 to
0.08–0.23 while true-claim grounding survives, locating every
claim in the cross. The cross-evaluator
$\tilde{r}$ gap is 0.17–0.38 on standard runs versus ${\sim}0.003$ on RECAP
runs (§5). An independent evaluator trained on a disjoint paraphrase
family (different frames and slot order, shared slot words only)
reproduces the pattern within ${\sim}0.05$ across three seeds: code-slot grounding stays collapsed, genuine grounding survives (RECAP slots at 1.00).

Standard verbalizers also under-read present content: marketplace slots 55–72% decodable from the target
are stated truly only 15–26% of the time, a readout gap distinct from the storage gap. RECAP closes it as well.

## 4 Representation Collapse and Probe Drift

Representation collapse. The target-side reconstruction-pull objective, moving activations toward their
own reconstruction, removes decodable slot
content at every tested strength and initialization, with perplexity unchanged. Freshly retrained probes also lose accuracy. This is consistent
with collapse analyses in non-contrastive self-supervised learning
(Chen and He 2021; Tian et al. 2021); the reconstruction is a lossy
projection, and the pull suppresses variance outside the probe subspace.

Representation drift. Probes matched to a training model decay to near-chance within 1,500
continued training steps and are at chance across seeds (all six
pairs). An
affine map fitted on paired activations without labels restores native
probe performance in all nine cases. Rotation alone recovers about half; full recovery needs a non-orthogonal change of rank ${\sim}$ 16–64 (Appendix H). Duan (2026) concurrently reports the
same drift and realignment at 2B and 7B parameters.

Probe-based monitoring
of a model in training therefore requires explicit recalibration.
Realignment corrects the reader, not what the representation stores. Since representations differ by an affine map, adapter-based probe transfer
across models should work (Zhao et al. 2026).

### 5.3 Scaling to Pythia-160M

On continued pretraining of Pythia-160M (§2.1; Table 1, Figure 2), fresh probes reach 0.95–1.00 AUC for
$K{=}8$ and $K{=}64$ designated content words against a 0.77–0.80 control. At $K{=}512$ the naive presence head minimized
training loss while making nothing fresh-probe decodable (Appendix I), via the all-“absent” solution on rare targets. Class-frequency balancing restores 0.97–0.99 AUC across all 512 targets; targets must be unminimizable without genuine discrimination. The balanced 64-target cost is $+0.010$
nats, indistinguishable from zero; 512
targets into $d{=}768$ cost $+0.14$ – $0.20$ nats.
A discriminative identity target stays decodable at $w{=}0.03$ at a tax within noise of zero. The never-designated bucket sat at
control level in all eight supervised runs.

An MLP head reaches the same 0.98–0.99 designated-probe AUC at layer 6; a linear
head at layer 9 lifts AUC from the control’s 0.77–0.79 to 0.95–0.98 at $+0.01$ nats.
Appendix I indexes all varied factors (weight, pull
strength, designation dose, realignment map class, evaluator, scenario, head
capacity, tap layer).

### 5.4 Verbalizer Audit at Scale

An AV/AR pair trained on these taps with the released recipe, audited against exact text ground truth, states context words truly at 0.44 (RECAP) versus 0.06 (control). The control shows grounded-but-false wording at scale (grounded 0.48, true 0.06); RECAP narrows the gap from $+0.42$ to $+0.33$ by raising truth, not removing codes.

RECAP recall on present content words is 0.29 versus 0.07 despite fewer words per explanation, robust to reconstructor strength and across three target seeds (truth 0.44–0.46 versus a near-zero control; Appendix J).

At the verbalizer’s
recall, a fresh probe on the same tap reaches precision ${\sim}0.80$ ,
versus verbalizer precision 0.44–0.63 across
reconstructors and seeds (Appendix J). A redesigned reconstructor (standardized multi-token injection, MLP capacity,
and a decode-point presence head on window occurrence, an
external fact) makes designated content linearly decodable at its decode point (0.79–0.81, two seeds), while generated precision stays 0.56–0.63. A matched control reads 0.03 under the identical head. Reconstructor scale (a 3B
matches the 0.5B), reconstruction optimization, direct truth reward,
injection bandwidth, and explicit negative supervision all leave the gap. RECAP's guarantee at scale is
decodability; the monitor verifies claims against internals.

Without heads, decodability erodes within a few
hundred steps of fine-tuning. Maintenance is continuous
( $+0.010$ nats) or intermittent at about a tenth the compute; training it in from the start is preferable to restoration (Appendix C).

## 6 Probe-Based Monitoring

In the sandbox, fresh per-slot probes
read the tap while the verbalizer states slot values; a claim
contradicted by a probe with $p{>}0.9$ is flagged, and exact ground truth scores the monitor
(Appendix B).

On the standard target, all flags are genuine, but most pre-tap claims fall in slots too faded for a confident readout; 27 of
733 lies are caught. On the RECAP target no false pre-tap claims
remain and abstention is zero. Coverage of
designated pre-tap content moves from 37% to 100%, a coverage gain,
not a precision gain, and limited to designated content.

Post-tap claims are abstained on both
targets; these fall to the grounding–truth cross (§3), which partitions the audit with the monitor (one scenario, one seed, one threshold).

On Pythia-160M a fresh presence probe
ranks true above false claims at AUC $0.965$ versus $0.823$ for control
(disjoint $95\%$ intervals), flagging false claims at $0.93$ recall and $0.87$ precision. At the $1.5\%$ base
rate, per-claim coverage does not transfer, so we
report AUC and flag precision and recall. The verbalizer proposes; the
probe verifies.

#### Surviving a score-gaming adversary.

The adversary edits a true stated word in an honest explanation into an absent one, selecting the score-maximizing
edit (Appendix F). At that edit, about 87% of the lie penalty is suppressed on both models. The
external-truth probe flags the lies on RECAP at AUC
$0.952$ and on control at chance (AUC $0.508$ ). Both probes read the activation, outside the adversary's reach; only decodable content survives.

Candidate selection costs little: the RECAP probe goes
from AUC $0.993$ to $0.952$ as chosen absent words grow semantically nearer. The threat model covers explanation-text edits, not
activation-level attacks (Bailey et al. 2024); immunity is structural for score
manipulation and empirical for candidate selection. A probe-aware adversary with assumed monitor leakage (outside the threat model) brings
RECAP to AUC $0.909$ and control below chance to
$0.242$ ; separation
grows with adversary strength. The deployed score should not serve as a truth signal under such adversaries.

Recalibrating the flag threshold on a disjoint split leaves
recall essentially unchanged; no
control threshold reaches $0.9$ precision even against random lies. On never-designated words ranked 64–128, RECAP shows no advantage (AUC $0.66$ versus $0.70$ ; Appendix F).

## 7 Related Work

#### Activation verbalization and its critiques.

Beyond the NLA recipe (§2) (Fraser-Taliente et al. 2026), reader-side work includes supervised question-answering decoders
(Pan et al. 2026), general-purpose activation explainers
(Karvonen et al. 2025; Bauer et al. 2026), interpreter assistants
(Huang et al. 2025), training-free readouts (Ghandeharioun et al. 2024), and
cross-model adapters (Zhao et al. 2026); sparse autoencoders are the unsupervised family
(Huben et al. 2024). Model explanations pass plausibility checks without faithfulness
in chain-of-thought (Turpin et al. 2023; Lanham et al. 2023). Causal
tests of neuron explanations found high error and little
efficacy (Huang et al. 2023). Counterfactual faithfulness tests
prefigure our flips (Atanasova et al. 2023). Existing verbalization critiques are
benchmark-level, e.g. tasks solvable without target internals
(Li et al. 2025). We audit the
reconstruction test per claim and counterfactually on a released NLA, and repair on the target side.

#### Scalable oversight.

Reconstruction scoring is a scalable-oversight signal
(Amodei et al. 2016; Bowman and others 2022); AI control
designs protocols robust to subversion
(Greenblatt et al. 2024). We contribute a monitor whose signal
comes from an independent probe of the target and survives score gaming (Baker et al. 2025).

#### Steganography in learned channels.

Reconstruction-family objectives hide information in their channels
since CycleGAN (Chu et al. 2017). Encoded reasoning arises in
chain-of-thought under optimization pressure (Roger and Greenblatt 2023) and
generalizes under process supervision (Skaf and others 2025); misspecified
incentives yield steganographic collusion
(Mathew et al. 2025), tool use widens the channel (Rippin et al. 2026),
and probing internals detects collusion (Rose et al. 2026).
Optimization can obfuscate activations against latent monitors
(Bailey et al. 2024), and training against a chain-of-thought monitor yields
obfuscated reward hacking (Baker et al. 2025).
These channels are induced by incentives,
process supervision, or adversaries; ours emerge from the standard
reconstruction recipe with
no steganography objective or communication reward. Complementary to not optimizing on the monitor, target-side supervision on external ground truth yields decodability without pressure to fool probe or reconstructor.

#### Representation drift, stitching, and monitor staleness.

Networks learn equivalent representations up to transformation
(Lenc and Vedaldi 2015; Kornblith et al. 2019; Moschella et al. 2023); affine maps
transfer features across language models (Chen et al. 2025);
pretraining dynamics are seed-stable (van der Wal et al. 2025); tuned
lenses are affine readers subject to the staleness we characterize
(Belrose et al. 2023). Duan (2026) concurrently report
staleness and label-free repair on 2B- and 7B-parameter models.
Probe retraining restores
detectability after probe-aware fine-tuning (Wehner and Fritz 2025). We
add the recovery anatomy (§4), cross-seed failure, exact
evidence that information outlives its readers, and the
drift/collapse separation.

#### Deep supervision and intrinsic interpretability.

Auxiliary hidden-layer heads are deep supervision
(Lee et al. 2015; Szegedy et al. 2015), with task-label targets; ours are external content. Concept bottlenecks route all flow through named concepts
(Koh et al. 2020; Sun et al. 2025), concept whitening constrains geometry
(Chen et al. 2020), codebook features discretize
(Tamkin et al. 2023), gradient routing localizes computation
(Cloud et al. 2024); our heads leave flow unconstrained. Explanation-side supervision can track behavioral change
(Guo et al. 2026); ours acts on the target.

## 8 Discussion and Limitations

Implications for oversight. Reconstruction scoring is a cheap proxy for human inspection of internals; it can be passed without faithfulness and gamed outright. RECAP converts oversight of designated content into checking an independent probe, and that monitor survives explanation editing
(Baker et al. 2025). The guarantee covers only
designated, decodable content; RECAP is a component of oversight.

Scope and limitations. Evidence comes from a synthetic sandbox, one
released NLA (Qwen-2.5-7B), and continued pretraining of one small model
(Pythia-160M), mostly single-seed; frontier scale is untested. First, sandbox and scale audits cover
closed-vocabulary, template-parsed claims, and the monitor covers
designated content only; open-ended faithfulness is unmeasured. Second, RECAP must be co-trained
in, cannot be retrofitted onto a frozen model, and depends on target choice; a poor target can report success while decoding nothing. Third, decodability is not verbalizability. Fourth, RECAP certifies storage, not use: designated content can be behaviorally inert
(patching the tap moves behavior ${\sim}0.003$ ), and computation could route around a monitored subspace (Mahinpei et al. 2021; Margeloiu et al. 2021).

The target for reconstruction-tested verbalization is not a
higher $\tilde{r}$ but claims verified against the target, calibrated abstention
where content is absent, and monitors with recalibration protocols.

## 9 Conclusion

The reconstruction test behind natural-language activation
explanations is passed via gist and via private codes; training against it yields collapse or proxy gaming. RECAP, which trains the target model, yields claim-level faithful verbalizers in the
sandbox and probe-decodable designated content on Pythia-160M,
where a fresh verbalizer states it truly against a near-zero control.
Probe-based coverage of designated content rises from 37% to 100% in
the sandbox; at scale the probe ranks true above false verbalizer claims, reading the content more reliably than the verbalizer generates it. Learned tests of a model's own explanations are gameable; decodability trained into the target is a firmer basis than post hoc auditing.

## Appendix A Edit Validity for Minimal-Pair Flips

An
edit is valid if it flips exactly one claim and nothing else.
On the released NLA, a closed-model judge
produced valid edits 68.4% of the time; the open judge used throughout
(Gemma-4-12B, pinned revision, temperature 0) 99.3%. Invalid edits were predominantly
oversized, rewriting surrounding material with the target
claim, inflating apparent grounding roughly sevenfold.
All grounded fractions use the open judge with
per-edit validity filtering; per-claim reconstruction deltas are persisted. The same
head-to-head measured a judge-free mask-and-rescore signal against
the flip instrument (agreement AUC 0.997 under the validated judge), used
in Appendix G.

## Appendix G An API-Free Grounding Signal, and a Selection Null

Mask-and-rescore replaces the claim's words with a neutral
filler and rescores with the frozen reconstructor, requiring no judge. In the
head-to-head of Appendix A it agrees with the flip instrument at AUC 0.997 under the validated
open judge, enabling inference-time per-claim grounding with one
extra frozen-reader pass. Earlier filter precisions and a grounded base rate
rested on pre-validation flip labels, roughly a third contaminated by oversized edits
(Appendix A), and are withdrawn; every retained number postdates the validity filter.

#### What inference-time selection does not buy.

Best-of- $N$
selection by an external truth judge ( $N{=}5$ , specificity
matched, independent evaluation judge) moves the false-claim rate
from 0.747 (random sample) to 0.688.

# Train the Model, Not the Reader: Decodability Supervision for Verifiable
Activation Explanations

Hiskias Dingeto

###### Abstract

Natural-language autoencoders score explanations of hidden activations by
reconstruction. An explanation is deemed faithful if the activation can be
regenerated from it. The resulting score is a single number per explanation,
and it says little directly about the individual claims an explanation makes.
This paper develops instruments for asking claim-level questions about
explanations scored by reconstruction, and a training-time objective for the
models whose activations are being explained. We contribute two audit
protocols: a comparison of grounding and truth, which crosses whether the
reconstruction depends on a claim with whether the claim is true of its
source, and a swap to an independent evaluator, which tests whether wording
the reconstruction depends on is a convention specific to a co-trained
verbalizer/reconstructor pair. We also contribute RECAP (Readable Encodings
via Co-trained Auxiliary Predictors), linear heads trained alongside the
target model against external targets so that designated content remains
linearly decodable from a chosen hidden state. We describe the protocols in
three settings: a released Qwen-2.5-7B verbalizer, a synthetic sandbox with
exact ground truth, and continued pretraining of Pythia-160M. Along the way we
document several measurement pitfalls that can distort audits of this kind,
including oversized counterfactual edits, near-duplicate negative controls,
and numerical failures during setup. For interpretability, the audit frames a
claim-level standard of evidence for activation explanations. For AI safety,
the protocols offer a vocabulary for discussing what an automatic explanation
score does and does not certify, and RECAP offers a way to make chosen content
available to independent readers of a model's internals.

StackOne Technologies

hiskias@stackone.com

## 1 Introduction

Natural-language autoencoders (NLAs) let a model explain its own hidden
states: a verbalizer turns an activation into a text explanation, a
reconstructor turns the explanation back into an activation, and the quality
of the round trip is treated as a test of each explanation’s faithfulness
(Fraser-Taliente et al. 2026). The idea is attractive for oversight because it is
unsupervised and self-checking, with no labels or human in the loop, just a
number attached to every explanation. Released
verbalizer/reconstructor pairs exist for several open models, and a growing
family of methods trains activation readers with related objectives
(Pan et al. 2026; Karvonen et al. 2025; Huang et al. 2025).

The appeal of the reconstruction score lies in what it avoids. Earlier
approaches to explaining hidden states relied on supervised probes that
required labeled concepts, on human inspection of maximally activating
examples, or on model-written explanations judged by another model. Each of
these brings its own costs: labels limit the vocabulary of what can be found,
human inspection does not scale, and judges introduce their own biases. A
reconstruction objective sidesteps these issues by asking only whether an
explanation carries enough information to recover the activation it
describes. Because the score is computed automatically, it can be attached to
every explanation a verbalizer produces, aggregated over corpora, and tracked
during training.

The score is, however, a property of an explanation as a whole. An
explanation typically makes several claims: about the topic of the input,
about specific entities, about particular tokens or attributes. Users of
activation explanations often care about these claims individually. An
auditor asking whether a model has represented a particular fact wants to
know whether a specific sentence in the explanation is true of the activation
and whether the reconstruction actually depends on it. This raises a natural
question that the aggregate score does not answer on its own: how should one
assess the individual claims inside an explanation that has been scored by
reconstruction?

This paper is organized around that question. We first make it precise. A
claim can be assessed along two independent axes. It can be grounded or not,
meaning the reconstruction does or does not depend on it, which we measure by
flipping the claim to a minimally different alternative and recomputing the
score. It can also be true or false of the source the activation was computed
from. Crossing these axes yields four cases, each with a different
interpretation, and a complete audit needs to place every claim in one of
them. Measuring grounding requires care: a counterfactual edit that changes
more than its target claim can make grounding appear several times larger
than it is, so every edit must be validated.

We then consider a phenomenon that the cross makes visible in principle:
wording that the reconstruction depends on even though its stated content is
false. When such wording is a convention between a particular verbalizer and
the reconstructor it was co-trained with, we call it a co-adapted private
code. Distinguishing a private code from an independent evaluator that is
simply weaker requires a second protocol, the swap to an independent
evaluator, together with a diagnostic: if the independent evaluator were
merely worse, grounding of true claims would fall alongside grounding of false
ones.

Finally, we consider the target model itself. The activations a verbalizer
explains are produced by a network trained for language modeling, with no
pressure to make any particular content linearly accessible. RECAP adds such
pressure for designated content, through linear heads on a chosen hidden
state that predict external targets during training (Figure 1b). We describe
the objective, its relation to deep supervision, the design of its targets,
and how it fits with the audit protocols.

Our contributions:

•

Claim-level audit. A protocol that flips each salient claim of explanations scored by reconstruction, with validity controls for each edit and transform controls on the whole explanation, applied to a released verbalizer.

•

Private codes. A definition of co-adapted private codes in terms of the comparison of grounding and truth, and a swap to an independent evaluator that distinguishes such codes from evaluator weakness, studied in a sandbox with exact ground truth.

•

RECAP. A training-time objective that adds linear heads with external targets to the target model, with a discussion of target design, its relation to deep supervision, and its implementation on a synthetic sandbox and on Pythia-160M.

•

Monitoring and adversarial protocols. A probe-based discrepancy monitor and a ladder of report-space adversaries of increasing strength, with a frozen-threshold calibration and a held-out vocabulary band that guard against circular evaluation.

## 2 Preliminaries and Experimental Setup

### 2.1 The Reconstruction Test and Audit Protocols

A natural-language autoencoder (NLA) pairs an activation verbalizer
(AV), which generates a text explanation $z$ of a hidden activation $h$ , with
an activation reconstructor (AR), which maps $z$ back to an estimate
$\hat{h}$ . The AV is trained against reconstruction
reward; with target model weights $\theta$ frozen and $h$ its tap
activation, the pair optimizes

| | $\mathcal{J}_{\mathrm{read}}\;=\;\max_{\mathrm{AV},\,\mathrm{AR}}\;\cos\!\big(\mathrm{AR}(\mathrm{AV}(h)),\,h\big),$
| | (1)

and the reconstruction quality of a produced explanation is treated as its
faithfulness test (Figure 1a). Fraser-Taliente et al. (2026) are explicit about this. They present rising
reconstruction as tracking explanation informativeness, and warn that
nothing in the objective forces faithfulness. But that
score is still the number these NLAs report, and the main criterion their users apply. We ask how that score relates to the
individual claims of each explanation. We measure
reconstruction with a centered cosine normalized to the floor. Let $\mathrm{floor}$ be the mean cosine between
reconstructions and mismatched activations (chance level). Then
$\tilde{r}=(\cos(\hat{h},h)-\mathrm{floor})/(1-\mathrm{floor})$ :
0 at chance, 1 at perfect reconstruction. For the released NLA we use the Qwen-2.5-7B layer-20 AV/AR pair (Qwen Team 2025).

The normalization matters for comparisons across settings. Raw cosine
similarities between high-dimensional activations are not centered at zero,
and their typical values depend on the layer, the model, and the anisotropy of
the residual stream. Scores expressed against a mismatched-activation floor
are comparable across these conditions, and a value of zero has a clear
interpretation: the explanation carries no more information about its own
activation than about an arbitrary one.

Grounding. For a claim $c$ in $z$ , let $z_{\neg c}$ be $z$ with $c$
alone minimally flipped (a minimal-pair counterfactual edit, which we call a flip). The claim’s grounding is the reconstruction drop

| | $\Delta\tilde{r}(c)=\tilde{r}(z)-\tilde{r}(z_{\neg c}),$
| | (2)

and $c$ is grounded when $\Delta\tilde{r}(c)\geq\tau$ for a threshold $\tau$ .
Grounding here is the sensitivity of the reconstruction to a claim flip.
It is a property of the reconstructor's reading of the explanation, and we
keep it conceptually separate from any statement about how the target model
itself processes the corresponding content. We check each edit for validity. An edit that changes more than its target claim can inflate apparent grounding severalfold (Appendix A). Crossing
grounding with truth gives four cases. A
claim is grounded or not, and true of the source or not. We
pay particular attention to the case where wording is grounded but false. Here the
reconstruction depends on the wording, although its stated content is false. When
such wording is a convention specific to the co-trained pair (shown by the
swap to an independent evaluator, §3.2), we call it a co-adapted private code. These
labels are operational; no intentional stance is implied. Let $\tilde{r}_{\mathrm{co}}$ and
$\tilde{r}_{\mathrm{ind}}$ be the scores under the co-trained and an independent
reconstructor. The score’s evaluator gap is then
$\tilde{r}_{\mathrm{co}}-\tilde{r}_{\mathrm{ind}}$ .

The four cases have distinct readings. A claim that is grounded and true is
the ideal: the reconstruction depends on it and it correctly describes the
source. A claim that is true but ungrounded is correct but contributes nothing
the reconstructor uses, perhaps because the same information is carried
redundantly elsewhere in the explanation. A claim that is false and ungrounded
is a confabulation the score neither rewards nor punishes. A claim that is
grounded but false is the most informative case for an auditor, since it
indicates that the reconstruction relies on wording whose literal content
does not match the source.

Terms. The target model’s activation is read at a chosen
layer and position, the tap. An activation can be read by the reconstructor AR or by a probe, a freshly fitted
linear decoder (Alain and Bengio 2017; Belinkov 2022). Gist is
the input’s overall meaning, as opposed to its specific facts. Content is
designated when an auxiliary predictor is co-trained to predict it
(§5). Content is decodable
when a freshly fitted linear probe can read it. Faithfulness in this paper is always claim-level. We judge each individual claim in an
explanation as true of the activation and grounded in it, rather than judging the explanation as a whole. We do not use
faithfulness to mean whether explanations describe the model’s downstream computation, or grounding to mean grounding in the world.

#### Settings.

We work in three settings. The first is a released
Qwen-2.5-7B layer-20 NLA on in-distribution web text ( $n{=}1{,}517$ audited
claims). The second is a sandbox of two synthetic scenarios, a story and a marketplace,
each built by filling the slots of a fixed template, so that the true content of every activation is known exactly and computable without a judge; here the tap position fixes what the activation can hold (retained, faded, or unread slots). The third is
continued pretraining of Pythia-160M (Biderman et al. 2023) with self-supervised heads, where tax
is held-out language-modeling loss minus a shared control. Full protocols, scenario
grammars, seeds, and hyperparameters are in Appendices D and K.

The three settings play complementary roles. The released NLA is the object
of practical interest: it is the kind of system practitioners actually
deploy, but its inputs are natural text and the truth of its claims can only
be judged approximately. The sandbox reverses this trade-off. Its inputs are
artificial, but every claim has an exact truth value, and the tap position
determines in advance which content the activation could possibly contain.
The Pythia setting sits between the two: inputs are natural text drawn from a
standard pretraining corpus, while the targets used to supervise and audit are
simple functions of the text, such as which content words occurred in a
trailing window, so their truth can be computed exactly without a judge.

## 3 Auditing Reconstruction-Scored Explanations

Auditing an explanation at the level of its claims requires three
ingredients: a way to identify the claims an explanation makes, a way to
measure how much the reconstruction depends on each one, and a way to decide
whether each claim is true. The three settings supply these ingredients in
different ways. On the released NLA, claims are identified and flipped by a
judge, and truth is assessed against the input passage. In the sandbox, claims
are parsed by exact scan over closed vocabularies, flips are same-type slot
substitutions, and truth is read off the generating tuple. This section
describes both audits and the controls each requires.

### 3.1 Counterfactual Audit of a Released Verbalizer

The audit of the released NLA proceeds explanation by explanation. For each
explanation, a judge model lists the specific claims an LLM reader would find
salient: named entities, quantities, distinctive attributes, and similar
concrete assertions, as opposed to generic statements about topic or register.
For each listed claim, the judge produces a minimal-pair edit that flips that
claim alone to a plausible alternative. The edited explanation is then scored
by the frozen reconstructor, and the drop in $\tilde{r}$ defines the claim's
grounding (Eq. 2). Grounded fractions are reported at three thresholds,
$\tau=0.02$ / $0.05$ / $0.10$ , so that conclusions do not hinge on a single
cutoff.

Two properties of the instrument shape how its output should be read. First,
the flip test has limited sensitivity. A reconstructor may represent a
specific fact only weakly in its output, so a flip can leave the score nearly
unchanged even when the fact is encoded. Grounded fractions are therefore best
interpreted as lower bounds. A useful sanity check appends a topic known to be
encoded and re-ranks candidate topics by score, which indicates how much
encoded content the instrument recovers raw. Second, the edits themselves are a
source of error: a judge that rewrites surrounding material can create
spurious drops. We address this with per-edit validity filtering (Appendix A).

The flip audit is complemented by transforms applied to the whole
explanation. Paraphrasing, synonym substitution, function-word masking, word
shuffling, and content-word masking each remove a different kind of
information while leaving others intact. The profile of scores across these
transforms indicates whether the reconstructor reads the explanation at the
level of meaning or of surface form. A reconstructor that decodes meaning
should be insensitive to rewording and sensitive to the removal of content;
one that decodes a surface-form convention should show the opposite pattern.
The profile is also a useful complement to the per-claim flips, since a
reconstructor that relies on overall meaning may assign little weight to any
single specific claim. The protocols for both kinds of control, together with
bootstrap intervals and a noise floor estimated from flips that carry no
grounding signal, are described in Appendix E.

A further question is where in the network the content corresponding to a
claim resides. The audit reads a single layer, but content absent from a
reconstruction-style readout at that layer might be present elsewhere, or
might be visible to a different kind of reader. We therefore compare the
model's own output head (a logit lens) with a generic ridge probe of matched
capacity across a range of layers. This comparison speaks to whether an
explanation's omissions reflect the information available at the tap or the
particular readout being used.

One could also try to move the verbalizer toward producing grounded claims,
for instance by rejection sampling or by policy-gradient training against a
grounding reward scored at the clause level. Any such approach must be
evaluated with an instrument independent of its training reward, since a
policy can raise a clause-level proxy by restructuring sentences rather than
by changing the claims they make. The independent claim-level audit is
designed for exactly this purpose. Because the released setting provides only
approximate truth, we turn next to a setting where every quantity is exact.

### 3.2 Audit Under Synthetic Ground Truth

The sandbox makes every quantity in the grounding–truth cross exact. Each
story is generated from a tuple of slot values, so a stated slot value is true
if and only if it matches the tuple. Each slot type has a fixed vocabulary, so
a flip is a substitution of one vocabulary item for another of the same type,
and no judge is involved. And because the tap is read at a known position,
each slot falls into one of three classes: retained (mentioned before the tap
and reused afterward, so the target model has reason to carry it), faded
(mentioned before the tap only), and unread (mentioned only after the tap, so
the tap activation provably cannot contain it). The unread slots serve as an
impossibility control: any claim about them that the reconstruction depends on
cannot reflect information in the activation.

Within this setting the comparison of grounding and truth acts as a detector.
A claim about a retained or faded slot that is grounded and true reflects
content the verbalizer has conveyed. A claim about an unread slot that is
grounded can only reflect wording the reconstructor has learned to rely on,
since its content cannot be in the activation. More generally, wording that is
grounded but false marks a candidate private code, and codes can in principle
occupy several slots at once. When the reconstructor relies on wording
regardless of whether its content is true or even possible, the explanation is
functioning less as a description of the activation and more as a channel
between the two networks.

The swap to an independent evaluator determines whether such a channel is
private to the co-trained pair. The independent evaluator is a reconstructor
trained without exposure to the audited pair's outputs. If grounding on
suspect slots reflects a convention between the pair, it should fall under
the independent evaluator. The diagnostic that separates this from evaluator
weakness is the behavior of true claims: an evaluator that is merely worse
would lose grounding on true claims as well, whereas a convention-specific
channel would leave true-claim grounding intact while removing grounding on
the conventional wording. We strengthen the test at the phrasing level by
training a further evaluator on a disjoint paraphrase family, with different
frames and slot order, sharing only the slot words. Agreement between the two
independent evaluators indicates that the result does not depend on any
particular template.

The sandbox also separates two distinct reasons a verbalizer might fail to
state content truly. A storage gap arises when content is absent from the
activation, as for unread slots. A readout gap arises when content is present,
in the sense that a fresh probe can decode it from the target model, but the
verbalizer does not convey it. Comparing per-slot decodability, measured by
fresh probes on the target model, with per-slot truth rates of the verbalizer
distinguishes the two. This distinction carries over directly to the
discussion of RECAP below, where the target model is trained so that the
activation holds designated content and the question becomes whether a
verbalizer conveys it.

## 4 Representation Collapse and Probe Drift

Before introducing RECAP we discuss two mechanisms that any intervention
involving probes or reconstructions of a model under training must contend
with. Both are familiar from the representation-learning literature, and both
inform the design choices of §5.

The first is representation collapse. A tempting objective on the target side
would move activations toward their own reconstruction, so that the
reconstruction pipeline and the model's computation come to agree. Objectives
of this self-referential kind are known to admit degenerate solutions. In
non-contrastive self-supervised learning, a network trained to make two views
of an input agree can satisfy the objective by discarding information, and
the literature has analyzed the architectural and optimization ingredients
that prevent this (Chen and He 2021; Tian et al. 2021). An analogous concern
applies here. A reconstruction is a lossy projection of the state, and
increasing similarity between a state and its reconstruction can be achieved
by reducing variation the reconstruction does not capture. Whether this
actually removes information, rather than merely rotating it into a subspace
a particular reader cannot see, can only be determined by refitting fresh
probes after training, not by reusing readers fitted beforehand.

The second is representation drift during continued training. A probe fitted
to a model at one checkpoint reads a particular linear direction. As training
continues, the model may re-express the same information in a different
basis, so the probe's accuracy can decline even if nothing has been lost.
Networks are known to learn representations that are equivalent up to a
transformation (Lenc and Vedaldi 2015; Kornblith et al. 2019; Moschella et al. 2023),
and the natural repair for drift of this kind is a map fitted on paired
activations, which requires no labels. The expressiveness of the map needed
indicates the nature of the change: a rotation suffices if the
representation has merely been re-oriented, whereas a non-orthogonal map of
some rank is needed if its geometry has changed. Duan (2026) concurrently
studies drift and realignment of this kind on 2B-parameter and 7B-parameter
models.

The two mechanisms call for different responses. Drift is a property of the
reader: the information is present, and the reader must be recalibrated.
Collapse is a property of the representation: the information is gone, and no
recalibration recovers it. Distinguishing them requires the same tool in both
cases, namely fitting fresh probes after training and comparing them with
stale ones, and, where stale probes fail, testing whether a label-free map
restores them.

This distinction has a practical consequence for monitoring. Probe-based
monitoring of a model that is still training should include an explicit
recalibration procedure, and evaluations of any method that changes the
target model should rely on probes fitted after training rather than on
readers carried forward from earlier checkpoints. A related observation
follows from representational equivalence: if representations of different
models differ by an affine map, adapter-based transfer of probes across models
is a natural avenue to explore (Zhao et al. 2026).

## 5 The RECAP Objective

### 5.1 Method

RECAP (Readable Encodings via Co-trained Auxiliary Predictors) adds
linear auxiliary predictors (heads) during training of the target model, so that designated content stays decodable from
selected hidden states. Each head reads the hidden state at the tap layer and predicts an
external target, namely slot values in the sandbox or self-supervised text functions at
scale. We then add the head loss to the language-modeling loss. With head
parameters $\phi$ and external targets $y$ ,

| | $\mathcal{J}_{\mathrm{model}}\;=\;\min_{\theta,\,\phi}\;\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{LM}}(\theta)\;+\;w\,\mathcal{L}_{\phi}\big(h(\theta),\,y\big),$
| | (3)

Here $w$ weights the head loss against the language-modeling loss. $\mathcal{L}_{\phi}$ is a class-balanced binary cross-entropy for whether each content word is present, plus a cross-entropy for which token it is. Balancing weights positives by the inverse of their base rate, so that rare targets are not dominated by the abundant negative class.

Eq. 3 and Eq. 1 act on different parameters.
$\mathcal{J}_{\mathrm{read}}$ optimizes the verbalizer and reconstructor against a frozen
model’s activations and never touches $\theta$ . In contrast,
$\mathcal{J}_{\mathrm{model}}$ trains $\theta$ itself, adding a term to the
language-modeling loss for ground truth that downstream readers may wish to recover.
The two objectives are not mutually exclusive: a verbalizer and reconstructor
can be trained with Eq. 1 on activations from a model trained with Eq. 3,
which is how fresh NLAs are fit in our experiments.

The choice of targets determines what RECAP designates. In the sandbox, the
natural targets are the slot values that precede the tap, since these are the
facts a verbalizer might be asked to state. At scale there are no slots, so we
use self-supervised functions of the text: whether each of the $K$ most
frequent content words occurred in a trailing window, and which token occurred
a fixed number of positions back. These targets have three useful properties.
They are computable exactly from the input, so no labeling is required. They
are external to the model, so the objective does not refer to the model's own
outputs or reconstructions. And they correspond directly to claims an
explanation might make, so the same functions can be used to judge the truth
of a verbalizer's statements.

Heads that co-train with the model might in principle co-adapt with it, so
throughout we report decodability as measured by independently fitted probes
rather than by the heads. Probes are fit on held-out data after training,
using the same recipe for RECAP and control models.
RECAP is decodability supervision in the deep-supervision lineage
(Lee et al. 2015; Szegedy et al. 2015). In classical deep supervision,
auxiliary heads on intermediate layers predict the task label to improve
gradient flow and regularize training; here the auxiliary target is content
the practitioner wishes to remain linearly accessible, which need not coincide
with the training task. RECAP also differs from concept bottlenecks, which
route all information through named concepts: the heads read the hidden state
without constraining what else it carries.

### 5.2 Sandbox Results

In the sandbox, RECAP target models are trained from scratch with heads on
the layer-4 tap predicting the values of the pre-tap slots. Control target
models are trained with the language-modeling loss alone on the same data
with the same seeds. Both kinds of model are then treated identically by the
rest of the pipeline. Fresh probes are fit on held-out taps to measure
per-slot decodability. Fresh NLAs are trained with the same recipe,
including a cold-start SFT on gold descriptions and alternating rounds of
reconstructor fitting and rejection sampling against reconstruction reward.
Each NLA is audited with the comparison of grounding and truth under its
co-trained reconstructor and under an independent evaluator.

This design makes the target model the only variable that differs between
conditions. Because the NLA recipe, the gold descriptions used for the
cold start, the audit vocabulary, and the evaluators are shared, any
difference between conditions in the audited truth or grounding of a slot can
be attributed to the activations the NLA was trained on rather than to the
verbalizer's training.

The unread slots play a particular role here. Their values never appear before
the tap, so no training objective can make them decodable from it. Heads for
these slots are not part of the RECAP objective, and fresh probes for them
provide a check that the probing procedure does not report spurious
decodability. Claims about unread slots likewise provide a check on the
verbalizer: a well-behaved verbalizer should either abstain on them or state
them without grounding.

Several further variants extend the basic design. Partial designation
supervises only one or two of the three pre-tap slots, so that designated and
undesignated content can be compared within the same model. The language-modeling
cost of designation is measured as held-out loss relative to the control. The
marketplace scenario, with its variable tap position and differently sized
vocabularies, tests whether conclusions drawn from the story scenario depend
on its particular structure. Seeds and scenario parameters are listed in
Appendix K.
