### 5.3 Scaling to Pythia-160M

At scale, RECAP is applied during continued pretraining of Pythia-160M, following
the setup of §2.1. Targets are self-supervised from the text: presence of each of
the top- $K$ content words in a trailing 64-token window, and identity of the
token eight positions back among the top- $K$ content vocabulary. Heads are
linear on the layer-6 hidden state. The configurations of interest vary the
number of targets $K$ , the auxiliary weight $w$ , and whether the presence loss
is naive or class-balanced.

Class balance becomes the central design issue as $K$ grows. With many rare
targets, a presence classifier can achieve low training loss by predicting
"absent" almost everywhere, without discriminating anything. This is precisely
the kind of failure that a head's own loss cannot reveal and that independently
fitted probes are designed to expose. We therefore adopt a design rule for
targets: a target is acceptable only if its loss cannot be minimized without
genuine discrimination. The class-balanced variant implements this rule for
presence targets by weighting positives by the inverse window base rate, and the
identity target satisfies it naturally because cross-entropy over many classes
rewards discrimination directly.

The tax is measured as held-out language-modeling loss minus a shared control,
on 20M held-out tokens, with paired differences across seeds where available.
Fresh probes are closed-form ridge per rank bucket at fixed regularization,
evaluated on disjoint held-out blocks, and a never-designated rank bucket is
included in every run as a control for spillover. Robustness factors include
head capacity (linear versus MLP) and tap layer (6 versus 9). Appendix I
indexes the full set of factors with the values tested.

### 5.4 Verbalizer Audit at Scale

At scale, the question of whether decodability reaches a fresh verbalizer can
be posed with exact truth, because the targets are defined from the text. We
train an AV/AR pair on Pythia-160M taps with the structure of the released
recipe and audit its explanations against ground truth computed from the text:
a stated context word is true if and only if it occurs in the trailing 64-token
window. Grounding flips swap a stated word for another top-64 vocabulary word.
The audit reports truth, grounding at several thresholds, recall on present
words, and the grounded-minus-true gap, for a RECAP target model and a matched
control, with tap-clustered bootstrap intervals (Appendix J).

Two comparisons are central to interpreting such an audit. The first compares
truth with recall: a verbalizer can raise its truth rate by stating fewer words,
so truth must be read alongside recall on the shared set of present words. The
second compares the verbalizer's generated precision–recall behavior with the
precision–recall curve of a fresh probe on the same tap. This comparison
separates decodability, the property that a linear reader can recover content,
from verbalizability, the property that a generator states it in text. The two
need not coincide, and the readout gap of §3.2 is the sandbox analogue of their
difference.

The reader side admits many redesigns that can be explored in this comparison:
standardized injection across multiple tokens, MLP capacity in the adapter, a
presence head trained at the decode point on whether each word occurred in the
window (an external fact, not a learned monitor), larger reconstructors,
reconstruction optimization, direct truth rewards, and explicit negative
supervision. A matched control evaluated under the identical decode-point head
is essential, so that any decodable content at the decode point can be
attributed to the target model rather than to the head.

A final consideration is persistence. Decodability trained in by auxiliary heads
may or may not survive subsequent training that omits them, as real
post-training pipelines typically do. Appendix C describes a protocol that
fine-tunes RECAP and control checkpoints without heads, re-probes at regular
snapshots with freshly fitted probes, and compares continuous, intermittent, and
absent head supervision.

## 6 Probe-Based Monitoring

A natural use of decodable content is monitoring. We specify a simple monitor
for the sandbox. Fresh probes, one per slot, read the tap activation while the
verbalizer states slot values. Any claim that a confident probe ( $p{>}0.9$ )
contradicts is flagged as a candidate discrepancy, and claims on which the probe
is not confident are abstained. Exact ground truth then scores every decision
(full protocol in Appendix B).

Three quantities summarize such a monitor. Precision is the fraction of flags
that are genuinely false claims. Recall is the fraction of false claims flagged.
Coverage is the fraction of claims on which the monitor does not abstain, that
is, the fraction it can verify against internals at all. In the sandbox, these
quantities are reported separately for pre-tap claims, which concern content
the activation can hold, and post-tap claims, which concern content the
activation provably lacks. Post-tap claims should be abstained on by any sound
activation monitor, since reading an activation cannot adjudicate content it
does not contain. Catching confabulations about such content is the job of the
comparison of grounding and truth (§3); the two tools partition the audit.

At scale, where false claims about a given word are rare, per-claim coverage is
not an informative summary. We therefore specify the monitor in ranking terms: a
fresh presence probe scores each stated word, and the monitor is evaluated by the
AUC with which it ranks true claims above false ones, together with the
precision and recall of a flag at a fixed operating point. In this formulation,
the verbalizer proposes and the probe verifies. The appropriate division of
labor between the two depends on how decodability and verbalizability compare at
the tap, which is exactly what §5.4 is designed to measure.

#### Surviving a score-gaming adversary.

Any monitor intended for oversight should be evaluated against an adversary.
The threat model we specify is report-space: the adversary edits the explanation
text but cannot alter the activation. Starting from an honest explanation, the
adversary edits a true stated word into an absent one, choosing among candidates
according to rungs of increasing strength: a random absent word, the
embedding-nearest absent word, and the absent word that maximizes the recomputed
reconstruction score (full protocol in Appendix F). The last rung directly tests
whether a deployment that trusted the reconstruction score could be fooled,
because it selects the lie the score is least able to penalize.

Two quantities are measured at each rung. The first is the residual lie penalty
under the reconstruction score: how much the score falls when a true word is
replaced by the chosen lie, relative to a random lie. The second is the
monitor's AUC and flag recall when an external presence probe, trained on ground
truth and never on verbalizer outputs, scores the edited explanation. A
probe-aware rung, which assumes the private monitor leaks and selects lies the
probe is most likely to mistake for present, is included as a worst-case bound
outside the threat model. Activation-level attacks (Bailey et al. 2024), which
move the activation itself, are out of scope.

Two controls guard against circularity. First, the flag threshold is calibrated
on a disjoint split rather than on the evaluation set, so the operating point
cannot be inflated by evaluation-time tuning. Second, the monitor is also
evaluated on a held-out band of words (ranked 64–128) that no head ever
supervised. Because the monitor probes the same presence predicate that RECAP
supervises, the held-out band is the right test of whether any monitoring
behavior extends beyond designated content or is confined to it (band protocol in
Appendix F).

## 7 Related Work

#### Activation verbalization and its critiques.

Beyond the NLA recipe (§2) (Fraser-Taliente et al. 2026), a fast-growing family
improves the reader. Examples include supervised question-answering decoders
(Pan et al. 2026), general-purpose activation explainers
(Karvonen et al. 2025; Bauer et al. 2026), interpreter assistants
(Huang et al. 2025), readouts that need no training (Ghandeharioun et al. 2024), and
cross-model adapters (Zhao et al. 2026). Sparse autoencoders are the unsupervised reader family
(Huben et al. 2024). These approaches differ in how they supervise the reader,
in whether they require labeled data, and in the form of the readout, but they
share the assumption that the target model is a fixed object to be interpreted.
Model-produced explanations can pass plausibility checks without faithfulness
in chain-of-thought (Turpin et al. 2023; Lanham et al. 2023). Causal
tests of neuron explanations found high error and little
efficacy (Huang et al. 2023). Counterfactual faithfulness tests
prefigure our flip protocol (Atanasova et al. 2023). Existing critiques of verbalization are
benchmark-level; for example, many tasks are solvable without the target's internals
(Li et al. 2025). Our audit is complementary: it operates per claim and
counterfactually on the reconstruction score itself, and our intervention
places supervision on the target model rather than on the reader.

The broader literature on explanation evaluation offers useful vocabulary.
Work on faithfulness of feature attributions distinguishes plausibility, the
degree to which an explanation convinces a human, from faithfulness, the degree
to which it reflects the model's reasoning, and has repeatedly found that the two
can diverge. Counterfactual and erasure-based tests, which remove or alter parts
of an input or explanation and measure the effect, are the standard instruments
for faithfulness in that literature, and our flip protocol is a direct
adaptation of them to explanations of activations. The distinction we draw
between claim-level and explanation-level evaluation parallels the distinction
between local and global evaluation in attribution work.

#### Scalable oversight.

Reconstruction scoring sits within scalable oversight, which substitutes cheap
automatic signals for costly human judgment of model behavior and internals
(Amodei et al. 2016; Bowman and others 2022). A parallel line, AI control,
designs protocols that remain safe even when the model tries to subvert them
(Greenblatt et al. 2024). Both lines emphasize that automatic signals must be
evaluated against adversaries, not only on benign data, since an optimizer with
access to a signal may find ways to satisfy it that its designers did not
intend (Baker et al. 2025). Our monitoring protocol and adversary ladder are
designed with this lesson in mind. Interpretability-based oversight in
particular is often motivated by the hope that internal signals are harder to
game than behavioral ones; evaluating that hope requires specifying which
internal signal, read by which reader, under which threat model.

#### Steganography in learned channels.

Objectives in the reconstruction family have hidden information in their channels
since CycleGAN (Chu et al. 2017). In LLMs, encoded reasoning arises in
chain-of-thought under optimization pressure (Roger and Greenblatt 2023) and
generalizes under process supervision (Skaf and others 2025). Misspecified
incentives yield steganographic collusion
(Mathew et al. 2025), tool use widens the channel (Rippin et al. 2026),
and probing internals detects collusion (Rose et al. 2026).
Optimization can obfuscate activations against latent monitors
(Bailey et al. 2024), and training against a chain-of-thought monitor yields
obfuscated reward hacking rather than honesty (Baker et al. 2025).
In these settings channels are induced by incentives, process supervision, or an
adversary. The co-adapted private codes defined in §2.1 are a related notion
within the interpretability pipeline, and the grounding–truth cross and
evaluator swap are instruments for looking for them in a setting where no
steganography objective or communication reward is present. A recurring
prescription in this literature is not to optimize directly on the monitor;
target-side supervision against external ground truth is one way of adding
supervision that does not reward fooling the probe or the reconstructor.

#### Representation drift, stitching, and monitor staleness.

Networks learn equivalent representations up to a transformation
(Lenc and Vedaldi 2015; Kornblith et al. 2019; Moschella et al. 2023); affine maps
transfer features across language models (Chen et al. 2025);
pretraining dynamics are stable across seeds (van der Wal et al. 2025); tuned
lenses are affine readers whose staleness is a practical concern
(Belrose et al. 2023). Concurrently, Duan (2026) study
staleness and its repair without labels on 2B- and 7B-parameter models.
Retraining probes also restores detectability after fine-tuning that is aware of
the probe (Wehner and Fritz 2025). Our contribution here is conceptual and
methodological: the separation between drift, which a label-free affine map can
diagnose, and collapse, which only freshly retrained probes can diagnose, and a
decomposition of realignment maps by expressiveness class (§4, Appendix H).

#### Deep supervision and intrinsic interpretability.

Auxiliary heads on hidden layers are deep supervision
(Lee et al. 2015; Szegedy et al. 2015); there the target is the task
label; our target is external content to keep decodable. Concept bottlenecks route all information flow through named concepts
(Koh et al. 2020; Sun et al. 2025), concept whitening constrains the geometry
(Chen et al. 2020), codebook features discretize the representation
(Tamkin et al. 2023), and gradient routing localizes computation
(Cloud et al. 2024); RECAP adds linear heads without constraining
flow. Supervision on the explanation side can track behavioral change
(Guo et al. 2026); ours acts on the target model. The general tradeoff in
intrinsic interpretability is between how strongly the representation is
constrained and how much task performance is preserved; RECAP occupies the
lightly constrained end of that spectrum, which is why the tax measurement of
§5.3 is a necessary part of its evaluation.

## 8 Discussion and Limitations

Implications for oversight. Scoring explanations by reconstruction is a form
of scalable oversight, a cheap automatic signal meant to stand in for expensive
human checking of a model's internals. As with any such signal, its value for
oversight depends on what it measures at the level that users act on, which for
explanations is the level of individual claims, and on how it behaves under
optimization pressure. The instruments in this paper are meant to make both
questions answerable: the flip audit and transform battery for what the score
responds to, the grounding–truth cross and evaluator swap for distinguishing
genuine dependence from pair-specific convention, and the adversary ladder for
behavior under pressure. Placing supervision on the target model is one design
response to these questions, and its scope is necessarily limited to the
content that is designated; RECAP is at most a component of oversight, not a
solution to it.

The perspective of supervising the target model has broader appeal. Much of
interpretability treats the model as a natural object to be studied as found.
Yet models are artifacts whose training objectives are chosen by their
developers, and there is no principled reason that interpretability
considerations should enter only after training. Deep supervision, concept
bottlenecks, and related methods show that intermediate representations can be
shaped at modest cost. If a developer knows in advance which content an
oversight process will need to inspect, training that content to remain
readable is a natural design option, and its costs and benefits deserve
systematic measurement.

Scope and limitations. The settings considered here comprise a synthetic
sandbox, one released NLA (Qwen-2.5-7B), and continued pretraining of one small
model (Pythia-160M), mostly at single seeds; frontier scale is untested. Four
limitations constrain the conclusions one can draw from this program. First,
the sandbox and scale audits cover only closed-vocabulary claims parsed from a
template, and the monitor covers only designated content; open-ended
faithfulness is not addressed. Second, RECAP must be co-trained in rather than
retrofitted onto a frozen model, and it depends on choosing good targets. A
poorly chosen target can report low head loss while decoding nothing, which is
why independently fitted probes are mandatory. Third, decodability is not
verbalizability; a probe and a generator reading the same tap need not convey
the same content, and evaluation must measure both. Fourth, RECAP concerns what
an activation stores, not what the model uses. Designated content can be present
yet behaviorally inert, and a model could route computation around a monitored
subspace (Mahinpei et al. 2021; Margeloiu et al. 2021).

What success would look like. Success for verbalization evaluated by
reconstruction is not simply a higher $\tilde{r}$ . It means explanations whose
specific claims can be verified against the target model, calibrated abstention
where content is absent, and monitors with recalibration protocols for models
that continue to train. Reaching that standard requires instruments that operate
at the level of individual claims, controls that separate reader conventions
from genuine content, and adversarial evaluation of any signal intended for
oversight.

## 9 Conclusion

We have developed a methodology for studying the reconstruction score behind
natural-language activation explanations at the level of individual claims. It
comprises a counterfactual flip audit with per-edit validity controls and a
transform battery; a synthetic sandbox with exact ground truth in which grounding
can be crossed with truth; an independent-evaluator swap for separating
pair-specific conventions from general properties of the text; a conceptual and
diagnostic distinction between representation collapse and probe drift; RECAP,
a training-time objective that co-trains linear heads on external targets with
the target model, with a class-balanced loss design and a strict rule that
decodability is measured by independently fitted probes; and a probe-based
monitoring protocol with a report-space adversary ladder and anti-circularity
controls. The common thread is that claims about what an explanation conveys,
and about what a model's activations contain, should be checked by instruments
independent of the components being evaluated. For oversight of increasingly
capable models, explanations that can be checked against internals offer a
firmer basis for trust than explanations that must be taken on faith, and the
instruments described here are intended to make that distinction measurable.

## Appendix A Edit Validity for Minimal-Pair Flips

Grounding measurements are only as good as the edits that produce them. An
edit is valid if it flips exactly one claim and changes nothing else.
We audited two edit generators on the released NLA: a closed-model judge
produced valid edits 68.4% of the time, while the open judge used throughout
the paper (Gemma-4-12B, pinned revision, temperature 0) produced valid
edits 99.3% of the time. The invalid edits were predominantly
oversized: they rewrote surrounding material along with the target
claim, and the extra damage inflated apparent grounding roughly sevenfold.
All grounded fractions in the audit protocol therefore use the open judge with
per-edit validity filtering, and the audit artifacts persist per-claim
reconstruction deltas. The same head-to-head also measured a judge-free
mask-and-rescore signal against the flip instrument (agreement AUC 0.997 under
the validated judge), used in Appendix G.

Two lessons generalize. First, edit validity should be checked per edit rather
than assumed from the generator's instructions, because even capable judges
frequently over-edit when asked for a minimal change. Second, the direction of
the bias from invalid edits is predictable: an edit that changes more than its
target removes more information from the explanation, so it can only inflate
the reconstruction drop. Unfiltered flip audits therefore overstate grounding,
and any reported grounded fraction should state its validity filter.

## Appendix B Safety Experiment 1: The Discrepancy Detector

#### Question.

If an auditor can read a target model's activation with
probes and can also read what the verbalizer says, disagreements
between the two are candidate lies. How should such a detector be built and
scored, and what properties of the target model govern how useful it can be?

#### Protocol.

Sandbox, scenario 1, seed 1, 400 held-out taps per
target model.
For each slot type we fit a fresh multinomial logistic probe (linear,
256-dimensional input) on the probe split of taps, reading the slot value
from the tap activation. On evaluation taps, the verbalizer generates an
explanation; the first stated word of each slot type is compared with the
probe's prediction.
A claim is flagged when a probe with confidence above 0.9 disagrees
with the stated word, and abstained when probe confidence is below
threshold. Exact tuple ground truth then scores every decision.
Precision is the fraction of flags that are genuinely false claims; recall is
the fraction of false claims flagged; abstention is the fraction of claims the
probe could not adjudicate at threshold. Each statistic is reported separately
for pre-tap and post-tap claims, for a RECAP target model and a control.

#### Findings.

The detector's structure determines how its outputs should be read. Its
precision depends on probe calibration: a flag is raised only when a confident
probe disagrees with the stated word, so false alarms require confident probe
errors. Its recall and coverage depend on target-model decodability: on slots
too faded for a confident readout, the detector abstains, and false claims in
those slots go uncaught regardless of the detector's design. Post-tap claims
should be fully abstained on any target model, since content the activation
provably lacks cannot be adjudicated by reading the activation; catching those
confabulations is the grounding cross's job. The useful summary is that
verification coverage is bounded by decodability, so comparisons between target
models should focus on coverage of pre-tap content rather than on precision
alone.

#### Caveats.

One scenario, one seed, one threshold (0.9); "decodable"
means linearly readable throughout. The protocol compares only the first stated
word per slot type; explanations that state several values for a slot are
scored on the first.

## Appendix C Safety Experiment 2: Legibility Persistence Under Head-Free
Fine-Tuning

#### Question.

Does decodability trained in by RECAP heads survive later
training that drops the heads, as real post-training pipelines do, and how
should persistence be measured?

#### Protocol.

Starting from a RECAP Pythia-160M checkpoint
( $K{=}64$ , class-balanced presence, $w{=}0.1$ ) and the control checkpoint,
both are fine-tuned with the language-modeling loss only (no heads) on 131M
tokens of a deliberately shifted corpus (FineWeb (Penedo and others 2024), versus the Pile training
distribution). Training uses batch $64\times 1024$ , learning rate $10^{-4}$ , and
2,000 steps, with snapshots at 250/1,000/2,000. Every snapshot is re-probed with the
standard fresh-probe pipeline: ridge probes fit and evaluated on disjoint
held-out sequence blocks, so the measurement is immune to reader staleness
by design: probes are refit at each snapshot, never carried forward.
Reported quantities are mean AUC on the two designated rank buckets, 64-class
identity accuracy, and the never-designated bucket in the RECAP run.

#### Findings.

Because probes are refit at every snapshot, any change in readability across
snapshots reflects a change in linear decodability itself, which is strictly
stronger than the frozen-reader staleness of §4: there, information can persist
while a frozen reader fails; here, fresh probes are refit and any loss is a loss
of access. The control run and the never-designated bucket serve as baselines
against which any change specific to designated content can be identified. The
deployment-relevant question is whether decodability is a one-time property
established during training or a running cost that must be maintained, and the
protocol is designed to answer it directly.

#### Follow-up runs.

Two further runs separate the obvious confounds. A head-free fine-tune on unseen
same-distribution data (fresh Pile tokens with no overlap with training,
validation, or probe data) separates the effect of removing the heads from the
effect of corpus shift. A run that applies the head loss every tenth step during
the shifted fine-tune tests whether intermittent supervision at one tenth the
frequency provides protection comparable to continuous supervision. The
original training logs, which record how quickly readability establishes at
$w{=}0.1$ , bear on whether establishing decodability after the fact would be a
quick repair or a substantial training pass.

#### Caveats.

Single seed per run; 2,000 steps; the intermittent
run's own language-modeling tax is not separately measured (the question is
about supervision frequency).

## Appendix E Released-NLA Audit Details

#### Setup.

All released-NLA measurements use the public Qwen-2.5-7B
layer-20 AV/AR pair on in-distribution web text, with greedy decoding and
direction-only reconstruction. Minimal-pair edits come from a pinned-revision
open judge with per-edit validity filtering (Appendix A); every
per-claim reconstruction delta is persisted ( $n{=}1{,}517$ base-NLA claims).
Grounded fractions are reported at $\tau{=}0.02/0.05/0.10$ with bootstrap 95%
intervals. The flip-noise floor is estimated from the empirical null as the
95th percentile of $|\Delta\tilde{r}|$ and the rate of wrong-direction drops,
and thresholds are chosen to sit above it. A decodability ceiling is estimated
with ridge probes on single-position residual vectors across layers 16–27 and
across prefix positions, and on mean-pooled vectors for gist. These ceiling
measurements bound reconstruction-style readouts only; the model's own
unembedding may see late-layer specifics in next-token form, which the
late-layer inventory below addresses.

#### Instrument validity controls.

Three controls validate the audit
instrument itself (598 in-distribution passages, positions ${\geq}50$ ).
Floor: reconstructions scored against mismatched activations give a
mean centered cosine of $-0.001$ , so the floor normalization in $\tilde{r}$
is calibrated and mismatched pairs collapse to chance. Input echo:
the explanation's reconstruction is compared with reconstructions from the raw
input prefix and from a paraphrased prefix, which tests whether the explanation
carries signal beyond restating the input, with the caveat that reconstructor
specialization to explanation-style text can account for part of any
difference. Transform profile: the transform battery of §3.1 records
reconstruction retained under paraphrase, synonym substitution, function-word
masking, word shuffling, and content-word masking, each applied to the
explanation $z$ . Meaning-level decoding and surface-form conventions predict
opposite profiles, so the battery is a direct test between them.

#### Late-layer inventory.

For each audited false claim with a clean
single-token true value ( $n{=}316$ ), the true value is ranked in two readouts per
layer: the model's own logit lens (final norm + unembedding) and a
document-folded ridge probe of matched capacity. Comparing the two across layers
indicates whether any late-layer signal lives in the model's own output basis or
is accessible to a generic trained probe, and therefore whether reading later
layers is a promising lever for reconstruction-style readers. Hidden states are
indexed by output position (embeddings at 0), so the layer-20 tap is index 21;
the decodability sweep (16–27) uses the same indexing.

#### A control-design lesson.

The ceiling probe's negative control
(scoring probes against a different document's activation) initially
shifted by one row and landed above chance at 0.163, because adjacent rows
are often two positions of the same document and encode the same
specifics; shifting by half the dataset restored exact chance. We report it
because near-duplicate controls are an easy way for audits of this kind to
flatter themselves.

## Appendix F Adversarial Monitor: the Lie-Ladder

#### Question.

If a deployment trusted the reconstruction score $\tilde{r}$
as a truth signal, could a report-space adversary who edits the explanation to
maximize $\tilde{r}$ slip a false claim past it, and how should an
activation-probe monitor be evaluated against that adversary?

#### Protocol.

RECAP and control Pythia-160M ( $K{=}64$ balanced). On
held-out taps we take the honest verbalizer generation and, for each stated word,
edit it into an absent top-64 word (a true-to-absent lie). We then recompute
$\tilde{r}$ on the edited text through the real reconstructor and score the lie with the
external-truth presence probe (trained on train taps, never on verbalizer
outputs). Adversary rungs of increasing strength: L1 a random
absent word; L2 the embedding-nearest absent word; L3 the per-claim
$\arg\max$ - $\tilde{r}$ absent word over all candidates (the strongest
$\tilde{r}$ -gaming lie in the edit family); and, as a worst-case bound outside the
threat model, L4 a probe-aware adversary that assumes the private monitor leaks
and, among absent lies keeping $\tilde{r}$ within $0.05$ of honest, picks the one the
probe most mistakes for present. The $0.05$ budget is chosen to be generous
relative to the score cost of pure-score lies, so that L4 is a conservative
bound rather than a tuned tolerance. Decoupled design (positive $=$ any
truly-present word; edit slot $=$ the verbalizer's stated word) so both arms are
well powered: RECAP $n{=}758$ , control $n{=}200$ . Edit-based, no reinforcement
learning.

#### Findings.

The ladder is designed so that each rung isolates one source of adversarial
leverage. The gap between L1 and L3 under $\tilde{r}$ measures how much of the
lie penalty a score-maximizing adversary can suppress, which is the quantity a
deployment trusting $\tilde{r}$ would care about. The monitor's AUC across L1–L3
measures how much the adversary's freedom to choose which absent word to state
costs the monitor; because the probe reads the activation, which the adversary
cannot touch, immunity to score manipulation is structural, and any degradation
across rungs reflects candidate selection. L4 bounds the worst case. Comparing
the RECAP and control arms at each rung separates the contribution of reading a
signal that predates the editable report from the contribution of that signal
being decodable; a probe positioned to read the activation is necessary for
robust monitoring but is not by itself sufficient.

#### Caveats.

Report-space adversaries; a probe-aware report-space
selection adversary is included as a worst-case bound (L4). Activation-level
attacks (probe-aware training of the target, input perturbation), which
move the activation itself rather than selecting which word to state, remain out
of scope. Any residual sensitivity of $\tilde{r}$ to individual lies is an
aggregate effect and should not be assumed usable on a per-instance basis.

#### Anti-circularity: frozen threshold and a held-out band.

Because the
monitor probes the same top-64 presence predicate RECAP supervises, two additions
test whether it merely re-measures the trained margin ( $n{=}2800$ audit taps).
(a) Frozen threshold. The $0.9$ -precision flag threshold is calibrated on a
disjoint split and then applied unchanged to the evaluation split, so the
operating point cannot be inflated by evaluation-time tuning; if no threshold
reaches $0.9$ precision for an arm, its recall is reported as undefined rather
than low. (b) Held-out band. Presence of words ranked 64–128, which the RECAP
heads never supervised, is monitored with the same ladder. Honest-case AUC on
this band leaves headroom for spillover to show, and a Hanley–McNeil standard
error is used to state the gap the comparison is powered to detect.

The band comparison is scoped to linear decodability at this tap, not evidence
about whether the band is represented elsewhere in the model. The frozen
threshold is a disjoint split of the same run, not a temporally held-out
deployment threshold. The band arm is unpaired. Taken together, the two controls
determine whether any monitoring behavior should be attributed to designation
itself, and therefore what scope a monitor built on RECAP could claim.

## Appendix G An API-Free Grounding Signal, and a Selection Null

The flip instrument needs a judge to write one minimal-pair edit per
claim. A cheaper signal needs none: mask the claim's words with a neutral
filler and rescore the explanation with the frozen reconstructor. In the
judge head-to-head of Appendix A, this mask-and-rescore
signal agrees with the flip instrument at AUC 0.997 under the validated
open judge, so per-claim grounding can be monitored at inference with one
extra frozen-reader pass and no judge in the loop. An earlier version of
this experiment also reported filter precisions and a grounded base rate;
those rested on pre-validation flip labels, and the validity audit later found
roughly a third of them contaminated by oversized edits
(Appendix A). We therefore report only the agreement number,
measured under the validated judge, and withdraw the rest. The
contamination is confined to those withdrawn quantities: every number retained
in the paper postdates the validity filter.

#### What inference-time selection does not buy.

Inference-time selection is a natural reader-side diagnostic: draw several
explanations per activation and keep the one an external truth judge prefers.
The selection null is the reference condition in which one of the $N$ samples is
chosen at random, with specificity matched between conditions and an independent
judge used for evaluation so that the selecting judge is not also the grader.
Comparing best-of- $N$ with this null indicates how much faithful explanations
are available in the sample neighborhood of a given verbalizer, which in turn
indicates whether selection or reranking could substitute for changes to
training. We include the protocol ( $N{=}5$ ) because it is cheap to run and
clarifies the ceiling of any reranking-based approach.

## Appendix H Reader Drift and Realignment

Readers matched to a training target model can be tracked across
continued-training checkpoints and across seeds to characterize drift. The
realignment protocol fits an affine map on ${\sim}$ 7,000 paired activations (no
labels) from the new representation to the one on which the reader was fitted,
and evaluates the frozen reader through the map. Decomposing realignment by
expressiveness class (rank-1, rank-4, pure rotation via Procrustes, and
non-orthogonal changes of rank 16–64 up to full affine) across reader pairs (two
cross-seed, one stale) indicates how the representation has moved: whether a
rotation suffices or a non-orthogonal change is needed, and of what rank.
Collapse is distinguished from drift by refitting fresh probes: if they also
fail, no realignment can exist.

## Appendix J Scale Verbalizer Audit Protocol

The scale verbalizer audit (§5.4) uses an AV/AR pair trained with the
released recipe's structure on Pythia-160M taps. Reader: a
0.5B-parameter language model with LoRA adapters (rank 16) and a linear
dimension adapter from the 768-dimensional tap state to the reader's
embedding width, activations injected norm-matched at marked positions.
Training: cold-start SFT on gold descriptions generated from a fixed
template stating the trailing-window content words and the token eight
positions back, then alternating reconstructor fitting and two
rejection-sampling rounds against reconstruction reward. Both conditions use
the same procedure; only the underlying target model (RECAP versus control)
differs. Audit: 400 held-out taps per condition from the probe
region; explanations are template-parsed into stated context words and a
stated token-at- $-8$ . A stated word is true iff it occurs in the
trailing 64-token window (exact, self-supervised, no judge); grounding
flips swap a stated word for another top-64 vocabulary word and measure
$\Delta\tilde{r}$ under the co-trained reconstructor. Intervals are
tap-clustered bootstrap 95% intervals (10,000 resamples of taps with
their claims). The parser emits up to three claims per explanation, so
clustering by tap is the appropriate unit for resampling; unclustered Wilson
intervals are reported alongside for comparison.

One subtlety concerns the offset-8 token. Its truth and grounding are computed
over all taps, but the true offset-8 token is a designated top-64 target only in
a small fraction of taps, while the verbalizer is trained to emit a claim on
every tap. Offset-8 truth is therefore dominated by its base rate and should not
be interpreted as evidence about codes either way.

Figure 5: Decodability versus verbalizability at scale (Pythia-160M, designated
content). The figure overlays the precision–recall curve of a fresh probe
reading the reconstructor's decode-point hidden state (black) with the
reconstruction verbalizer's generated precision–recall curve (green, two
reconstructor seeds) and the control verbalizer (grey), so that the two readouts
of the same content can be compared at matched recall.

#### Robustness to reconstructor strength.

A stronger AV/AR pair (LoRA rank 32, more SFT, reconstructor, and
rejection-sampling rounds) can be trained on the same target models to check
whether audit outcomes depend on reconstructor strength. Because a stronger
verbalizer may also change how many words it states, the comparison should be
made on precision and recall over the shared set of present words, not on truth
rate alone, since a verbalizer that states fewer words can raise its truth rate
through selectivity. Stability across seeds is assessed by repeating the audit
over the three class-balanced RECAP target-model seeds and three control NLA
seeds.

#### Decodability exceeds verbalizability (readout redesign).

The title of this protocol names the hypothesis it is designed to test: that
content decodable from a tap by a linear probe may be only partly conveyed by a
generator reading the same tap. To test it, the verbalizer is placed on the
fitted probe's precision–recall curve, comparing the probe's precision at the
verbalizer's own recall with the verbalizer's generated precision. The reader
is then rebuilt: standardized (not per-sample norm-stripped) injection, six
injected tokens via an MLP adapter, MLP-LoRA, and a decode-point presence head
trained on the exact window-occurrence labels (external truth, never a learned
monitor). The decode-point head measures whether the designated content is
linearly readable from the reader's own last-prompt hidden state, and a matched
control evaluated under the identical head attributes any such content to the
target model rather than the head. A per-word confidence sweep traces the
verbalizer's generative precision–recall curve for comparison with the probe's
(Figure 5). Reader scale (0.5B vs. 3B), RAFT reconstruction reward, a direct
truth reward, injection bandwidth, and explicit negative supervision are the
further reader-side variations in this protocol, each of which bears on whether
any residual difference reflects missing information or a cost of serializing
sparse superposed features by generation.

# Train the Model, Not the Reader: Decodability Supervision for Verifiable
Activation Explanations

Hiskias Dingeto

###### Abstract

Natural-language autoencoders score explanations of hidden activations by
reconstruction: an explanation counts as faithful if the activation can be
regenerated from it. We audit what that score certifies at the level of
individual claims, and find two distinct ways it is passed without claim-level
faithfulness. On a released Qwen-2.5-7B verbalizer, explanations reconstruct
well above chance while as few as ${\sim}2\%$ of their specific claims are ones
the reconstruction depends on. Under exact synthetic ground truth, standard
training consistently develops co-adapted private codes, false wording the
reconstruction depends on. Fixes that leave the target model unchanged do not
help. We contribute two audit protocols (the comparison of grounding and truth,
and the swap to an independent evaluator) and RECAP (Readable Encodings via
Co-trained Auxiliary Predictors), linear heads trained alongside the target
model on designated content. On RECAP-trained sandbox models, fresh verbalizers
state the designated content truly and the codes vanish, at a $+0.001$ -nat
cost. This replicates on a pretrained Pythia-160M under a target-design rule
we identify. The content becomes reliably decodable by a probe, though a fresh
verbalizer conveys it only in part (truth 0.44–0.46 against a near-zero
control). For interpretability, the audit sets a claim-level standard of
evidence for activation explanations. For AI safety, RECAP makes designated
content checkable against probes. On the pretrained model, an independent probe
scores the verbalizer’s true claims above its false ones at AUC 0.96, versus
0.82 without RECAP. When an adversary edits an explanation to maximize the
score while lying, it suppresses about 87% of its lie penalty, yet the RECAP
probe still flags the lies at AUC 0.95, while the control probe falls to 0.51.

## 1 Introduction

Natural-language autoencoders (NLAs) let a model explain its own hidden
states: a verbalizer turns an activation into a text explanation, a
reconstructor turns the explanation back into an activation, and the quality
of the round trip is treated as a test of each explanation’s faithfulness
(Fraser-Taliente et al. 2026). The test is unsupervised and self-checking,
attaching a number to every explanation with no labels or human in the loop.
Released verbalizer/reconstructor pairs exist for several open models, and a
growing family of methods trains activation readers with related objectives
(Pan et al. 2026; Karvonen et al. 2025; Huang et al. 2025).

The reconstruction objective rewards an explanation $z$ for the cosine between
$h$ and $\mathrm{AR}(z)$; it contains no term referring to the truth of the
individual claims in $z$. We measure, per claim and counterfactually, how the
score responds when one claim is replaced by a false alternative, and cross
that sensitivity with exact truth where it is available.

The test is passed in two ways, neither faithful at the claim level. By gist:
on a released Qwen-2.5-7B-based NLA, explanations reconstruct well above
chance, yet our flip audit detects grounding in only ${\sim}2\%$ of their
salient specific claims, a lower bound given the flip test’s low sensitivity.
By codes: in a synthetic sandbox with exact ground truth, co-trained
verbalizer/reconstructor pairs consistently develop private codes, false
wording that the reconstruction depends on (gaps between grounded and true
rates of 0.30–0.80), under standard training in two scenarios. The two natural
training fixes also fail. Minimizing the distance between a hidden state and
its reconstruction removes content a probe could previously read; rewarding the
verbalizer for grounding raises the proxy through sentence restructuring with
no change in claim-level grounding.

The intervention that survives our controls trains the target model, not the
activation reader (Figure 1b): RECAP, linear heads on external targets
co-trained with the model (§5). Fresh NLAs then state the designated content
faithfully in the sandbox under both co-trained and independent evaluators, and
codes are absent. The reconstruction objective on the target side collapses
decodable content, and a frozen probe goes stale under representation drift;
a label-free affine realignment fully reverses the latter.

(Fraser-Taliente et al. 2026): AV maps an activation to text, AR maps it back, and
reconstruction quality is the test; only AV and AR train. The score can stay

(this work) trains the target model. Top: co-trained linear heads keep

an independent fresh probe (not the heads) recovers the content (AUC
0.95) and a fresh verbalizer states it truly.

Our contributions:

•

Claim-level audit. Validity-controlled flips of each salient claim of reconstruction-scored explanations show that a released verbalizer passes the test with largely ungrounded specific claims; the score survives paraphrase and collapses under content-word masking.

•

Private codes. Co-trained verbalizer/reconstructor pairs develop private codes in a sandbox with exact ground truth, detected and quantified by the grounding–truth cross and the independent-evaluator swap.

•

RECAP. Target-model training with co-trained linear heads on external targets restores claim-level faithfulness in the sandbox and transfers to Pythia-160M, where designated content becomes probe-decodable at a measured cost; target-side reconstruction pull collapses decodable content and frozen probes go stale under drift.

•

Adversarial monitor. A score-gaming adversary that edits the explanation suppresses ${\sim}87\%$ of its lie penalty on both models, yet RECAP’s activation probe still flags the lies (AUC $0.95$ ) while the control probe falls to $0.51$ .

## 2 Preliminaries and Experimental Setup

### 2.1 The Reconstruction Test and Audit Protocols

A natural-language autoencoder (NLA) pairs an activation verbalizer
(AV), which generates a text explanation $z$ of a hidden activation $h$ , with
an activation reconstructor (AR), which maps $z$ back to an estimate
$\hat{h}$ . The AV is trained against reconstruction
reward; with target model weights $\theta$ frozen and $h$ its tap
activation, the pair optimizes

| | $\mathcal{J}_{\mathrm{read}}\;=\;\max_{\mathrm{AV},\,\mathrm{AR}}\;\cos\!\big(\mathrm{AR}(\mathrm{AV}(h)),\,h\big),$
| | (1)

and the reconstruction quality of a produced explanation is treated as its
faithfulness test (Figure 1a). Fraser-Taliente et al. (2026) present rising
reconstruction as tracking explanation informativeness and note that nothing in
the objective forces faithfulness; the score nonetheless remains the number
these NLAs report and the main criterion their users apply. We measure
reconstruction with a centered cosine normalized to the floor, the mean cosine
between reconstructions and mismatched activations:
$\tilde{r}=(\cos(\hat{h},h)-\mathrm{floor})/(1-\mathrm{floor})$ .
For the released NLA we use the Qwen-2.5-7B layer-20 AV/AR pair (Qwen Team 2025).

Grounding. For a claim $c$ in $z$ , let $z_{\neg c}$ be $z$ with $c$
alone minimally flipped. Then

| | $\Delta\tilde{r}(c)=\tilde{r}(z)-\tilde{r}(z_{\neg c}),$
| | (2)

and $c$ is grounded when $\Delta\tilde{r}(c)\geq\tau$ . Every edit is
validity-filtered; oversized edits inflate apparent grounding severalfold
(Appendix A). Each claim is grounded or not and true of the source or not; the
grounded-but-false cell, when specific to the co-trained pair under the
independent-evaluator swap (§3.2), is a co-adapted private code. The labels are
operational. With $\tilde{r}_{\mathrm{co}}$ and $\tilde{r}_{\mathrm{ind}}$ the
scores under the co-trained and an independent reconstructor, the evaluator gap
is $\tilde{r}_{\mathrm{co}}-\tilde{r}_{\mathrm{ind}}$ .

Terms. The tap is the layer and position read. A probe is a freshly fitted
linear decoder (Alain and Bengio 2017; Belinkov 2022). Gist is the input’s
overall meaning. Content is designated when an auxiliary predictor is
co-trained on it (§5), and decodable when a fresh linear probe reads it.
Faithfulness is claim-level throughout, true of the activation and grounded in
it; we do not use it for downstream computation, nor grounding for grounding in
the world.

#### Settings.

We evaluate in three settings. The first is a released
Qwen-2.5-7B layer-20 NLA on in-distribution web text ( $n{=}1{,}517$ audited
claims). The second is a sandbox of two synthetic scenarios, a story and a
marketplace, each built by filling the slots of a fixed template so that the
true content of every activation is exact and judge-free; the tap position
partitions slots into retained, faded, and unread. The third is continued
pretraining of Pythia-160M (Biderman et al. 2023) with self-supervised heads,
where tax is held-out language-modeling loss minus a shared control. Full
protocols, scenario grammars, seeds, and hyperparameters are in Appendices D
and K.

## 3 Auditing Reconstruction-Scored Explanations

On the released NLA the missing specifics are largely absent from the tap
under reconstruction-style readouts. In the sandbox the content is present,
and the verbalizer states it in wording interpretable only by its co-trained
reconstructor.

### 3.1 Counterfactual Audit of a Released Verbalizer

On in-distribution web text, the released NLA’s explanations reconstruct
at $\tilde{r}=0.84$ , yet the audit finds grounding in only about $2\%$ of
the specific claims an LLM finds salient ( $4.2\%$ / $2.1\%$ /
$1.6\%$ at $\tau=0.02$ / $0.05$ / $0.10$ ; full table in Appendix E).
This is a lower bound: a control that appends and re-ranks recovers a topic
known to be encoded at only $28\%$ raw. The relative gap is more robust: a
probe recovers specific facts about $3\times$ less accurately than gist
( ${\sim}6\%$ versus ${\sim}18\%$ chance-corrected at each position;
mean-pooled gist reaches ${\sim}50\%$ ; Appendix E).

Across the $n{=}1{,}517$ audited specific claims, reconstruction depends weakly
on most. Under transforms of $z$, reconstruction survives paraphrase and
collapses when content words are masked (Appendix E). The effect holds across
layers 16–27 and is specific to reconstruction-style readouts; the model’s own
output head sees late-layer specifics in next-token form (Appendix E).
Appendix E also reports bootstrap intervals and a noise floor from flips
carrying no grounding signal, below the smallest threshold.

We also trained the verbalizer toward grounding directly, with rejection
sampling and with GRPO against a clause-level grounding reward. Both raised
their proxy while the independent claim-level audit stayed null at every
$\tau$ (confidence intervals straddle zero). Text statistics attribute the gains
to sentence restructuring, merging and packaging the units the policy
controls.

### 3.2 Audit Under Synthetic Ground Truth

In every sandbox run the toy NLA asserts every slot confidently while passing
the test at $\tilde{r}$ 0.71–0.86 (both scenarios; representative example in
Appendix D). The fully decodable slot is stated truly at 0.44–0.96 across seeds
(grounded 0.76–0.88 in all), partially decodable slots at 0.15–0.26, and unread
slots no better than chance.

In 5/5 runs of standard training the co-trained pair develops co-adapted
private codes, with gaps between grounded and true rates of 0.30–0.80. Codes
can occupy several slots at once; in the marketplace scenario one code occupies
an unread slot, whose value is provably absent from the activation.

Under an independent evaluator, trained without exposure to the audited
pair’s outputs, grounding on code-carrying slots collapses from 0.53–0.89 to
0.08–0.23, while grounding of true claims survives. The cross-evaluator
$\tilde{r}$ gap is 0.17–0.38 on standard runs versus ${\sim}0.003$ on RECAP
runs (§5). An independent evaluator trained on a disjoint paraphrase family
(different frames and slot order, sharing only the slot words) reproduces the
same pattern within ${\sim}0.05$ across three seeds: code-slot grounding stays
collapsed while genuine grounding survives (RECAP slots at 1.00).

Standard-training verbalizers also under-read content that is present: in the
marketplace scenario, slots that are 55–72% decodable from the target model are
stated truly only 15–26% of the time, a readout gap in addition to the storage
gap. RECAP also closes it.

## 4 Representation Collapse and Probe Drift

The first failure mode is representation collapse. The natural target-side
objective pulls activations toward their own reconstruction. At every tested
strength, regardless of initialization, it removes decodable slot content while
perplexity is unchanged. Freshly retrained probes lose accuracy too, so the
loss is of information, not of a readable subspace. This is consistent with
prior analyses of collapse in non-contrastive self-supervised learning
(Chen and He 2021; Tian et al. 2021).

The second failure mode is representation drift during continued training.
Probes matched to a training model decay to near-chance within 1,500
continued training steps and are at chance across seeds (all six
pairs). An affine map fitted on paired activations (no labels) restores native
probe performance in all nine cases. Decomposing the map (mode sweep in
Appendix H), rotation alone recovers about half; full recovery needs a
non-orthogonal change of rank ${\sim}$ 16–64. Duan (2026) concurrently report
the same drift and realignment on 2B-parameter and 7B-parameter models.

Probe-based monitoring of a model still in training therefore requires a
recalibration procedure. Realignment corrects the readout; it does not alter
what the representation contains. Since representations differ by an affine
map, adapter-based cross-model probe transfer should work (Zhao et al. 2026).

## 5 The RECAP Objective

### 5.1 Method

RECAP (Readable Encodings via Co-trained Auxiliary Predictors) adds linear
auxiliary predictors (heads) during target-model training. Each head reads the
hidden state at the tap layer and predicts an external target: slot values in
the sandbox, self-supervised text functions at scale. With head parameters
$\phi$ and external targets $y$ ,

| | $\mathcal{J}_{\mathrm{model}}\;=\;\min_{\theta,\,\phi}\;\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{LM}}(\theta)\;+\;w\,\mathcal{L}_{\phi}\big(h(\theta),\,y\big),$
| | (3)

where $w$ weights the head loss against the language-modeling loss and
$\mathcal{L}_{\phi}$ at scale is a class-balanced binary cross-entropy on
content-word presence plus a cross-entropy on token identity (§5.3).

$\mathcal{J}_{\mathrm{read}}$ (Eq. 1) optimizes AV and AR against a frozen
model and never touches $\theta$ ; $\mathcal{J}_{\mathrm{model}}$ (Eq. 3) trains
$\theta$ , with targets taken from the input rather than from the model’s own
reconstruction, and heads that read the activation with no intervening text.

Every decodability number we report comes from independently fitted probes,
never from the heads. RECAP sits in the deep-supervision lineage
(Lee et al. 2015; Szegedy et al. 2015).

### 5.2 Sandbox Results

Designated content reaches 100% decodability by independently fitted probes, at
$+0.001$ nats, in all five runs. On unread slots, whose values never appear
before the tap, the heads decode nothing in any run. At scale the tax is
re-estimated as $+0.010$ nats and depends on target design (§5.3).

Fresh NLAs trained on RECAP target models state the designated content at
${\sim}1.00$ truth and grounding, under both the co-trained and the independent
evaluator, and the remaining false content sits at grounding ${\sim}0$ . No
codes appear in any RECAP run (emergence ledger in Appendix D). Both NLAs
receive identical training, including a cold-start SFT on gold descriptions;
only the target model producing the activations differs.

Figure 2: Decoding content from a real model’s hidden state (one held-out Pile (Gao et al. 2020)
passage; fresh probes read the layer-6 state at the marked position). On the
RECAP-trained model the probes recover the trailing-window content words and the
offset-8 token; on the control the readout is scrambled. Same probe recipe and
data; only the target model differs.

### 5.3 Scaling to Pythia-160M

We apply RECAP in continued pretraining of Pythia-160M (§2.1); Table 1 and
Figure 2 report the results. Fresh probes reach 0.95–1.00 AUC for $K{=}8$ and
$K{=}64$ designated content words, against a 0.77–0.80 control baseline. At
$K{=}512$ the naive presence head minimized its training loss while making
nothing decodable to a fresh probe (Appendix I); class-frequency balancing
restores 0.97–0.99 AUC across all 512 targets. Targets must therefore be ones
whose loss cannot be minimized without discrimination. The cost depends on
target design: $+0.010$ nats for 64 balanced targets, indistinguishable from
zero; $+0.14$ – $0.20$ nats for 512 targets into $d{=}768$ . A discriminative
identity target stays decodable at $w{=}0.03$ at a tax within noise of zero. The
never-designated probe bucket sat at control level in all eight supervised
runs.

Decodability is robust to head capacity and tap choice. An MLP head reaches the
same 0.98–0.99 designated-probe AUC at layer 6, and a linear head at layer 9
lifts AUC from the control’s 0.77–0.79 to 0.95–0.98 at $+0.01$ nats.
Appendix I indexes, with outcomes, the full weight sweep and the other factors
varied (pull strength, designation dose, realignment map class, evaluator,
scenario, head capacity, tap layer).

### 5.4 Verbalizer Audit at Scale

We train an AV/AR pair on Pythia-160M taps with the released NLA’s procedure
and audit it against exact ground truth from the text. It states context words
truly at 0.44 on the RECAP model versus 0.06 on the control. On the control,
stated words are grounded at 0.48 and true at only 0.06; RECAP narrows the
grounded-minus-true gap from $+0.42$ to $+0.33$ without eliminating it.

RECAP recovers more of the present content words, at recall 0.29 versus the
control’s 0.07, while stating fewer words per explanation. The result is robust
to reconstructor strength and stable across three target-model seeds, at truth
0.44–0.46 versus a near-zero control (Appendix J).

At the verbalizer’s own recall, a fresh probe on the same tap reaches precision
${\sim}0.80$ , versus the verbalizer’s 0.44–0.63 across reconstructors and
seeds (precision–recall figure in Appendix J). A redesigned reader
(standardized multi-token injection, MLP capacity, and a decode-point presence
head on whether each word occurred in the window, an external fact rather than
a learned monitor) makes the designated content linearly decodable at its
decode point (0.79–0.81, two seeds), while its generated precision stays
0.56–0.63. A matched control’s decode-point state reads at chance (0.03) under
the identical head. Neither reconstructor scale, reconstruction optimization, a
direct truth reward, injection bandwidth, nor explicit negative supervision
closes the gap (a 3B reconstructor matches the 0.5B). At scale RECAP’s guarantee
is decodability: the designated content is present and probe-verifiable, and
the reconstruction-family verbalizer conveys it into text only in part.

Without the heads, decodability erodes within a few hundred steps of
fine-tuning. Maintenance is either continuous ( $+0.010$ nats) or intermittent
at about a tenth of the compute (Appendix C).

## 6 Probe-Based Monitoring

In the sandbox, fresh probes, one per slot, read the tap activation while the
verbalizer states slot values. A claim contradicted by a confident probe
( $p{>}0.9$ ) is flagged, and exact ground truth scores the monitor (Appendix B).

On the standard target model every flag is a genuine false claim, but most
pre-tap claims fall in slots whose decodability is too low for a confident
readout, so the monitor catches 27 of 733. On the RECAP target model no false
pre-tap claims remain and abstention falls to zero. Verification coverage of
the designated pre-tap content moves from 37% to 100%; the gain is in coverage,
not precision, and is confined to designated content.

Post-tap claims are abstained on both target models; they fall to the
grounding–truth cross (§3), the two tools partitioning the audit (one scenario,
one seed, one threshold).

On Pythia-160M a fresh presence probe ranks true claims above false ones at AUC
$0.965$ versus $0.823$ for the control (disjoint $95\%$ intervals), flagging
false claims at $0.93$ recall and $0.87$ precision. At scale’s $1.5\%$ base
rate per-claim coverage does not transfer, so we report AUC and the flag’s
precision and recall.

#### Surviving a score-gaming adversary.

The adversary edits a true stated word in an honest explanation into an absent
one, choosing the edit that maximizes the recomputed score (Appendix F). At the
score-optimal edit the lie penalty is about 87% suppressed on both models. The
external-truth probe still flags the lies on the RECAP model at AUC $0.952$ ;
on the control it falls to AUC $0.508$ , despite also reading the activation,
which the text-editing adversary cannot touch.

Candidate selection costs little: the RECAP probe drifts from AUC $0.993$ to
$0.952$ as the chosen absent words grow semantically nearer. The threat model
covers edits to the explanation text, not activation-level attacks
(Bailey et al. 2024); within it, immunity is structural for score manipulation
and empirical for candidate selection. A probe-aware adversary assuming monitor
leakage (outside the threat model) degrades the RECAP monitor to AUC $0.909$ ,
while the control falls below chance to $0.242$ ; the separation grows with
adversary strength.

Recalibrating the flag threshold on a disjoint split leaves recall essentially
unchanged, and no control threshold reaches $0.9$ precision even against random
lies. On held-out words never designated (ranked 64–128), the RECAP monitor has
no advantage over the control (AUC $0.66$ versus $0.70$ ; band table in
Appendix F).

## 7 Related Work

#### Activation verbalization and its critiques.

Beyond the NLA recipe (§2) (Fraser-Taliente et al. 2026), a fast-growing family
improves the reader: supervised question-answering decoders
(Pan et al. 2026), general-purpose activation explainers
(Karvonen et al. 2025; Bauer et al. 2026), interpreter assistants
(Huang et al. 2025), training-free readouts (Ghandeharioun et al. 2024), and
cross-model adapters (Zhao et al. 2026). Sparse autoencoders are the
unsupervised reader family (Huben et al. 2024). Model-produced explanations pass
plausibility checks without faithfulness in chain-of-thought
(Turpin et al. 2023; Lanham et al. 2023). Causal tests of neuron explanations
found high error and little efficacy (Huang et al. 2023). Counterfactual
faithfulness tests prefigure our flip protocol (Atanasova et al. 2023).
Existing critiques of verbalization are benchmark-level; many tasks are
solvable without the target’s internals (Li et al. 2025). We audit the
reconstruction test itself, per claim and counterfactually, on a released NLA,
and our repair trains the target model rather than the reader.

#### Scalable oversight.

Reconstruction scoring sits within scalable oversight, which substitutes cheap
automatic signals for costly human judgment of model behavior and internals
(Amodei et al. 2016; Bowman and others 2022). AI control designs protocols
that stay safe even when the model tries to subvert them
(Greenblatt et al. 2024). We contribute a monitor whose signal comes from an
independent probe of the target model and which survives gaming of the
reconstruction score (Baker et al. 2025).

#### Steganography in learned channels.

Objectives in the reconstruction family have hidden information in their
channels since CycleGAN (Chu et al. 2017). In LLMs, encoded reasoning arises in
chain-of-thought under optimization pressure (Roger and Greenblatt 2023) and
generalizes under process supervision (Skaf and others 2025). Misspecified
incentives yield steganographic collusion (Mathew et al. 2025), tool use widens
the channel (Rippin et al. 2026), and probing internals detects collusion
(Rose et al. 2026). Optimization can obfuscate activations against latent
monitors (Bailey et al. 2024), and training against a chain-of-thought monitor
yields obfuscated reward hacking (Baker et al. 2025). These channels are
induced by incentives, process supervision, or an adversary; our codes emerge
from the standard reconstruction recipe alone, with no steganography objective
or communication reward. Complementary to not optimizing on the monitor,
supervising the target model against external ground truth makes its content
decodable without pressure on probe or reconstructor.

#### Representation drift, stitching, and monitor staleness.

Networks learn equivalent representations up to a transformation
(Lenc and Vedaldi 2015; Kornblith et al. 2019; Moschella et al. 2023); affine maps
transfer features across language models (Chen et al. 2025);
pretraining dynamics are stable across seeds (van der Wal et al. 2025); tuned
lenses are the affine readers whose staleness we characterize
(Belrose et al. 2023). Concurrently, Duan (2026) report the
same staleness and its label-free repair on 2B- and 7B-parameter models.
Retraining probes also restores detectability after probe-aware fine-tuning
(Wehner and Fritz 2025). We add the recovery anatomy (§4), the cross-seed
failure, exact evidence that information outlives its readers, and the
separation between drift and collapse.

#### Deep supervision and intrinsic interpretability.

Auxiliary heads on hidden layers are deep supervision
(Lee et al. 2015; Szegedy et al. 2015), with the task label as target; ours is
external content to keep decodable. Concept bottlenecks route all information
through named concepts (Koh et al. 2020; Sun et al. 2025), concept whitening
constrains the geometry (Chen et al. 2020), codebook features discretize the
representation (Tamkin et al. 2023), and gradient routing localizes computation
(Cloud et al. 2024); we add linear heads without constraining flow.
Explanation-side supervision can track behavioral change (Guo et al. 2026);
ours acts on the target model.

## 8 Discussion and Limitations

Implications for oversight. Reconstruction scoring is a scalable-oversight
signal. RECAP-trained designated content is checkable by an independent probe,
and that monitor survives an attacker editing the explanation, a requirement
against models capable of gaming the metrics used to judge them
(Baker et al. 2025). The guarantee covers only designated, decodable content;
RECAP is a component of oversight, not a solution to it.

Scope and limitations. Our evidence comes from a synthetic sandbox, one
released NLA (Qwen-2.5-7B), and continued pretraining of one small model
(Pythia-160M), mostly at single seeds; frontier scale is untested. First,
sandbox and scale audits cover only closed-vocabulary, template-parsed claims,
and the monitor covers only designated content; open-ended faithfulness is
unmeasured. Second, RECAP must be co-trained in and cannot be retrofitted onto
a frozen model, and a poorly chosen target can report success while decoding
nothing. Third, decodability is not verbalizability. Fourth, RECAP certifies
what an activation stores, not what the model uses: designated content can be
present and checkable yet behaviorally inert (patching the tap barely moves
behavior, ${\sim}0.003$ ), and a model could route computation around a
monitored subspace (Mahinpei et al. 2021; Margeloiu et al. 2021).

The target for reconstruction-tested verbalization is not a higher
$\tilde{r}$ but explanations whose specific claims are verified against the
target model, calibrated abstention where content is absent, and monitors with
recalibration protocols.

## 9 Conclusion

Models pass the reconstruction test behind natural-language activation
explanations via gist and via private codes, and training that targets the test
produces collapse or proxy gaming. RECAP, which trains the target model rather
than the reader, yields claim-level faithful verbalizers in the sandbox and
probe-decodable designated content on Pythia-160M, where a fresh verbalizer
states it truly against a near-zero control. Probe-based coverage of designated
content rises from 37% to 100% in the sandbox. At scale a probe ranks the
verbalizer’s true claims above its false ones, reading the content more
reliably than the verbalizer generates it. Training decodability into the
target model is more reliable than auditing a trained model after the fact.

## Appendix A Edit Validity for Minimal-Pair Flips

An edit is valid if it flips exactly one claim and changes nothing else.
We audited two edit generators on the released NLA: a closed-model judge
produced valid edits 68.4% of the time, while the open judge used throughout
the paper (Gemma-4-12B, pinned revision, temperature 0) produced valid
edits 99.3% of the time. Invalid edits were predominantly oversized,
rewriting surrounding material along with the target claim, and inflated
apparent grounding roughly sevenfold. All grounded fractions in the paper use

persist per-claim reconstruction deltas. The same head-to-head also measured
a judge-free mask-and-rescore signal against the flip instrument (agreement

## Appendix B Safety Experiment 1: The Discrepancy Detector

#### Question.

Disagreements between a probe readout of the activation and the verbalizer’s
statement are candidate lies. How useful is that detector, and what does its
usefulness depend on?

#### Protocol.

Sandbox, scenario 1, seed 1, 400 held-out taps per
target model.
For each slot type we fit a fresh multinomial logistic probe (linear,
256-dimensional input) on the probe split of taps, reading the slot value
from the tap activation. On evaluation taps, the verbalizer generates an
explanation; the first stated word of each slot type is compared with the
probe’s prediction.
A claim is flagged when a probe with confidence above 0.9 disagrees
with the stated word, and abstained when probe confidence is below
threshold. Exact tuple ground truth then scores every decision.

## Appendix F Adversarial Monitor: the Lie-Ladder

#### Question.

Can a report-space adversary editing the explanation to maximize $\tilde{r}$
slip a false claim past a deployment that trusts $\tilde{r}$ , and does an
activation-probe monitor survive it?

#### Protocol.

RECAP and control Pythia-160M ( $K{=}64$ balanced). On
held-out taps we take the honest verbalizer generation and, for each stated word,
edit it into an absent top-64 word (a true-to-absent lie). We recompute
$\tilde{r}$ on the edited text through the real reconstructor and score the lie with the
external-truth presence probe (trained on train taps, never on verbalizer
outputs). Adversary rungs: L1 a random absent word; L2 the embedding-nearest
absent word; L3 the per-claim $\arg\max$ - $\tilde{r}$ absent word over all
candidates; and, as a worst-case bound outside the threat model, L4 a
probe-aware adversary that assumes the private monitor leaks and, among absent
lies keeping $\tilde{r}$ within $0.05$ of honest, picks the one the probe most
mistakes for present. The $0.05$ budget is over twice the $0.022$ score cost of
the L3 lie. Decoupled design (positive $=$ any truly-present word; edit slot $=$
the verbalizer’s stated word): RECAP $n{=}758$ , control $n{=}200$ ; honest
$\tilde{r}$ $0.304$ / $0.275$ . Edit-based, no reinforcement learning.

| adversary rung | RECAP AUC / recall | control AUC / recall

| L1 random | 0.993 / 0.99 | 0.729 / 0.06

| L2 embedding-near | 0.971 / 0.93 | 0.635 / 0.06

| L3 $\tilde{r}$ -optimal | 0.952 / 0.86 | 0.508 / 0.01

| L4 probe-aware∗ | 0.909 / 0.70 | 0.242 / 0.00

Table 9: Lie-ladder: probe-monitor AUC and flag recall (at $0.9$ precision)
against report-space adversaries of increasing strength, RECAP vs control. At the
$\tilde{r}$ -optimal rung, on a stated true word the optimal lie lowers RECAP
$\Delta\tilde{r}$ by only $0.022$ , CI $[0.017,0.027]$ , versus $0.173$ for a
random lie. ∗L4 is a probe-aware selection adversary outside the report-space
threat model (it assumes the private monitor leaks), reported as a worst-case

#### Findings.

(i) At L3 the optimal lie suppresses $\sim$ 87% of the penalty a random lie
incurs (RECAP $\Delta\tilde{r}$ $0.022$ , CI $[0.017,0.027]$ ). (ii) The RECAP
probe stays at AUC 0.952; the control probe is at 0.508. (iii) Selection

$0.909$ (recall $0.70$ ) while the control falls to $0.242$ , the expected
signature of a white-box attack selecting absent words the weak control probe
over-scores. The RECAP–control separation is $0.27$ at L1 and $0.67$ at L4.

#### Caveats.

Report-space adversaries, with a probe-aware report-space selection adversary
as worst-case bound (L4). Activation-level attacks (probe-aware training of the
target, input perturbation) remain out of scope. $\tilde{r}$ is nearly, not
literally, claim-insensitive: the residual is an aggregate effect with no
practically usable per-instance signal.

no control threshold reaches $0.9$ precision even against random (L1) lies, so
control recall is undefined. (b) Held-out band: presence of words ranked

## Appendix G An API-Free Grounding Signal, and a Selection Null

A judge-free alternative to the flip instrument masks the claim’s words with a
neutral filler and rescores the explanation with the frozen reconstructor. In
the judge head-to-head of Appendix A, this mask-and-rescore signal agrees with
the flip instrument at AUC 0.997 under the validated open judge, requiring one
extra frozen-reader pass at inference. An earlier version also reported filter
precisions and a grounded base rate resting on pre-validation flip labels,
roughly a third of which the validity audit found contaminated by oversized
edits (Appendix A); we report only the agreement number and withdraw the rest.
Every number retained in the paper postdates the validity filter.

#### What inference-time selection does not buy.

Best-of- $N$ selection by an external truth judge ( $N{=}5$ , specificity
matched, independent judge for evaluation) moves the false-claim rate only
from 0.747 (random sample) to 0.688.

## Appendix H Reader Drift and Realignment

Readers matched to a training target model decay to near-chance within
1,500 continued-training steps (3/3 seeds) and read nothing across seeds
(6/6 pairs). An affine map fitted on ${\sim}$ 7,000 paired activations (no
labels) restores native reader performance in 9/9 cases. By expressiveness
class across the three reader pairs (two cross-seed, one stale): rank-1 and
rank-4 maps recover almost nothing, pure rotation (Procrustes) recovers about
half, and rank 16–64 of non-orthogonal change restores nearly all of it. Under
collapse, freshly retrained probes also fail.

## Appendix K Hyperparameters and Reproducibility Notes

#### Scale runs (Pythia-160M).

Continued pretraining on
pile-uncopyrighted, 500M tokens per run, identical data and order across
runs; batch $64\times 1024$ tokens, AdamW ( $10^{-4}$ , cosine to 10%, warmup
100, weight decay 0.01, gradient clip 1.0), bf16 autocast with fp32 weights.
Heads: linear on the layer-6 hidden state. Presence targets use BCE averaged
over $K$ ; the class-balanced variant weights positives by the empirical
inverse window base rate, clamped at 100, estimated from the first 2M
training tokens. Identity targets use cross-entropy over the top- $K$ content
vocabulary at offset $-8$ . Fresh probes: closed-form ridge per rank bucket at fixed
$\lambda{=}10^{4}$ , fit on the first 80% of held-out probe sequences and evaluated
on the last 20% (disjoint contiguous blocks; long documents may straddle the
boundary); identity probes are 64-class logistic. An earlier version selected
$\lambda$ per bucket from $\{10,10^{2},10^{3},10^{4}\}$ by evaluation-split AUC; a full
rerun with $\lambda$ fixed reproduces every reported bucket AUC to three decimals.
Optimizer hyperparameters (learning rate, warmup, weight decay, gradient clip)
were fixed to standard values and not swept; the method-specific
hyperparameters (aux weight, target count $K$ , designation dose, tap layer,
head capacity) are varied, with ranges and selection rule in the Ablation Index.
Held-out language-modeling loss is measured on 20M tokens. Significance is
assessed by 95% bootstrap confidence intervals and disjoint-interval
comparisons (with a Hanley–McNeil power analysis for the held-out-band null),
not fixed-level hypothesis tests. All experiments run on single NVIDIA
A100-80GB GPUs under Modal (Debian-slim, Python 3.12; PyTorch, Transformers,
Accelerate, and NumPy, with exact versions pinned in the released environment
file). Recent library defaults load fp16 checkpoints natively, and AdamW in
fp16 destroys all weights in a single step through epsilon underflow while loss
and gradients still read finite; all runs force fp32 parameters.

#### Sandbox runs.

Two synthetic scenarios (story; marketplace) over closed vocabularies; target
models are 8-layer, $d{=}256$ transformers trained from scratch; the toy NLA
uses a 0.5B-parameter AV/AR pair with a dimension adapter, norm-matched
activation injection, cold-start SFT on full-story descriptions, then
alternating reconstructor fitting and rejection-sampling rounds against
reconstruction reward (the released recipe’s structure). Audits parse stated
specifics by exact closed-vocabulary scan; grounding flips swap one stated word
for a same-type vocabulary word and measure the reconstruction drop. RECAP runs
use aux weight 0.3, 3,000 steps, batch 128, learning rate $3{\times}10^{-4}$ ,
and 30,000 probe taps. Seeds: three (scenario 1) plus two (scenario 2); each run
is controlled by a single integer seed passed to torch.manual_seed (with a
matched CUDA generator for sampling), fixing initialization, data order, and
stochastic training and evaluation; RECAP ceilings are evaluated by
independently fitted probes on tuple-disjoint splits in scenario 1 and held-out
splits in scenario 2.

# Train the Model, Not the Reader: Decodability Supervision for Verifiable
Activation Explanations

Hiskias Dingeto

###### Abstract

Natural-language autoencoders score explanations of hidden activations by
reconstruction: an explanation counts as faithful if the activation can be
regenerated from it. Flipping a single claim to a false alternative often
leaves the reconstruction unchanged. We show the test is passed without
faithfulness in two distinct ways. On a released Qwen-2.5-7B verbalizer,
explanations reconstruct well above chance while as few as ${\sim}2\%$ of their
specific claims are flip-grounded. Under exact synthetic ground truth, standard
training consistently yields co-adapted private codes. Interventions that leave
the target model fixed do not help. We contribute two audit protocols (the
grounding–truth cross and the independent-evaluator swap) and RECAP (Readable
Encodings via Co-trained Auxiliary Predictors), linear heads co-trained with the
target model on designated content. On RECAP-trained sandbox models, fresh
verbalizers state the designated content truly and codes vanish, at a
$+0.001$ -nat cost. The result replicates on a pretrained Pythia-160M under a
target-design rule we identify: the content becomes reliably probe-decodable,
while a fresh verbalizer conveys it only in part (truth 0.44–0.46 against a
near-zero control). For interpretability, the audit sets a claim-level standard
of evidence for activation explanations. For AI safety, RECAP makes designated
content checkable against probes rather than taken on trust from gameable
verbalizer prose. On the pretrained model, an independent probe scores the
verbalizer’s true claims above its false ones at AUC 0.96, versus 0.82 without
RECAP. An adversary editing an explanation to maximize the score while lying
suppresses about 87% of its lie penalty, yet the RECAP probe flags the lies at
AUC 0.95 while the control probe falls to chance at 0.51.
