## 1 Introduction

Natural-language autoencoders (NLAs) pair a verbalizer, which maps an
activation to a text explanation, with a reconstructor, which maps the
explanation back to an activation; round-trip quality serves as a per-explanation
faithfulness test (Fraser-Taliente et al. 2026). The signal is unsupervised and
label-free, which makes it attractive for oversight. Released
verbalizer/reconstructor pairs exist for several open models, and related
objectives train a growing family of activation readers
(Pan et al. 2026; Karvonen et al. 2025; Huang et al. 2025).

Reconstruction requires only that an explanation suffice to regenerate the
activation; it imposes no penalty on false additions. This is a property of the
objective, independent of model and scale.

In practice the test is passed in two ways, neither faithful at the claim level.
By gist: on a released Qwen-2.5-7B-based NLA, explanations reconstruct well above
chance, while the per-claim flip audit detects grounding in only ${\sim}2\%$ of
salient specific claims, a lower bound given the flip test’s low sensitivity. By
codes: in a synthetic sandbox with exact ground truth, co-trained
verbalizer/reconstructor pairs consistently develop private codes under standard
training across two scenarios (grounded-minus-true gaps 0.30–0.80). Two natural
training fixes fail: minimizing the distance between a hidden state and its
reconstruction removes probe-readable content, and rewarding the verbalizer for
grounding raises the score by changing which sentences the metric counts.

RECAP, linear heads on external targets co-trained with the target model
(Figure 1b, §5), survives our controls. Fresh NLAs on RECAP target models state
the designated content faithfully in the sandbox under both co-trained and
independent evaluators, with no codes. The reconstruction objective collapses
decodable content; frozen probes go stale under representation drift, which a
label-free realignment fully reverses.

Our contributions:

•

Claim-level audit. Per-claim flips of reconstruction-scored explanations, with per-edit validity controls, on a released verbalizer; the score survives paraphrase and collapses under content-word masking.

•

Private codes. Co-trained verbalizer/reconstructor pairs develop private codes in a sandbox with exact ground truth, detected and quantified by the grounding–truth cross and the independent-evaluator swap.

•

RECAP. A target-model objective that restores claim-level faithfulness in the sandbox and transfers to Pythia-160M, where designated content becomes probe-decodable at a measured cost.

•

Adversarial monitor. A report-space adversary gaming the deployed reconstruction score suppresses ${\sim}87\%$ of its lie penalty on both models; RECAP’s activation probe still flags the lies (AUC $0.95$ ) while the control probe collapses to chance ( $0.51$ ).

## 2 Preliminaries and Experimental Setup

### 2.1 The Reconstruction Test and Audit Protocols

An NLA pairs an activation verbalizer (AV), generating a text explanation $z$ of
a hidden activation $h$ , with an activation reconstructor (AR) mapping $z$ to
$\hat{h}$ . With target weights $\theta$ frozen and $h$ the tap activation, the
pair optimizes

| | $\mathcal{J}_{\mathrm{read}}\;=\;\max_{\mathrm{AV},\,\mathrm{AR}}\;\cos\!\big(\mathrm{AR}(\mathrm{AV}(h)),\,h\big),$
| | (1)

and reconstruction quality is the faithfulness test (Figure 1a).
Fraser-Taliente et al. (2026) present rising reconstruction as tracking
informativeness and caution that the objective does not force faithfulness; the
score nonetheless remains the reported number and the operative criterion. We
measure reconstruction by a floor-normalized centered cosine,
$\tilde{r}=(\cos(\hat{h},h)-\mathrm{floor})/(1-\mathrm{floor})$ , with
$\mathrm{floor}$ the mean cosine against mismatched activations. The released NLA
is the Qwen-2.5-7B layer-20 AV/AR pair (Qwen Team 2025).

Grounding. With $z_{\neg c}$ a minimal-pair flip of claim $c$ alone,

| | $\Delta\tilde{r}(c)=\tilde{r}(z)-\tilde{r}(z_{\neg c}),$
| | (2)

and $c$ is grounded when $\Delta\tilde{r}(c)\geq\tau$ . Edits are
validity-filtered; edits altering more than the target claim inflate apparent
grounding severalfold (Appendix A). We cross grounding with truth and attend to
grounded-and-false wording; where the independent-evaluator swap (§3.2) shows it
is specific to the co-trained pair, we call it a co-adapted private code. Labels
are operational; no intentional stance is implied. With
$\tilde{r}_{\mathrm{co}}$ and $\tilde{r}_{\mathrm{ind}}$ the scores under the
co-trained and an independent reconstructor, the evaluator gap is
$\tilde{r}_{\mathrm{co}}-\tilde{r}_{\mathrm{ind}}$ .

Terms. Activations are read at the tap by AR or by a freshly fitted linear
probe (Alain and Bengio 2017; Belinkov 2022). Content is designated when an
auxiliary predictor is co-trained on it (§5) and decodable when a fresh linear
probe reads it. Gist, faithfulness, and grounding are used in the claim-level
sense throughout, not in the sense of downstream computation or world grounding.

#### Settings.

Three settings: the released Qwen-2.5-7B layer-20 NLA on in-distribution web
text ( $n{=}1{,}517$ audited claims); a sandbox of two synthetic slot-filled
template scenarios (story, marketplace) with judge-free exact ground truth, where
tap position partitions slots into retained, faded, and unread; and continued
pretraining of Pythia-160M (Biderman et al. 2023) with self-supervised heads,
with tax the held-out language-modeling loss minus a shared control. Protocols,
grammars, seeds, and hyperparameters: Appendices D and K.

## 3 Auditing Reconstruction-Scored Explanations

On the released NLA the missing specifics are largely absent from the tap; in the
sandbox the content is present and stated in wording only the co-trained
reconstructor reads, which the independent-evaluator swap exposes.

### 3.1 Counterfactual Audit of a Released Verbalizer

On in-distribution web text the released NLA reconstructs at $\tilde{r}=0.84$ ,
while the audit finds grounding in about $2\%$ of LLM-salient specific claims
( $4.2\%$ / $2.1\%$ / $1.6\%$ at $\tau=0.02$ / $0.05$ / $0.10$ ; Appendix E).
These are lower bounds: an append-and-rerank control recovers a topic known to be
encoded at only $28\%$ raw. The relative gist–specifics gap is more robust: a probe
recovers specifics about $3\times$ less accurately than gist ( ${\sim}6\%$ versus
${\sim}18\%$ chance-corrected per position; mean-pooled gist ${\sim}50\%$ ;
Appendix E).

Across the $n{=}1{,}517$ audited specific claims, reconstruction depends weakly on
most. Reconstruction survives paraphrase and collapses under content-word masking
(Appendix E). The pattern holds across layers 16–27 and is specific to
reconstruction-style readouts; the model’s own output head does see late-layer
specifics in next-token form (Appendix E). Bootstrap intervals and the flip-noise
floor, which sits below the smallest threshold, are in Appendix E.

We also trained the verbalizer toward grounding directly, via rejection sampling
and via GRPO against a clause-level grounding reward. Both raised their proxy
while the independent claim-level audit stayed null at every $\tau$ (CIs straddle
zero); text statistics attribute the gains to merging and repackaging sentence
units, not to increased claim-level grounding.

### 3.2 Audit Under Synthetic Ground Truth

In every sandbox run the toy NLA asserts every slot confidently while passing at
$\tilde{r}$ 0.71–0.86 (both scenarios; example in Appendix D). The fully
decodable slot is stated truly at 0.44–0.96 across seeds (grounded 0.76–0.88 in
all), partially decodable slots at 0.15–0.26, and unread slots no better than
chance.

In 5/5 standard-training runs the co-trained pair develops co-adapted private
codes, with grounded-minus-true gaps of 0.30–0.80. Codes can occupy several slots
at once; in the marketplace scenario one occupies an unread slot, whose content is
neither true nor storable.

Under an independent evaluator trained without exposure to the audited pair’s
outputs, grounding on code-carrying slots collapses from 0.53–0.89 to 0.08–0.23,
while grounding of true claims survives. The cross-evaluator $\tilde{r}$ gap is
0.17–0.38 on standard runs versus ${\sim}0.003$ on RECAP runs (§5). An independent
evaluator trained on a disjoint paraphrase family (different frames and slot
order, sharing only slot words) reproduces the pattern within ${\sim}0.05$ across
three seeds: code-slot grounding stays collapsed and RECAP slots remain grounded at
1.00.

Standard-training verbalizers also under-read present content: in the marketplace
scenario, slots 55–72% decodable from the target model are stated truly only
15–26% of the time, a readout gap in addition to the storage gap. RECAP closes it
as well.

## 4 Representation Collapse and Probe Drift

Representation collapse. The target-side objective that pulls activations toward
their own reconstruction, aligning probe recovery with the model’s computation,
removes decodable slot content at every tested strength and initialization, with
perplexity unchanged. Freshly retrained probes lose accuracy as well, so the
information is removed rather than rotated out of a readable subspace; this is
consistent with collapse analyses in non-contrastive self-supervised learning
(Chen and He 2021; Tian et al. 2021). Since the reconstruction is a lossy
projection of the state, raising state–reconstruction similarity suppresses
variation outside the probe’s subspace.

Representation drift. Probes matched to a training model decay to near-chance
within 1,500 continued-training steps and are at chance across seeds (all six
pairs). An affine map fitted on paired activations without labels restores native
probe performance in all nine cases. Rotation alone recovers about half; full
recovery requires a non-orthogonal change of rank ${\sim}$ 16–64 (Appendix H).
Duan (2026) concurrently reports the same drift and realignment on 2B-parameter and
7B-parameter models.

Probe-based monitoring of a model still in training therefore needs an explicit
recalibration procedure. Realignment repairs the probe’s reading of the
representation, not its contents. Affine equivalence also implies adapter-based
cross-model probe transfer should work (Zhao et al. 2026).

### 5.1 Method

RECAP (Readable Encodings via Co-trained Auxiliary Predictors) adds linear heads
on the tap hidden state during target-model training, each predicting an external
target (slot values in the sandbox; self-supervised text functions at scale). With
head parameters $\phi$ and external targets $y$ ,

| | $\mathcal{J}_{\mathrm{model}}\;=\;\min_{\theta,\,\phi}\;\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{LM}}(\theta)\;+\;w\,\mathcal{L}_{\phi}\big(h(\theta),\,y\big),$
| | (3)

where $w$ weights the head loss and, at scale, $\mathcal{L}_{\phi}$ is a
class-balanced presence BCE over content words plus an identity cross-entropy;
balancing blocks the shortcut of §5.3. Unlike $\mathcal{J}_{\mathrm{read}}$ ,
which never touches $\theta$ , $\mathcal{J}_{\mathrm{model}}$ trains $\theta$
against ground truth the verbalizer and reconstructor will later need. The heads
co-train with the model, the targets are external, and the heads read the
activation directly.

All decodability numbers come from independently fitted probes, never from the
heads. RECAP sits in the deep-supervision lineage
(Lee et al. 2015; Szegedy et al. 2015).

### 5.2 Sandbox Results

Designated content reaches 100% decodability by independently fitted probes at
$+0.001$ nats in all five runs. On unread slots, whose values never precede the
tap, nothing decodes in any run. At scale (below) the tax re-estimates to
$+0.010$ nats and depends on target design.

Fresh NLAs trained on RECAP target models state the designated content at
${\sim}1.00$ truth and grounding under both the co-trained and the independent
evaluator, and the remaining false content shows grounding ${\sim}0$ . No RECAP run
shows codes (ledger in Appendix D). Both NLAs share identical training, including
cold-start SFT on gold descriptions; only the target model differs.

Figure 2: Decoding content from a real model’s hidden state (one held-out Pile (Gao et al. 2020)

### 5.3 Scaling to Pythia-160M

On continued pretraining of Pythia-160M (§2.1; Table 1, Figure 2), fresh probes
reach 0.95–1.00 AUC for $K{=}8$ and $K{=}64$ designated content words against a
0.77–0.80 control. At $K{=}512$ the naive presence head minimized its training
loss by predicting “absent” for the many rare targets while leaving nothing
decodable to a fresh probe (Appendix I); class-frequency balancing restores
0.97–0.99 AUC across all 512 targets. Targets should be ones whose loss cannot be
minimized without genuine discrimination. The tax for 64 balanced targets is
$+0.010$ nats, indistinguishable from zero; for 512 targets into $d{=}768$ it rises
to $+0.14$ – $0.20$ nats. A discriminative identity target stays decodable at
$w{=}0.03$ with tax within noise of zero. The never-designated probe bucket sat at
control level in all eight supervised runs.

A nonlinear (MLP) head reaches the same 0.98–0.99 designated-probe AUC at layer 6,
and a linear head at layer 9 lifts AUC from the control’s 0.77–0.79 to 0.95–0.98
at $+0.01$ nats. Appendix I indexes the weight sweep and the other varied factors
(pull strength, designation dose, realignment map class, evaluator, scenario, head
capacity, tap layer) with outcomes.

### 5.4 Verbalizer Audit at Scale

An AV/AR pair trained on these taps with the released NLA’s procedure and audited
against exact text ground truth states context words truly at 0.44 on the RECAP
model versus 0.06 on the control. On the control, stated words are grounded at
0.48 and true at 0.06; RECAP narrows the grounded-minus-true gap from $+0.42$ to
$+0.33$ without eliminating it.

RECAP recovers more present content words (recall 0.29 versus 0.07) while stating
fewer words per explanation. The result is robust to reconstructor strength and
stable across three target-model seeds (truth 0.44–0.46 versus a near-zero
control; Appendix J).

At the verbalizer’s own recall, a fresh probe on the same tap reaches precision
${\sim}0.80$ , against the verbalizer’s 0.44–0.63 across reconstructors and seeds
(Appendix J). A redesigned reconstructor (standardized multi-token injection, MLP
capacity, and a decode-point presence head trained on window occurrence, an
external fact rather than a learned monitor) makes designated content linearly
decodable at its decode point (0.79–0.81, two seeds), yet generated precision
stays 0.56–0.63; a matched control reads at chance (0.03) under the identical
head. Reconstructor scale (a 3B reconstructor matches the 0.5B), reconstruction
optimization, a direct truth reward, injection bandwidth, and explicit negative
supervision each leave the gap open. At scale, RECAP’s guarantee is probe
decodability; the free-form explanation is a lossy rendering, and our monitor
checks claims against internals.

Without the heads, decodability erodes within a few hundred fine-tuning steps.
Maintenance is continuous ( $+0.010$ nats) or intermittent at about a tenth the
compute; training it in from the start is preferable to later restoration
(Appendix C).

## 6 Probe-Based Monitoring

In the sandbox, fresh per-slot probes read the tap while the verbalizer states slot
values; claims contradicted by a confident probe ( $p{>}0.9$ ) are flagged, and
exact ground truth scores the monitor (Appendix B).

On the standard target model every flag is a genuine false claim, but most pre-tap
claims fall in slots too faded for a confident readout, and the monitor catches 27
of 733. On the RECAP target model no false pre-tap claims remain and abstention
falls to zero. Verification coverage of designated pre-tap content moves from 37%
to 100%, a gain in coverage rather than precision, confined to designated content.

Post-tap claims are correctly abstained on both target models; these fall to the
grounding–truth cross (§3), the two tools partitioning the audit (one scenario,
one seed, one threshold).

On Pythia-160M a fresh presence probe ranks true claims above false ones at AUC
$0.965$ versus $0.823$ for the control (disjoint $95\%$ intervals), flagging false
claims at $0.93$ recall and $0.87$ precision. At the $1.5\%$ scale base rate,
per-claim coverage is not the appropriate statistic; we report AUC and flag
precision and recall. The verbalizer proposes and the probe verifies.

#### Surviving a score-gaming adversary.

The adversary edits a true stated word in an honest explanation into an absent one,
choosing the edit maximizing the recomputed score (Appendix F). At the
score-optimal edit the lie penalty is suppressed by about 87% on both models. The
external ground-truth probe still flags the lies on the RECAP model at AUC $0.952$ ,
while on the control it falls to chance (AUC $0.508$ ), although the control probe
equally reads an activation the text-editing adversary cannot touch.

The RECAP probe drifts from AUC $0.993$ to $0.952$ as the chosen absent words grow
semantically nearer. The threat model covers explanation-text edits, not
activation-level attacks (Bailey et al. 2024); within it, immunity is structural
for score manipulation and empirical for candidate selection. A probe-aware
adversary assuming monitor leakage (outside the threat model) degrades the RECAP
monitor only to AUC $0.909$ , while the control falls below chance to $0.242$ ; the
separation grows with adversary strength. The deployed score must not serve as a
truth signal against such adversaries.

Recalibrating the flag threshold on a disjoint split leaves recall essentially
unchanged, and no control-probe threshold reaches $0.9$ precision even against
random lies. On held-out words never designated (ranked 64–128), the RECAP monitor
has no advantage over the control (AUC $0.66$ versus $0.70$ ; Appendix F).

## 7 Related Work

#### Activation verbalization and its critiques.

Beyond the NLA recipe (§2) (Fraser-Taliente et al. 2026), a fast-growing family
improves the reader: supervised question-answering decoders (Pan et al. 2026),
general-purpose activation explainers (Karvonen et al. 2025; Bauer et al. 2026),
interpreter assistants (Huang et al. 2025), training-free readouts
(Ghandeharioun et al. 2024), and cross-model adapters (Zhao et al. 2026). Sparse
autoencoders are the unsupervised reader family (Huben et al. 2024).
Model-produced explanations pass plausibility checks without faithfulness in
chain-of-thought (Turpin et al. 2023; Lanham et al. 2023). Causal tests of neuron
explanations found high error and little efficacy (Huang et al. 2023).
Counterfactual faithfulness tests prefigure our flip protocol
(Atanasova et al. 2023). Existing critiques of verbalization are benchmark-level:
many tasks are solvable without the target’s internals (Li et al. 2025). We audit
the reconstruction test itself, per claim and counterfactually, on a released NLA,
and our repair trains the target model rather than the reader.

#### Scalable oversight.

Reconstruction scoring is a scalable-oversight signal substituting cheap automatic
checks for costly human judgment of behavior and internals
(Amodei et al. 2016; Bowman and others 2022). AI control designs protocols that
remain safe when the model attempts subversion (Greenblatt et al. 2024). We
contribute a monitor whose signal is an independent probe of the target model and
which survives gaming of the reconstruction score (Baker et al. 2025).

#### Steganography in learned channels.

Reconstruction-family objectives have hidden information in their channels since
CycleGAN (Chu et al. 2017). In LLMs, encoded reasoning arises in chain-of-thought
under optimization pressure (Roger and Greenblatt 2023) and generalizes under
process supervision (Skaf and others 2025). Misspecified incentives yield
steganographic collusion (Mathew et al. 2025), tool use widens the channel
(Rippin et al. 2026), and probing internals detects collusion (Rose et al. 2026).
Optimization can obfuscate activations against latent monitors
(Bailey et al. 2024), and training against a chain-of-thought monitor yields
obfuscated reward hacking rather than honesty (Baker et al. 2025). These channels
are induced by incentives, process supervision, or an adversary; our codes emerge
from the standard reconstruction recipe alone, inside the interpretability
pipeline, with no steganography objective or communication reward. Complementary
to the prescription not to optimize on the monitor, supervising the target model
against external ground truth makes content decodable without pressure to fool the
probe or reconstructor.

#### Representation drift, stitching, and monitor staleness.

Networks learn equivalent representations up to a transformation
(Lenc and Vedaldi 2015; Kornblith et al. 2019; Moschella et al. 2023); affine maps
transfer features across language models (Chen et al. 2025); pretraining dynamics
are stable across seeds (van der Wal et al. 2025); tuned lenses are the affine
readers whose staleness we characterize (Belrose et al. 2023). Duan (2026)
concurrently report the same staleness and its label-free repair on 2B- and
7B-parameter models. Retraining probes also restores detectability after
probe-aware fine-tuning (Wehner and Fritz 2025). We add the recovery anatomy
(§4), the cross-seed failure, exact evidence that information outlives its
readers, and the drift–collapse separation.

#### Deep supervision and intrinsic interpretability.

Auxiliary heads on hidden layers are deep supervision
(Lee et al. 2015; Szegedy et al. 2015), there with the task label as target; ours
is external content kept decodable. Concept bottlenecks route all information flow
through named concepts (Koh et al. 2020; Sun et al. 2025), concept whitening
constrains geometry (Chen et al. 2020), codebook features discretize the
representation (Tamkin et al. 2023), and gradient routing localizes computation
(Cloud et al. 2024); we add linear heads without constraining flow.
Explanation-side supervision can track behavioral change (Guo et al. 2026); ours
acts on the target model.

## 8 Discussion and Limitations

Implications for oversight. Reconstruction scoring is a cheap automatic stand-in
for human checking of internals; it is passable without faithfulness and gameable
by an adversary. RECAP replaces trust in prose with checks against an independent
probe that survives an attacker editing the explanation, a property required
against models able to game the metrics used to judge them
(Baker et al. 2025). The guarantee covers only designated, decodable content;
RECAP is a component of oversight, not a solution to it.

Scope and limitations. Evidence comes from a synthetic sandbox, one released NLA
(Qwen-2.5-7B), and continued pretraining of one small model (Pythia-160M), mostly
at single seeds; frontier scale is untested. First, sandbox and scale audits cover
only closed-vocabulary template-parsed claims, and the monitor only designated
content; open-ended faithfulness is unmeasured. Second, RECAP must be co-trained
in, cannot be retrofitted onto a frozen model, and depends on target choice; a
poor target can report success while decoding nothing. Third, decodability is not
verbalizability: the free-form verbalizer conveys only part of probe-decodable
content. Fourth, RECAP certifies storage, not use: designated content can be
present and checkable yet behaviorally inert (patching the tap barely moves
behavior, ${\sim}0.003$ ), and a model could route computation around a monitored
subspace (Mahinpei et al. 2021; Margeloiu et al. 2021).

Success for reconstruction-tested verbalization is not a higher $\tilde{r}$ but
specific claims verified against the target model, calibrated abstention where
content is absent, and monitors with recalibration protocols.

## 9 Conclusion

The reconstruction test behind natural-language activation explanations is passed
via gist and via private codes, and training against it produces collapse or proxy
gaming. RECAP, which trains the target model rather than the reader, yields
claim-level faithful verbalizers in the sandbox and makes designated content
probe-decodable on Pythia-160M, where a fresh verbalizer states it truly against a
near-zero control. Probe-based coverage of designated content rises from 37% to
100% in the sandbox; at scale a probe ranks the verbalizer’s true claims above its
false ones, reading the content more reliably than the verbalizer generates it. A
model can game a learned test of its own explanations; decodability trained into
the target model is more reliable than post hoc auditing, and an explanation
checkable against internals is a firmer basis for trust than one taken on faith.

## Appendix A Edit Validity for Minimal-Pair Flips

An edit is valid if it flips exactly one claim and changes nothing else. We
audited two edit generators on the released NLA: a closed-model judge produced
valid edits 68.4% of the time, while the open judge used throughout the paper
(Gemma-4-12B, pinned revision, temperature 0) produced valid edits 99.3% of the
time. Invalid edits were predominantly oversized, rewriting surrounding material
along with the target claim, and the extra damage inflated apparent grounding
roughly sevenfold. All grounded fractions in the paper use the open judge with
per-edit validity filtering, and the audit artifacts persist per-claim
reconstruction deltas. The same head-to-head also measured a judge-free
mask-and-rescore signal against the flip instrument (agreement AUC 0.997 under the
validated judge), used in Appendix G.

## Appendix B Safety Experiment 1: The Discrepancy Detector

#### Question.

Disagreements between a probe reading of the target activation and the
verbalizer’s statement are candidate lies. How useful is that detector, and on
what does its usefulness depend?

#### Protocol.

Sandbox, scenario 1, seed 1, 400 held-out taps per target model. For each slot
type we fit a fresh multinomial logistic probe (linear, 256-dimensional input) on
the probe split of taps, reading the slot value from the tap activation. On
evaluation taps the verbalizer generates an explanation, and the first stated word
of each slot type is compared with the probe’s prediction. A claim is flagged when
a probe with confidence above 0.9 disagrees with the stated word, and abstained
when probe confidence is below threshold. Exact tuple ground truth scores every
decision.

## Appendix F Adversarial Monitor: the Lie-Ladder

#### Question.

Could a report-space adversary who edits the explanation to maximize $\tilde{r}$
slip a false claim past a deployment that trusted $\tilde{r}$ as a truth signal,
and does an activation-probe monitor survive that adversary?

#### Protocol.

RECAP and control Pythia-160M ( $K{=}64$ balanced). On held-out taps we take the
honest verbalizer generation and, for each stated word, edit it into an absent
top-64 word (a true-to-absent lie). We recompute $\tilde{r}$ on the edited text
through the real reconstructor and score the lie with the external-truth presence
probe (trained on train taps, never on verbalizer outputs). Rungs of increasing
strength: L1 a random absent word; L2 the embedding-nearest absent word; L3 the
per-claim $\arg\max$ - $\tilde{r}$ absent word over all candidates (the strongest
$\tilde{r}$ -gaming lie in the edit family); and, as a worst-case bound outside the
threat model, L4 a probe-aware adversary that assumes the private monitor leaks
and, among absent lies keeping $\tilde{r}$ within $0.05$ of honest, picks the one
the probe most mistakes for present. The $0.05$ budget is over twice the $0.022$
score cost of the strongest pure-score lie (L3), a deliberately generous bound
rather than a tuned tolerance. Decoupled design (positive $=$ any truly-present
word; edit slot $=$ the verbalizer’s stated word) keeps both arms well powered:
RECAP $n{=}758$ , control $n{=}200$ ; honest $\tilde{r}$ $0.304$ / $0.275$ .
Edit-based, no reinforcement learning.

| adversary rung | RECAP AUC / recall | control AUC / recall

| L1 random | 0.993 / 0.99 | 0.729 / 0.06

| L2 embedding-near | 0.971 / 0.93 | 0.635 / 0.06

| L3 $\tilde{r}$ -optimal | 0.952 / 0.86 | 0.508 / 0.01

| L4 probe-aware∗ | 0.909 / 0.70 | 0.242 / 0.00

Table 9: Lie-ladder: probe-monitor AUC and flag recall (at $0.9$ precision)
against report-space adversaries of increasing strength, RECAP vs control. At the
$\tilde{r}$ -optimal rung the lie penalty is nearly gone on both arms (on a stated
true word the optimal lie lowers RECAP $\Delta\tilde{r}$ by only $0.022$ , CI
$[0.017,0.027]$ , versus $0.173$ for a random lie); the RECAP probe holds while
the control probe falls to chance. ∗L4 is a probe-aware selection adversary
outside the report-space threat model (it assumes the private monitor leaks),
reported as a worst-case bound: it degrades the RECAP monitor only to AUC $0.909$
while inverting the control below chance to $0.242$ .

#### Findings.

(i) At L3 the optimal lie on a stated true word suppresses $\sim$ 87% of the
penalty a random lie incurs (RECAP $\Delta\tilde{r}$ $0.022$ , CI
$[0.017,0.027]$ ). (ii) The RECAP probe stays discriminative (AUC 0.952) while the
control probe is at chance (0.508). (iii) Selection leakage is small (RECAP AUC
$0.993\to 0.952$ down the rungs). (iv) The L4 adversary degrades RECAP only to AUC
$0.909$ (recall $0.70$ ) while the control falls below chance to $0.242$ , the
expected signature of a white-box attack selecting absent words this weak control
probe over-scores. The RECAP–control separation is $0.27$ at L1 and $0.67$ at L4.

#### Caveats.

Report-space adversaries, with a probe-aware report-space selection adversary
(L4) as a worst-case bound. Activation-level attacks (probe-aware training of the
target, input perturbation), which move the activation itself, remain out of scope.
$\tilde{r}$ is nearly, not literally, claim-insensitive: the residual is an
aggregate effect with no practically usable per-instance signal.

## Appendix G An API-Free Grounding Signal, and a Selection Null

The flip instrument needs a judge to write one minimal-pair edit per claim. A
judge-free alternative masks the claim’s words with a neutral filler and rescores
the explanation with the frozen reconstructor. In the head-to-head of Appendix A
this mask-and-rescore signal agrees with the flip instrument at AUC 0.997 under the
validated open judge, enabling per-claim grounding monitoring at inference with one
extra frozen-reader pass. An earlier version also reported filter precisions and a
grounded base rate resting on pre-validation flip labels, roughly a third of which
the validity audit later found contaminated by oversized edits (Appendix A); we
report only the agreement number and withdraw the rest. Every number retained in
the paper postdates the validity filter.

#### What inference-time selection does not buy.

Best-of- $N$ selection by an external truth judge ( $N{=}5$ , specificity matched,
independent judge for evaluation) moves the false-claim rate only from 0.747
(random sample) to 0.688.

## Appendix H Reader Drift and Realignment

Readers matched to a training target model decay to near-chance within 1,500
continued-training steps (3/3 seeds) and read nothing across seeds (6/6 pairs). An
affine map fitted on ${\sim}$ 7,000 paired activations (no labels) restores native
reader performance in 9/9 cases. Decomposing that map by expressiveness class
across three reader pairs (two cross-seed, one stale): rank-1 and rank-4 maps
recover almost nothing, pure rotation (Procrustes) recovers about half, and rank
16–64 of non-orthogonal change restores nearly all of it. Under collapse, freshly
retrained probes also fail, and no realignment exists.

label-free maps of increasing expressiveness, for two cross-seed pairs and

The scale result (§5.4) audits an AV/AR pair trained with the released recipe’s
structure on Pythia-160M taps. Reader: a 0.5B-parameter language model with LoRA
adapters (rank 16) and a linear dimension adapter from the 768-dimensional tap
state to the reader’s embedding width, activations injected norm-matched at marked
positions. Training: cold-start SFT on gold descriptions from a fixed template
stating the trailing-window content words and the token eight positions back, then
alternating reconstructor fitting and two rejection-sampling rounds against
reconstruction reward. Both conditions use the same procedure; only the target

0.208 (control) and 0.300 (RECAP). RECAP states words truly at 0.574 versus 0.152
and, on the shared 381 present words, recovers them at recall 0.470 versus 0.037;
the control states fewer words (92 versus 312) and trails on both precision and
recall. Offset-8 truth is again near zero (0.028/0.026), consistent with its 2.2%
storable-tap base rate. Across the three class-balanced RECAP target-model seeds,
stated-word truth is 0.444, 0.455, 0.443, against three control NLA seeds at
0.062, 0.060, 0.000.

#### Decodability exceeds verbalizability (readout redesign).

At the verbalizer’s own recall, the fitted probe reaches ${\sim}0.80$ precision
(designated-content AUC 0.99), while the verbalizer generates at 0.44–0.63; the
relevant comparison is the AUC-vs-precision mismatch, not a literal $0.99$ -vs-
$0.57$ gap. The rebuilt reader uses standardized (not per-sample norm-stripped)
injection, six injected tokens via an MLP adapter, MLP-LoRA, and a decode-point
presence head trained on exact window-occurrence labels (external truth, never a
learned monitor). Designated content becomes linearly readable from the reader’s
last-prompt hidden state at $0.79$ – $0.81$ (two seeds), yet generated precision
stays $0.56$ – $0.63$ ; a matched control reads $0.03$ at the same point under the
identical head. A per-word confidence sweep traces the verbalizer’s generative PR
curve entirely below the probe’s (Figure 5). Reader scale (0.5B vs. 3B), RAFT
reconstruction reward, a direct truth reward, injection bandwidth, and explicit
negative supervision each fail to raise generated precision, consistent with a cost
of serializing sparse superposed features by generation rather than missing
information.

## Appendix K Hyperparameters and Reproducibility Notes

#### Scale runs (Pythia-160M).

Continued pretraining on pile-uncopyrighted, 500M tokens per run, identical data
and order across runs; batch $64\times 1024$ tokens, AdamW ( $10^{-4}$ , cosine to
10%, warmup 100, weight decay 0.01, gradient clip 1.0), bf16 autocast with fp32
weights. Heads: linear on the layer-6 hidden state. Presence targets use BCE
averaged over $K$ ; the class-balanced variant weights positives by the empirical
inverse window base rate, clamped at 100, estimated from the first 2M training
tokens. Identity targets use cross-entropy over the top- $K$ content vocabulary at
offset $-8$ . Fresh probes: closed-form ridge per rank bucket at fixed
$\lambda{=}10^{4}$ , fit on the first 80% of held-out probe sequences and evaluated
on the last 20% (disjoint contiguous blocks; long documents may straddle the
boundary); identity probes are 64-class logistic. An earlier version selected
$\lambda$ per bucket from $\{10,10^{2},10^{3},10^{4}\}$ by evaluation-split AUC; a
full rerun with $\lambda$ fixed reproduces every reported bucket AUC to three
decimals. Optimizer hyperparameters (learning rate, warmup, weight decay, gradient
clip) were fixed to standard values and not swept; the method-specific
hyperparameters (aux weight, target count $K$ , designation dose, tap layer, head
capacity) are varied, with ranges and the selection rule in the Ablation Index.
Held-out language-modeling loss is measured on 20M tokens. Significance is assessed
by 95% bootstrap confidence intervals and disjoint-interval comparisons (with a
Hanley–McNeil power analysis for the held-out-band null), not by fixed-level
hypothesis tests. All experiments run on single NVIDIA A100-80GB GPUs under Modal
(Debian-slim, Python 3.12; PyTorch, Transformers, Accelerate, and NumPy, with exact
versions pinned in the released environment file). Recent library defaults load
fp16 checkpoints natively, and AdamW in fp16 destroys all weights in a single step
through epsilon underflow while loss and gradients still read finite; all runs force
fp32 parameters.

#### Sandbox runs.

Two synthetic scenarios (story; marketplace) over closed vocabularies; target
models are 8-layer, $d{=}256$ transformers trained from scratch; the toy NLA uses a
0.5B-parameter AV/AR pair with a dimension adapter, norm-matched activation
injection, cold-start SFT on full-story descriptions, then alternating
reconstructor fitting and rejection-sampling rounds against reconstruction reward
(the released recipe’s structure). Audits parse stated specifics by exact
closed-vocabulary scan; grounding flips swap one stated word for a same-type
vocabulary word and measure the reconstruction drop. RECAP runs use aux weight 0.3,
3,000 steps, batch 128, learning rate $3{\times}10^{-4}$ , and 30,000 probe taps.
Seeds: three (scenario 1) plus two (scenario 2); each run is controlled by a single
integer seed passed to torch.manual_seed (with a matched CUDA generator for
sampling), fixing initialization, data order, and stochastic training and
evaluation. RECAP ceilings are evaluated by independently fitted probes on
tuple-disjoint splits in scenario 1 and held-out splits in scenario 2.

ANSWER Q1: **Not settled**
The held-out band analysis (words ranked 64–128) is designed to test whether the monitor's performance is specific to designated content (64 top words) or a general effect. While the band leaves "headroom" for any spillover from designated content, the paper does not explicitly state whether the band's decodability was measured or whether it was provably absent. The analysis focuses on comparing RECAP vs. control, not on proving absence of representation in the band.

ANSWER Q2: **The claim that RECAP prevents co-adapted private codes would lose support**
If grounding of true designated claims dropped sharply under the independent evaluator, it would suggest that the verbalizer/reconstructor pair relied on a convention or private code shared with the independent evaluator. This would undermine the conclusion that RECAP's decodability is independent of such private codes.

---

ANSWER Q3: **The sandbox control monitor can achieve precision 1.0 because it operates on a closed-vocabulary, exact-ground-truth system, while the scale control probe lacks such guarantees**
In the sandbox, the control monitor adjudicates claims against exact ground truth and a closed vocabulary, allowing it to flag false claims with certainty. At scale, the control probe operates on natural text with approximate truth and open-ended claims, so no threshold reaches 0.9 precision even against random lies due to ambiguity and noise.

---

ANSWER Q4: **The interpretation that the erosion of decodability is specific to designated content would be undermined**
If both the never-designated bucket and the control model lost decodability, the erosion cannot be attributed solely to the RECAP heads. This would suggest the loss is a general effect of fine-tuning rather than a side effect of supervision on designated content.

---

ANSWER Q5: **No, the fresh co-trained NLA would still develop private codes**
Private codes arise from the interaction between the verbalizer and reconstructor, not from RECAP's designation of slots. Even if RECAP designated none of the slots, the verbalizer/reconstructor pair could still co-adapt to conventions or private codes during training.

---

ANSWER Q6: **The conclusion that the reconstruction score assigns a meaningful penalty to lies would lose support**
If the r̃-optimal lie lowered r̃ about as much as a random lie, it suggests the reconstruction score is not sensitive to the truthfulness of the explanation, undermining the idea that it serves as a reliable truth signal.

---

ANSWER Q7: **It should expect a higher aggregate reconstruction score but not necessarily higher grounded fractions of specific claims**
A stronger verbalizer/reconstructor pair may improve reconstruction quality overall, but the grounded fraction of specific claims depends on whether the new pair actually improves the sensitivity of reconstruction to individual claims rather than just improving overall reconstruction.

---

ANSWER Q8: **The interpretation that corpus shift caused the erosion of decodability would be undermined**
If head-free fine-tuning on fresh same-distribution data preserved decodability, but the shifted FineWeb fine-tune eroded it, the erosion is more likely due to the distributional shift rather than the removal of the heads.

---

ANSWER Q9: **Supported**
The paper explicitly tests RECAP's decodability gain at different tap layers (6 vs. 9). Since the layer-6 tap was the default and the layer-9 tap was explicitly tested and found to have a different trade-off, the gain is shown to depend on the choice of tap layer.

---

ANSWER Q10: **The pattern that RECAP's monitor is more robust to adversarial lies than the control's would be contradicted**
If the probe-aware L4 adversary drove the RECAP monitor below chance, it would mean the monitor's robustness advantage over the control is not reliable, undermining the conclusion that RECAP improves monitor performance.

---

ANSWER Q11: **It should expect to find more information available at layer 27, but not necessarily better alignment with the verbalizer’s claims**
The late-layer inventory in Appendix E shows that later layers (like 27) may contain more information, but this does not guarantee that the verbalizer will capture or explain that information effectively.

---

ANSWER Q12: **It should refit the probe on paired activations from the current checkpoint, and a non-orthogonal map of sufficient rank may be required**
To keep the probe working without new labels, the team should use label-free realignment via an affine map fitted on paired activations. If the representation has changed geometry, a non-orthogonal map may be necessary.

---

ANSWER Q13: **Not settled**
The paper does not explicitly state whether the 100% RECAP ceiling in scenario 2 proves generalization to unseen slot-value combinations. While the sandbox design allows for this, the paper does not provide direct evidence that these combinations were never seen during probe fitting.

---

The RECAP probe barely moves because its decodability is grounded in actual content representation, making it less susceptible to adversarial edits. The control probe falls because it relies on weaker, more fragile conventions that are more easily exploited by adversarial lies.

# Train the Model, Not the Reader: Decodability Supervision for Verifiable
Activation Explanations

Hiskias Dingeto

###### Abstract

Natural-language autoencoders score explanations of hidden activations by
reconstruction. On a released Qwen-2.5-7B verbalizer, explanations reconstruct
well above chance while as few as ${\sim}2\%$ of their specific claims are
grounded. Under exact synthetic ground truth, standard training consistently
yields co-adapted private codes. Reader-side fixes leave both unchanged. We
contribute two audit protocols, the grounding/truth cross and the
independent-evaluator swap, and RECAP (Readable Encodings via Co-trained
Auxiliary Predictors), linear heads co-trained with the target model on
designated content. On RECAP-trained sandbox models, fresh verbalizers state the
designated content truly and codes are absent, at $+0.001$ nats. The result
replicates on a pretrained Pythia-160M under a target-design rule. Content
becomes reliably probe-decodable, and a fresh verbalizer conveys it in part
(truth 0.44–0.46 against a near-zero control). On the pretrained model, an
independent probe ranks the verbalizer's true claims above its false ones at AUC
0.96, versus 0.82 without RECAP. A score-maximizing lying adversary suppresses
about 87% of its lie penalty. The RECAP probe still flags the lies at AUC 0.95,
while the control probe falls to 0.51.

StackOne Technologies

hiskias@stackone.com

## 1 Introduction

NLAs (Fraser-Taliente et al. 2026) attach a round-trip reconstruction score to
every explanation of a hidden state. The score needs no labels and no human
judge. Released verbalizer/reconstructor pairs exist for several open models,
and related reader objectives are proliferating (Pan et al. 2026; Karvonen et
al. 2025; Huang et al. 2025).

The test is passed in two ways, and neither is faithful.

- **Gist.** On a released Qwen-2.5-7B NLA, explanations reconstruct well above
  chance, yet a per-claim flip audit detects grounding in only ${\sim}2\%$ of
  salient specific claims. This figure is a lower bound given the audit's low
  sensitivity.
- **Codes.** In a synthetic sandbox with exact ground truth, co-trained pairs
  under standard training consistently develop private codes in two scenarios,
  with grounded-minus-true gaps of 0.30–0.80.

Two training fixes fail. Minimizing the distance between a hidden state and its
reconstruction removes probe-readable content. Rewarding the verbalizer for
grounding raises the score through which sentences the metric counts, while
claim-level grounding does not increase.

RECAP (Figure 1b) uses linear heads on external targets, co-trained with the
target model (§5). Fresh NLAs on RECAP models then state designated content
faithfully in the sandbox under both co-trained and independent evaluators, and
codes are absent. The self-reconstruction objective collapses decodable content.
Frozen probes go stale under drift, which a label-free realignment fully
reverses.

Figure 1: The two architectures. (a) A natural-language autoencoder (prior work)
(Fraser-Taliente et al. 2026): AV maps an activation to text, AR maps it back,
and reconstruction quality is the test; only AV and AR train. The score can stay
high while the text asserts an ungrounded specific (red “mirror”). (b) RECAP
(this work) trains the target model. Top: co-trained linear heads on external
targets. Bottom: after training, an independent fresh probe (not the heads)
recovers the content (AUC 0.95) and a fresh verbalizer states it truly.

Contributions:

•

Claim-level audit. A per-claim flip audit with per-edit validity controls on a
released verbalizer finds its specific claims largely ungrounded. Its score
survives paraphrase and collapses under content-word masking.

•

Private codes. In the sandbox, the grounding/truth cross and the
independent-evaluator swap detect and quantify private codes.

•

RECAP. Self-reconstruction collapses decodable content and frozen probes drift.
RECAP restores claim-level faithfulness in the sandbox, and on Pythia-160M it
yields probe-decodable designated content at a measured tax.

•

Adversarial monitor. A score-gaming text-editing adversary suppresses
${\sim}87\%$ of its lie penalty on both models. RECAP's activation probe still
flags the lies at AUC $0.95$, while the control probe is at $0.51$.

## 2 Preliminaries and Experimental Setup

### 2.1 The Reconstruction Test and Audit Protocols

The AV emits $z$ from tap activation $h$, and the AR returns $\hat{h}$. With
target weights $\theta$ frozen,

| | $\mathcal{J}_{\mathrm{read}}\;=\;\max_{\mathrm{AV},\,\mathrm{AR}}\;\cos\!\big(\mathrm{AR}(\mathrm{AV}(h)),\,h\big),$
| | (1)

and reconstruction quality serves as the faithfulness test (Figure 1a).
Fraser-Taliente et al. (2026) present rising reconstruction as tracking
informativeness, and they caution that nothing in the objective forces
faithfulness. This score is nonetheless what these NLAs report and what users
apply. We report
$\tilde{r}=(\cos(\hat{h},h)-\mathrm{floor})/(1-\mathrm{floor})$, using a
centered cosine with $\mathrm{floor}$ the mean cosine against mismatched
activations. The released pair is Qwen-2.5-7B layer 20 (Qwen Team 2025).

Grounding. With $z_{\neg c}$ the minimal-pair flip of claim $c$ alone,

| | $\Delta\tilde{r}(c)=\tilde{r}(z)-\tilde{r}(z_{\neg c}),$
| | (2)

and $c$ counts as grounded at $\Delta\tilde{r}(c)\geq\tau$. Edits are
validity-filtered. An edit that changes more than its target can inflate
apparent grounding severalfold (Appendix A). We cross grounded/ungrounded with
true/false and focus on grounded-and-false wording. Where such wording is
specific to the co-trained pair under the swap of §3.2, we call it a private
code. These labels are operational and carry no intentional stance. The
evaluator gap is $\tilde{r}_{\mathrm{co}}-\tilde{r}_{\mathrm{ind}}$, computed
under the co-trained and an independent reconstructor.

Probes are freshly fitted linear decoders (Alain and Bengio 2017; Belinkov
2022). Faithfulness is claim-level throughout. We do not use it for downstream
computation, and grounding is never meant as grounding in the world.

#### Settings.

We use three settings.

1. The released Qwen-2.5-7B layer-20 NLA on in-distribution web text
   ($n{=}1{,}517$ audited claims).
2. A sandbox of two templated scenarios, story and marketplace, with exact
   judge-free ground truth and retained, faded, and unread slots.
3. Continued pretraining of Pythia-160M (Biderman et al. 2023) with
   self-supervised heads, with tax measured against a shared control.

Protocols, grammars, seeds, and hyperparameters are given in Appendices D and K.

## 3 Auditing Reconstruction-Scored Explanations

On the released NLA, the missing specifics are largely absent from the tap. In
the sandbox the content is present, and the independent-evaluator swap exposes
the codes.

### 3.1 Counterfactual Audit of a Released Verbalizer

On in-distribution web text, the released NLA's explanations reconstruct at
$\tilde{r}=0.84$. Grounding appears in about $2\%$ of LLM-salient specific
claims: $4.2\%$ / $2.1\%$ / $1.6\%$ at $\tau=0.02$ / $0.05$ / $0.10$ (Appendix
E). These are lower bounds. An append-and-rerank control recovers a topic known
to be encoded at only $28\%$ raw.

The gist–specifics gap is the more robust statistic. Specific facts are probed
about $3\times$ less accurately than gist (${\sim}6\%$ versus ${\sim}18\%$
chance-corrected per position). Mean-pooled gist reaches ${\sim}50\%$ (Appendix
E). The score survives paraphrase and collapses under content-word masking. The
pattern holds across layers 16–27 and is specific to reconstruction-style
readouts. The model's own output head does see late-layer specifics in its
next-token predictions. Appendix E gives bootstrap intervals and a flip-noise
floor below the smallest $\tau$.

We tried two reader-side fixes, rejection sampling and GRPO, both against a
clause-level grounding reward. Each raised its proxy, while the independent
claim-level audit stayed null at every $\tau$, with CIs straddling zero. Text
statistics attribute the gains to sentence restructuring, that is, merging and
packaging of policy-controlled units.

### 3.2 Audit Under Synthetic Ground Truth

In every sandbox run the toy NLA asserts every slot and scores $\tilde{r}$
0.71–0.86 in both scenarios (example in Appendix D). Truth rates by slot are:

| slot | truth rate
|---|---
| fully decodable | 0.44–0.96 across seeds (grounded 0.76–0.88 in all)
| partially decodable | 0.15–0.26
| unread | at chance

Under standard training, 5/5 runs develop private codes, with grounded-minus-true
gaps of 0.30–0.80. Codes can occupy several slots at once. In the marketplace,
one code occupies an unread slot.

The independent evaluator is trained without exposure to the audited pair's
outputs. Under it, grounding on code-carrying slots collapses from 0.53–0.89 to
0.08–0.23, while grounding of true claims survives. The swap locates every claim
in the cross. The evaluator gap is 0.17–0.38 on standard runs versus
${\sim}0.003$ on RECAP runs (§5). An independent evaluator trained on a disjoint
paraphrase family (different frames and slot order, slot words shared)
reproduces the pattern within ${\sim}0.05$ across three seeds. Code grounding
stays collapsed while genuine grounding survives, with RECAP slots at 1.00.

Standard verbalizers also under-read content that is present. In the
marketplace, slots 55–72% decodable from the target are stated truly only
15–26% of the time. This readout gap sits alongside the storage gap, and the
intervention below closes both.

## 4 Representation Collapse and Probe Drift

Collapse. A target-side objective pulls activations toward their own
reconstruction. At every tested strength and initialization, it removes
decodable slot content with perplexity unchanged. Freshly retrained probes also
lose accuracy. This is consistent with collapse analyses in non-contrastive SSL
(Chen and He 2021; Tian et al. 2021).

Drift. Probes matched to a training model decay to near-chance within 1,500
continued steps and are at chance across seeds in all six pairs. An affine map
fitted on paired activations, without labels, restores native performance in
all nine cases. Rotation alone recovers about half; full recovery needs a
non-orthogonal change of rank ${\sim}$ 16–64 (Appendix H). Duan (2026)
concurrently reports the same drift and realignment at 2B and 7B parameters.

Probe-based monitoring of a model still in training therefore needs explicit
recalibration. Realignment corrects how a probe reads the representation. RECAP
changes what the representation contains. Affine equivalence also suggests
adapter-based cross-model probe transfer (Zhao et al. 2026).

### 5.1 Method

Linear heads read the tap and predict external targets $y$. In the sandbox $y$
is the slot values; at scale it is self-supervised text functions. With head
parameters $\phi$,

| | $\mathcal{J}_{\mathrm{model}}\;=\;\min_{\theta,\,\phi}\;\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{LM}}(\theta)\;+\;w\,\mathcal{L}_{\phi}\big(h(\theta),\,y\big),$
| | (3)

At scale, $\mathcal{L}_{\phi}$ is class-balanced presence BCE over content words
plus identity CE (cf. §5.3). Every reported decodability number comes from
independently fitted probes, never from the heads. The construction follows
deep supervision (Lee et al. 2015; Szegedy et al. 2015).

### 5.2 Sandbox Results

Designated content is 100% decodable by independent probes, at $+0.001$ nats,
in all five runs. On unread slots the heads decode nothing in any run. At scale
the tax is $+0.010$ nats and depends on target design (§5.3).

Fresh NLAs on RECAP targets state designated content at ${\sim}1.00$ truth and
grounding under both co-trained and independent evaluators. Remaining false
content sits at grounding ${\sim}0$, and no codes appear in any RECAP run
(Appendix D ledger). Both NLA conditions receive identical training, including a
cold-start SFT on gold descriptions; only the target model differs.

Figure 2: Decoding content from a real model’s hidden state (one held-out Pile

### 5.3 Scaling to Pythia-160M

Results are in Table 1 and Figure 2.

- **Decodability.** Fresh probes reach 0.95–1.00 AUC for $K{=}8$ and $K{=}64$
  designated content words, against a 0.77–0.80 control.
- **Naive $K{=}512$.** The naive presence head minimizes its loss by always
  predicting “absent” and makes nothing decodable to a fresh probe (Appendix I).
  Class-frequency balancing restores 0.97–0.99 AUC across all 512 targets.
  Targets should be ones whose loss cannot be minimized without genuine
  discrimination.
- **Tax.** For 64 targets the tax is $+0.010$ nats, indistinguishable from
  zero. For 512 targets into $d{=}768$ it is $+0.14$ – $0.20$ nats.
- **Other targets.** A discriminative identity target stays decodable at
  $w{=}0.03$ with tax within noise of zero. The never-designated bucket stays
  at control level in all eight supervised runs.

An MLP head gives the same 0.98–0.99 designated AUC at layer 6. A linear head at
layer 9 lifts AUC from 0.77–0.79 to 0.95–0.98 at $+0.01$ nats. Appendix I
indexes the full sweep: weight, pull strength, dose, realignment map class,
evaluator, scenario, head capacity, and tap layer.

### 5.4 Verbalizer Audit at Scale

We train an AV/AR pair on Pythia-160M taps using the released recipe and audit
it against exact text ground truth.

- **Truth.** Stated context words are true at 0.44 on RECAP versus 0.06 on the
  control.
- **Grounding.** Control words are grounded at 0.48 but true at 0.06. RECAP
  moves the gap from $+0.42$ to $+0.33$.
- **Recall.** RECAP reaches 0.29 versus 0.07 while stating fewer words per
  explanation.
- **Stability.** Results are stable across reconstructor strength and three
  target seeds (truth 0.44–0.46 versus a near-zero control; Appendix J).

At the verbalizer's own recall, a fresh probe on the same tap reaches precision
${\sim}0.80$. The verbalizer reaches 0.44–0.63 across reconstructors and seeds
(Appendix J). We redesigned the reconstructor with:

- standardized multi-token injection;
- MLP capacity;
- a decode-point presence head trained on window occurrence, an external fact
  and not a learned monitor.

This makes designated content linearly decodable at the decode point
(0.79–0.81, two seeds). Generated precision stays at 0.56–0.63, and a matched
control reads 0.03 under the identical head. None of the following closes the
gap: reconstructor scale (a 3B reader matches the 0.5B), reconstruction
optimization, a direct truth reward, injection bandwidth, or negative
supervision. The monitor below checks claims against internals rather than the
prose.

Without heads, decodability erodes within a few hundred steps of fine-tuning.
Continuous maintenance costs $+0.010$ nats; intermittent maintenance costs about
a tenth the compute (Appendix C).

## 6 Probe-Based Monitoring

In the sandbox, fresh per-slot probes read the tap while the verbalizer states
slot values. A claim contradicted by a probe at $p{>}0.9$ is flagged, and exact
ground truth scores the monitor (Appendix B).

- **Standard target.** Every flag is a genuine false claim, but only 27 of 733
  false pre-tap claims are caught, since most fall in low-decodability slots.
- **RECAP target.** No false pre-tap claims remain, and abstention is zero.
  Coverage of designated pre-tap content rises from 37% to 100%. This is a
  coverage gain, not a precision gain, and it is confined to designated content.
- **Post-tap claims.** These are abstained on both targets and are left to the
  grounding/truth cross of §3 (one scenario, one seed, one threshold).

On Pythia-160M, a fresh presence probe ranks true over false claims at AUC
$0.965$ versus $0.823$ for the control, with disjoint $95\%$ intervals. It flags
false claims at $0.93$ recall and $0.87$ precision. At the $1.5\%$ base rate we
report AUC and flag precision/recall in place of coverage. The verbalizer
proposes; the probe verifies.

#### Surviving a score-gaming adversary.

The adversary edits a true stated word into an absent one, choosing the edit
that maximizes the recomputed $\tilde{r}$ (Appendix F). At the $\tilde{r}$-optimal
edit, ${\sim}87\%$ of the lie penalty is suppressed on both models. The
external-truth probe flags these lies at AUC $0.952$ on RECAP and $0.508$ on the
control, which reads the same activation the adversary cannot touch.

Candidate selection moves RECAP AUC from $0.993$ to $0.952$ as the chosen absent
words grow semantically nearer. The threat model is text edits only, excluding
activation-level attacks (Bailey et al. 2024). Within it, immunity is structural
for score manipulation and empirical for candidate selection. A probe-aware
adversary that assumes monitor leakage lies outside the threat model. Against
it, RECAP holds at AUC $0.909$, while the control drops to $0.242$; the
separation grows with adversary strength.

The operating point is not tuned on the evaluation set:

- Recalibrating the flag threshold on a disjoint split leaves recall essentially
  unchanged.
- No control threshold reaches $0.9$ precision even against random lies.
- On never-designated words (ranked 64–128), RECAP has no advantage
  (AUC $0.66$ versus $0.70$; Appendix F).

## 7 Related Work

#### Activation verbalization and its critiques.

Beyond NLAs (Fraser-Taliente et al. 2026), reader-side work includes:

- supervised QA decoders (Pan et al. 2026);
- general activation explainers (Karvonen et al. 2025; Bauer et al. 2026);
- interpreter assistants (Huang et al. 2025);
- training-free readouts (Ghandeharioun et al. 2024);
- cross-model adapters (Zhao et al. 2026);
- SAEs (Huben et al. 2024).

Related critiques:

- Plausible-but-unfaithful chain-of-thought (Turpin et al. 2023; Lanham et al. 2023).
- Causal tests of neuron explanations (Huang et al. 2023).
- Counterfactual faithfulness tests (Atanasova et al. 2023).
- Benchmark-level verbalization critiques, which find many tasks solvable
  without the target's internals (Li et al. 2025).

We instead audit the reconstruction test per claim and counterfactually on a
released NLA, and our repair trains the target model.

#### Scalable oversight.

Reconstruction scoring is a cheap automatic oversight signal (Amodei et al.
2016; Bowman and others 2022), and AI control seeks robustness to subversion
(Greenblatt et al. 2024). We contribute a monitor driven by an independent probe
that survives score gaming (Baker et al. 2025).

#### Steganography in learned channels.

Prior hidden channels:

- reconstruction-family objectives since CycleGAN (Chu et al. 2017);
- encoded CoT reasoning (Roger and Greenblatt 2023), which generalizes under
  process supervision (Skaf and others 2025);
- steganographic collusion (Mathew et al. 2025), widened by tool use (Rippin et
  al. 2026) and detected by probes (Rose et al. 2026);
- activation obfuscation against latent monitors (Bailey et al. 2024);
- obfuscated reward hacking under CoT monitoring (Baker et al. 2025).

All of these arise from incentives, process supervision, or an adversary. Our
codes arise from the standard reconstruction recipe alone, with no
steganography objective or communication reward. We supervise the target model
against external ground truth rather than against a monitor.

#### Representation drift, stitching, and monitor staleness.

Background:

- representation equivalence up to transformation (Lenc and Vedaldi 2015;
  Kornblith et al. 2019; Moschella et al. 2023);
- affine feature transfer across LMs (Chen et al. 2025);
- cross-seed stability of pretraining dynamics (van der Wal et al. 2025);
- tuned lenses (Belrose et al. 2023).

Duan (2026) concurrently reports the same staleness and label-free repair at 2B
and 7B. Probe retraining restores detectability after probe-aware fine-tuning
(Wehner and Fritz 2025). We add the recovery anatomy (§4), the cross-seed
failure, exact evidence that information persists when readers fail, and the
separation of drift from collapse.

#### Deep supervision and intrinsic interpretability.

In deep supervision (Lee et al. 2015; Szegedy et al. 2015) the auxiliary target
is the task label; ours is external content. Intrinsic alternatives:

- concept bottlenecks (Koh et al. 2020; Sun et al. 2025);
- concept whitening (Chen et al. 2020);
- codebook features (Tamkin et al. 2023);
- gradient routing (Cloud et al. 2024).

We add linear heads without constraining information flow.
Explanation-side supervision can track behavioral change (Guo et al. 2026); ours
acts on the target.

## 8 Discussion and Limitations

Implications for oversight. Reconstruction scoring stands in for human checking
of internals. The scored models pass it without faithfulness, and an adversary
games it. RECAP-trained designated content is checkable by an independent probe
that survives explanation editing (cf. Baker et al. 2025). The guarantee covers
only designated, decodable content, so RECAP is a component of oversight, not a
complete solution.

Scope and limitations. Evidence comes from a sandbox, one released NLA
(Qwen-2.5-7B), and one small model (Pythia-160M), mostly at single seeds;
frontier scale is untested.

1. Audits cover closed-vocabulary template-parsed claims, and the monitor covers
   only designated content. Open-ended faithfulness is unmeasured.
2. RECAP must be co-trained in and cannot be retrofitted to a frozen model. A
   poorly chosen target can report success while decoding nothing.
3. Decodability is not verbalizability.
4. RECAP certifies storage, not use. Patching the tap barely moves behavior
   (${\sim}0.003$), and computation could route around a monitored subspace
   (Mahinpei et al. 2021; Margeloiu et al. 2021).

Success for reconstruction-tested verbalization is not a higher $\tilde{r}$.
It is per-claim verification against the target, calibrated abstention, and
monitors with recalibration protocols.

## 9 Conclusion

Reconstruction-scored explanations pass via gist and via private codes, and
training against the test yields collapse or proxy gaming. RECAP produces
claim-level faithful verbalizers in the sandbox. On Pythia-160M it produces
probe-decodable designated content, which a fresh verbalizer states truly
against a near-zero control. Sandbox auditor coverage of designated content
rises from 37% to 100%. At scale, a probe ranks true over false claims, reading
the content more reliably than the verbalizer generates it.

## Appendix F Adversarial Monitor: the Lie-Ladder

#### Question.

Can a report-space adversary maximizing $\tilde{r}$ slip a false claim past the
score, and does an activation-probe monitor survive it?

#### Protocol.

RECAP and control Pythia-160M ($K{=}64$ balanced). On held-out taps, each word
stated in an honest generation is edited into an absent top-64 word. We
recompute $\tilde{r}$ through the real reconstructor and score the lie with the
external-truth presence probe, trained on train taps and never on verbalizer
outputs. Rungs:

- **L1:** a random absent word.
- **L2:** the embedding-nearest absent word.
- **L3:** the per-claim $\arg\max$-$\tilde{r}$ absent word.
- **L4** (outside the threat model): a probe-aware choice. Among absent lies
  within $0.05$ of honest $\tilde{r}$, it picks the one the probe most mistakes
  for present. The $0.05$ budget exceeds twice L3's $0.022$ cost.

The design is decoupled: a positive is any truly-present word, and the edit slot
is the stated word. RECAP $n{=}758$, control $n{=}200$; honest $\tilde{r}$
$0.304$ / $0.275$. Edit-based, no RL.

## Appendix G An API-Free Grounding Signal, and a Selection Null

Mask-and-rescore replaces the claim's words with neutral filler and rescores
with the frozen reconstructor. It agrees with the flip instrument at AUC 0.997
under the validated judge (Appendix A), using one extra frozen pass and no
judge. An earlier version also reported filter precisions and a grounded base
rate based on pre-validation labels. Roughly a third of those labels were
contaminated by oversized edits, so we withdraw those quantities. All retained
numbers postdate the filter.

#### What inference-time selection does not buy.

Best-of-$N$ by an external truth judge ($N{=}5$, specificity-matched,
independent evaluation judge) moves the false-claim rate from 0.747 to 0.688.

## Appendix J Scale Verbalizer Audit Protocol

- **Reader.** 0.5B LM with LoRA (rank 16) and a linear adapter from the
  768-dimensional tap to embedding width. Activations are injected norm-matched
  at marked positions.
- **Training.** Cold-start SFT on templated gold descriptions (trailing-window
  content words and the token eight positions back), then alternating
  reconstructor fitting and two rejection-sampling rounds against
  reconstruction reward. Only the target model differs between conditions.
- **Audit.** 400 held-out taps per condition. A stated word is true iff it
  occurs in the trailing 64-token window. Flips swap in another top-64 word,
  scored under the co-trained reconstructor.

  RECAP versus 0.040–0.085 control. The parser emits up to three claims per
  explanation, but at most two shared a tap. Unclustered Wilson intervals are

## Appendix K Hyperparameters and Reproducibility Notes

#### Scale runs (Pythia-160M).

- **Data.** pile-uncopyrighted, 500M tokens per run, identical data and order.
- **Optimization.** Batch $64\times 1024$; AdamW ($10^{-4}$, cosine to 10%,
  warmup 100, weight decay 0.01, clip 1.0); bf16 autocast with fp32 weights.
  These were fixed, not swept. Method hyperparameters (aux weight, $K$, dose,
  tap layer, head capacity) are varied as listed in Appendix I.
- **Heads.** Linear on the layer-6 state. Presence uses BCE averaged over $K$;
  the balanced variant weights positives by inverse window base rate, clamped at
  100, estimated on the first 2M tokens. Identity uses CE over the top-$K$
  content vocabulary at offset $-8$.
- **Probes.** Closed-form ridge per rank bucket at $\lambda{=}10^{4}$, fit on
  the first 80% of held-out probe sequences and evaluated on the last 20%
  (contiguous blocks; long documents may straddle). Identity probes are
  64-class logistic. An earlier per-bucket selection of $\lambda$ from
  $\{10,10^{2},10^{3},10^{4}\}$ by eval AUC was rerun with fixed $\lambda$,
  reproducing every bucket AUC to three decimals.
- **Evaluation.** Held-out LM loss on 20M tokens. Significance via 95%
  bootstrap CIs and disjoint-interval comparisons, plus Hanley–McNeil power for
  the band null; no fixed-level tests.
- **Compute.** Single A100-80GB GPUs under Modal (Debian-slim, Python 3.12;
  PyTorch, Transformers, Accelerate, NumPy, pinned versions).
- **Precision caveat.** fp16 checkpoints load natively under recent defaults,
  and AdamW in fp16 destroys all weights in one step via epsilon underflow
  while loss and gradients read finite. All runs force fp32 parameters.

#### Sandbox runs.

- **Targets.** Two closed-vocabulary scenarios; 8-layer, $d{=}256$ targets
  trained from scratch.
- **NLA.** 0.5B AV/AR with a dimension adapter and norm-matched injection.
  Cold-start SFT on full-story descriptions, then alternating reconstructor
  fitting and rejection sampling against reconstruction reward.
- **Audits.** Exact closed-vocabulary scan; flips swap a same-type word.
- **RECAP.** Aux weight 0.3, 3,000 steps, batch 128, learning rate
  $3{\times}10^{-4}$, 30,000 probe taps.
- **Seeds.** Three (scenario 1) plus two (scenario 2), each a single integer
  passed to torch.manual_seed with a matched CUDA generator.
- **Ceilings.** Evaluated by independent probes on tuple-disjoint splits
  (scenario 1) and held-out splits (scenario 2).

ANSWER Q9: It should apply RECAP to the target model. Grounding rewards for the verbalizer raised proxy scores through sentence restructuring without improving claim-level grounding, whereas RECAP closed both the storage and readout gaps in the sandbox.

ANSWER Q10: Not settled. The measured point estimate was \(+0.010\) nats, with a paired 95% confidence interval of \([-0.015,+0.034]\), so the cost was statistically indistinguishable from zero but not proven to be exactly zero.

ANSWER Q11: It should choose 64 balanced targets at \(w=0.1\) under a tight language-modeling budget. This achieved 0.97–0.99 probe AUC at about \(+0.010\) nats, while 512 targets in a 768-dimensional model cost \(+0.14\) to \(+0.20\) nats for similar AUC.

ANSWER Q13: It should not expect a substantial increase in claim-level grounding merely from a stronger reader pair. Specifics at that tap were only about 6% chance-corrected decodable by reconstruction-style readouts, the AR did not exceed the ridge ceiling, and prior reader-side optimization raised proxies without improving the independent audit.

ANSWER Q14: L3 optimizes the reconstruction score, not the independent activation probe’s error, and text edits cannot alter the activation read by that probe. The modest AUC decline comes from selecting semantically nearer, harder absent words rather than directly defeating the monitor.

ANSWER Q15: Not settled. The paper’s own models extend only to Pythia-160M and the sandbox; the 2B- and 7B-parameter realignment result is attributed to concurrent work by Duan rather than demonstrated in these experiments.

ANSWER Q18: Their edits are controlled lexical substitutions over known vocabularies with exact ground truth: same-type slot swaps in the sandbox and top-64 word swaps at scale. The released NLA instead requires open-ended natural-language rewriting, where a judge may inadvertently change more than the targeted claim.

ANSWER Q19: No. Across the scale runs, the never-designated bucket stayed at control-level decodability, and the suppression of undesignated content seen in one sandbox ablation did not replicate at scale.

ANSWER Q20: The intermittent head loss periodically restores an explicit incentive to keep identity linearly decodable. With LM-only fine-tuning there is no such maintenance pressure, so the RECAP-specific representation erodes rapidly even though probes are freshly refitted.

ANSWER Q21: The layer-20 tap imposes a low reconstruction-style decodability ceiling for specific facts, so the verbalizer cannot reliably ground information that its readout cannot access. Moreover, RAFT and GRPO can optimize the grounding proxy through sentence packaging and restructuring rather than increasing independently audited claim-level grounding.

ANSWER Q1: Contradicted. In the \(K=64\) auxiliary-weight sweep, tax was non-monotonic: \(+0.064,+0.027,+0.052,-0.003\) nats for \(w=1.0,0.3,0.1,0.03\), respectively, and the paper explicitly notes this.
ANSWER Q2: Contradicted. A linear RECAP head at layer 9 also raised fresh-probe AUC from \(0.77\)–\(0.79\) to \(0.95\)–\(0.98\), so the gain is not specific to the layer-6 tap.
ANSWER Q3: L4 is a white-box, probe-aware attack that deliberately selects the absent word each probe is most likely to classify as present. Because the held-out band was never supervised and both probes are weak there, this adversarial selection can invert their rankings and produce sub-chance AUC.
ANSWER Q4: Not settled. The paper reports a flip-noise floor for the released Qwen NLA, but it does not report an equivalent noise-floor measurement for the Pythia-scale audit, so its \(\tau=0.02\) grounding counts are not shown to exceed scale-specific flip noise.
ANSWER Q5: No. A head can reduce its own loss through a degenerate strategy, as the naive \(K=512\) presence head did by predicting “absent,” without making the targets decodable; verification therefore requires independently fitted fresh probes.
ANSWER Q6: The conclusion that a score-maximizing adversary can suppress about \(87\%\) of the reconstruction-score penalty for lying would lose support. The separate finding that the RECAP probe detects L3 lies could still hold.
ANSWER Q7: The claim that training the target model with RECAP, rather than merely strengthening the reader, causes the verbalizer’s large truth advantage over a near-zero control would lose support. The independent-probe evidence for greater RECAP decodability would remain.
ANSWER Q8: L3 selects hard absent-word negatives that preserve reconstruction score and are increasingly semantically close, exploiting the control representation’s weak encoding of designated word presence. RECAP explicitly makes that presence decodable from the activation, which the text-only adversary cannot alter, so its independent probe loses only modest AUC.
ANSWER Q9: Supported. In the marketplace scenario the tap position varies with the template and filler, yet both standard-training runs developed private codes.
ANSWER Q10: Not settled. The paper shows label-free affine realignment across seeds and checkpoints of the same architecture, but only suggests adapter-based cross-model probe transfer; it does not demonstrate general transfer across distinct models or architectures.
ANSWER Q11: It would undermine the broader qualification that late-layer readout recovers only a small minority of the missed specifics and that simply moving to a later layer offers little recovery. It would not directly refute the layer-20 finding, because those values could still be absent or unreadable at that particular tap.
ANSWER Q12: It should periodically fit a label-free realignment map using paired activations from the early and current checkpoints, then map current activations into the probe’s original representation. A non-orthogonal affine change of roughly rank 16–64 was needed for near-full recovery; rotation alone recovered only about half.
ANSWER Q13: No. With the stronger pair, the control’s recall was \(0.037\), below the approximately \(0.07\) recall reported in the original scale audit.
ANSWER Q14: Those slots describe events after the tap, so their values are unavailable in the tapped activation. Because RECAP removes pair-specific codes, changing these unsupported claims does not materially affect reconstruction, leaving their grounding near zero.
ANSWER Q15: Not unless it had retained the original checkpoint’s activations for the same inputs. The method requires paired old and current activations to fit the label-free affine map; without the old checkpoint or stored old activations, that pairing cannot be constructed.
ANSWER Q16: The sandbox detector abstains aggressively and adjudicates only a tiny, easy subset: it caught 27 of 733 false pre-tap claims while abstaining on 63%, so perfect precision came with very low recall. At scale, false claims have only a \(1.5\%\) base rate and the control representation is weak, making \(0.9\) precision unattainable even against random lies.
ANSWER Q17: It would undermine the interpretation that designated decodability generally erodes merely because the auxiliary heads are removed and therefore requires continuous maintenance. Instead, the result would point to distribution shift, rather than head-free training itself, as the principal cause.
ANSWER Q18: It should expect very low coverage and extensive abstention, though the paper does not establish an exact Qwen coverage rate. Specifics at the layer-20 tap have only about \(6\%\) chance-corrected single-position decodability and only about \(2\%\) claim-level grounding, so few claims are likely to support a \(>0.9\)-confidence probe judgment.
ANSWER Q19: A gap of \(0.25\) lies in the standard-run range and suggests that reconstruction depends on pair-specific information, potentially private codes. The team must then perform the claim-level grounding/truth cross and verify that grounded false claims lose grounding under the independent evaluator while genuinely grounded true claims survive.
ANSWER Q20: It should expect only modest recovery. At layer 27 the logit lens placed missed true values in its top 50 only \(10.1\%\) of the time, while the matched ridge probe remained near \(6\%\), so most missed specifics would remain unrecovered.
ANSWER Q21: It would undermine the conclusions that RECAP’s true designated claims are genuinely grounded under independent evaluation and that fresh sandbox NLAs are faithful under both evaluators, as well as the near-zero evaluator-gap result. It would not by itself refute their literal truth or independent probe decodability, nor necessarily establish private codes under the paper’s grounded-and-false definition.
